body:
• Bunzl plc reported a good first half for the six months to 30 June 2026, upgraded its 2026 outlook and announced a new £500m buyback to run over the next 12 months.
  • Revenue rose 2.9% at constant exchange rates (4.1% CER reported in the narrative); underlying revenue up 3.2%, a fifth consecutive quarter of growth led by North America.
  • Operating margin expanded to 7.3% from 7.0%; adjusted operating profit up 8.0% CER, reported operating profit up 16.9%, and adjusted EPS up 11.4%.
  • Interim dividend per share increased 3.0%; adjusted net debt to EBITDA of 1.8x, below the 2.0-2.5x target range.
  • North America Distribution delivered 8% underlying revenue growth with restored service levels; two bolt-on acquisitions completed year-to-date (Scientifix in Australia, Ghessu Bath in Spain).
  • 2026 guidance upgraded: now expects operating margin broadly flat year-on-year (vs 7.6% in 2025) and modest adjusted operating profit growth at constant exchange rates.
headline: Bunzl posts a good H1 2026 with margins up, upgrades its 2026 outlook and launches a new £500m share buyback.
priority_reason: Half-year results with a 2026 guidance upgrade and a new £500m buyback.

figures.note: H1 to 30 June 2026; +4.1% CER cited in narrative

guidance.previous: Prior 2026 guidance not quoted in the announcement; group had guided to modest underlying revenue growth with a less favourable margin outlook.
guidance.current: Continues to expect modest underlying revenue growth; now expects group operating margin to be broadly flat year-on-year versus the 7.6% reported in 2025 (excluding an £8m share-based payment credit), and modest adjusted operating profit growth year-on-year at constant exchange rates. Net adjusted finance expense of £125-£130m; full-year effective tax rate around 26.0%.
guidance.commentary: Bunzl upgraded its 2026 outlook on the back of a robust first half, notably the stabilisation of North America Distribution and effective management of inflation. The margin outlook improved to broadly flat year-on-year, though management flags that much of the H1 margin gain is expected to be temporary.

explainer:
Bunzl reports at constant exchange rates (stripping out currency swings) and on an 'underlying' basis, which excludes acquisitions and disposals to show like-for-like growth. Underlying revenue rose 3.2%, driven by both higher volumes (led by North America) and inflation feeding through product costs, particularly plastic-related items. The operating margin rose to 7.3% from 7.0%, but the company stresses that much of this improvement comes from a temporary inflation benefit rather than a permanent structural gain.

The guidance upgrade centres on margins. Bunzl now expects the full-year 2026 operating margin to be broadly flat against the 7.6% recorded in 2025, and modest adjusted operating profit growth at constant currency — an improvement on its earlier, more cautious stance. Note the group excludes an £8m share-based payment credit (a reversal of prior-year charges) from these comparisons to keep the underlying picture clean.

Alongside the results, Bunzl launched a new £500m share buyback to be completed over the next 12 months. With leverage at 1.8x net debt to EBITDA — below its 2.0-2.5x target — the group says it has ample headroom to keep funding bolt-on acquisitions, which remain its priority, while returning excess cash to shareholders.

• Old Mutual Limited issued a voluntary operating update and trading statement for H1 2026 (six months ended 30 June 2026), with full interim results due 8 September 2026.
  • Life APE sales up 21% (up 12% excluding non-recurring Old Mutual Corporate risk sales); gross flows up 21%, aided by Wealth Management and the inclusion of 10X Investments.
  • Gross written premiums up 3%; net underwriting margin at Old Mutual Insure held at the upper end of its 5%-8% medium-term target range despite elevated catastrophe losses.
  • Adjusted headline earnings expected to decrease, driven by lower shareholder investment returns amid risk-off equity and bond conditions; results from operations grew on stronger Wealth Management and Old Mutual Investments revenue.
  • Per-share metrics benefited from the 2025 share repurchase programme (completed early May 2026), cutting the adjusted weighted average share count to 4,179m (from 4,352m).
  • Note: the announcement's EPS/HEPS guidance ranges and KPI tables did not carry through in the scraped text, so specific figures are not available here.
headline: Old Mutual reports strong new business growth in H1 2026 but lower adjusted headline earnings on weaker shareholder investment returns, ahead of interim results.
priority_reason: Pre-close voluntary operating update and trading statement flagging earnings ranges ahead of interim results on 8 September 2026.

guidance.current: Trading statement provides indicative ranges for headline EPS and basic EPS per JSE Listings Requirement 6.26; specific ranges were not captured in the scraped text.
guidance.commentary: Results from operations grew on stronger Wealth Management and Old Mutual Investments revenue and lower central costs, but adjusted headline earnings are expected to fall on weaker shareholder investment returns. Headline earnings and IFRS profits benefited from a strong Zimbabwe performance excluded from adjusted headline earnings.

explainer:
This is a pre-close trading statement: a South African-listed group is legally required (JSE rule 6.26) to flag likely earnings moves before publishing full results, here due on 8 September 2026. It signals direction and ranges rather than final audited figures, and the numbers are unaudited management estimates.

Operationally the half was strong — new business (Life APE sales) and client inflows both rose 21%, helped by the acquisition of 10X Investments and buoyant Wealth Management flows. Underwriting at Old Mutual Insure held up well despite heavy catastrophe claims. 'Results from operations', the group's preferred measure of underlying trading, grew.

However, adjusted headline earnings — the group's headline profit metric — are set to fall, because returns on the shareholder investment portfolio dropped as equity and bond markets sold off on Middle East geopolitical tensions. This is an investment-market effect rather than a deterioration in the core business.

Per-share figures are flattered by the 2025 buyback, which cut the share count by about 4%, so per-share growth will look better than absolute profit growth. Note too that headline earnings and IFRS profit include a strong Zimbabwe contribution that is stripped out of the adjusted headline figure, so the different profit lines can move in different directions.

• Old Mutual Limited issues a voluntary operating update and JSE trading statement for the six months ended 30 June 2026, ahead of interim results on 8 September 2026.
  • Adjusted headline earnings — the Group's primary profit metric — expected down 35% to 25% at R2,733m-R3,153m (prior R4,204m), with adjusted HEPS down 32% to 22% at 65.7-75.3 cents, driven by lower shareholder investment returns amid risk-off markets.
  • Results from operations expected up 2% to 12% at R5,039m-R5,533m (prior R4,940m), aided by stronger Wealth Management and Old Mutual Investments revenue and lower central costs.
  • Headline earnings guided -11% to -1% (R3,704m-R4,120m) and IFRS profit -10% to 0%, both supported by a strong performance in Zimbabwe not included in adjusted headline earnings.
  • Operating metrics strong: Life APE sales +21% (R7,857m), gross flows +21% (R128,911m), value of new business +32% (R569m); Old Mutual Insure net underwriting margin fell 210bps to 7.6% on catastrophe losses but stayed within the 5%-8% target.
  • Weighted average share count reduced to 4,179m (from 4,352m) following completion of the 2025 share repurchase programme in early May 2026.
headline: Old Mutual guides H1 adjusted headline EPS down 32%-22% on weaker shareholder investment returns, despite 21% higher life sales and robust operating earnings.
priority_reason: Voluntary operating update and JSE trading statement flagging a sharp fall in adjusted headline earnings ahead of interim results on 8 September.

figures.metric: Old Mutual Insure net underwriting margin

guidance.previous: Not applicable — this is a JSE Listings Requirements trading statement giving earnings ranges ahead of results.
guidance.current: Results from operations up 2% to 12% (R5,039m-R5,533m); adjusted headline earnings down 35% to 25% (R2,733m-R3,153m); adjusted HEPS down 32% to 22% (65.7-75.3 cents); headline earnings -11% to -1%; IFRS profit -10% to 0%.
guidance.commentary: The trading statement flags a sharp decline in the Group's primary profit metric, adjusted headline earnings, driven by lower shareholder investment returns as the portfolio tracked weaker equity and bond indices amid geopolitical risk-off conditions. Underlying operating performance, however, remained robust with results from operations rising.

explainer:
This is a JSE-mandated trading statement, which South African listing rules require once a company knows its earnings will differ materially (typically 20%+) from the prior period. Old Mutual has given ranges rather than final numbers because the actual interim results are still being finalised for release on 8 September 2026. The figures are unaudited and include non-IFRS measures.

The headline weakness is in adjusted headline earnings — the Group's preferred profit measure — expected down 22%-32% per share. This is not an operating problem: results from operations, which strip out investment market noise, are actually up 2%-12%. The gap is explained by shareholder investment returns, where Old Mutual's own capital portfolio followed sharply lower equity and bond markets driven by Middle East geopolitical conflict, versus a strong prior-period comparative.

Note the divergence between measures: headline earnings and IFRS profit fall far less (or are broadly flat) because they include a strong Zimbabwe contribution that is excluded from adjusted headline earnings. Per-share metrics also benefit from the completed 2025 buyback, which cut the weighted average share count from 4,352m to 4,179m, flattering the per-share numbers relative to the absolute earnings changes.

Operationally the update is strong: life sales (APE) and gross flows both up 21%, value of new business up 32%, and net client outflows sharply reduced. The one soft spot is Old Mutual Insure, where catastrophe losses pushed the net underwriting margin down 210bps to 7.6%, though this remains at the top of its 5%-8% target range.

body:
• Goodwin PLC reports record FY26 (year ended 30 April 2026) trading profit of £77.5m (2025: £35.5m), up 118%, on revenue of £280m, up 27%.
  • Ordinary dividend raised 18% to 330p (2025: 280p).
  • Board committed to a potential disposal of a substantial part of the Mechanical Engineering Division, with Rothschild & Co appointed adviser (announced post period-end 7 August 2026); assets for sale include Goodwin Steel Castings, Goodwin International, Noreva GmbH, Easat Group and Pumps; targeted completion within twelve months.
  • Board expects a substantial part of any disposal proceeds to be paid to shareholders, and is reviewing capital allocation and dividend policy.
  • Mechanical Engineering growth driven by high-integrity castings for UK and US Navy frigate and submarine programmes; Easat profits rose from breakeven to £4.5m; Refractory Division subsidiary trading profits up 15%.
  • New Technological Division (Duvelco and Internet Central) created; Duvelco production finalisation running behind schedule but progressing, with a partner agreement to manufacture stock shapes.
headline: Goodwin reports record FY26 trading profit of £77.5m, up 118%, on revenue of £280m, and lifts the dividend 18% to 330p while pursuing a Mechanical Engineering disposal.
priority_reason: Record full-year results with a 118% jump in trading profit, plus an active sale process for a substantial part of the Mechanical Engineering Division.

guidance.commentary: No formal earnings guidance issued; the Board flags that capital allocation and dividend policy will be reviewed and that a substantial part of any Mechanical Engineering disposal proceeds is expected to be returned to shareholders.

explainer:
These are preliminary (unaudited) full-year results for the twelve months to 30 April 2026. The headline figure is trading profit — operating profit before certain items — which more than doubled to £77.5m, well ahead of the prior year's £35.5m, on revenue up 27% to £280m. Goodwin attributes the step-change largely to its Mechanical Engineering division, which supplies precision-machined, high-integrity castings for UK and US naval submarine and frigate programmes; defence milestone payments also improved cash generation. The proposed dividend rises 18% to 330p.

The most market-relevant development is corporate rather than purely financial: the Board has committed to selling a substantial part of the Mechanical Engineering Division — the very division driving the profit surge — and has appointed Rothschild & Co to run a sale process, targeting completion within twelve months. The businesses earmarked for sale (Goodwin Steel Castings, Goodwin International, Noreva, Easat and Pumps) are now classed as assets held for sale.

Because the group's composition will change materially if the disposal completes, management has restated its internal reporting and carved out a new Technological Division (Duvelco and Internet Central), which is being retained. The Board indicates dividend policy and capital allocation are under review and that much of any sale proceeds would be returned to shareholders — so investors should treat the current dividend trajectory and divisional earnings mix as subject to change pending the outcome of the sale.

Note several figures (revenue prior-year comparative, Easat's change, precise divisional profits) are not fully quantified in this preliminary statement, with the full financial statements to follow shortly.

• Blanket Mine underground M&I resources up 22% to 2.178 million ounces of gold (17.7Mt at 3.83 g/t), from 1.789Moz at 31 December 2023 — driven by a 16% rise in tonnes and 5% higher grade.
  • Inferred underground resources down 30% to 0.748Moz (from 1.061Moz), largely reflecting conversion into higher-confidence M&I categories rather than depletion.
  • Maiden surface mineral resource declared for oxide, transitional and sulphide material; oxide heap-leach test work shows recoveries of up to 67%, with oxide mining potentially starting first half of 2027 at a target 40,000 tonnes/month.
  • CEO Mark Learmonth: $3.733m invested in deep drilling over 6 years added 1.279Moz M&I (before depletion) at a discovery cost of $2.92 per ounce; a study to deepen operations below 1,100m is due late 2026.
  • NI 43-101 technical report, including a restated Life of Mine Plan and new reserve estimate, to be filed on SEDAR+ within 45 days.
  • Resource comparison tables referenced in the announcement are not reproduced in the scraped text; Blanket is 64%-owned by Caledonia.
headline: Caledonia reports a **22% increase** in Blanket Mine underground measured and indicated resources to **2.178 million ounces** of gold, plus a maiden surface resource.
priority_reason: Material resource upgrade and maiden surface resource at the company's principal mine, with potential to extend mine-life and add near-term production.

figures.note: 17.7Mt at 3.83 g/t; effective date 30 June 2026 vs 31 December 2023
oxide, transitional and sulphide; no comparison as first estimate

explainer:
Mineral resource estimates classify how confident a miner is that gold is actually in the ground. "Measured and indicated" (M&I) resources carry enough geological evidence to support mine planning, while "inferred" resources are lower confidence. Caledonia's underground M&I ounces at Blanket rose 22% to 2.178 million ounces, and much of the 30% fall in inferred ounces reflects that material being upgraded into the more reliable M&I categories through further drilling — not gold being mined away. The figures are reported under Canada's NI 43-101 standard on a 100% project basis, though Caledonia owns 64% of Blanket.

Separately, the company declared a maiden (first-ever) surface resource. This covers near-surface oxide material that could be processed cheaply by heap leaching (test recoveries up to 67%), potentially adding incremental gold production from the first half of 2027, plus transitional and an unexpected shallow sulphide zone requiring further work.

This is an exploration and resource update rather than an earnings statement, so it does not change financial guidance. However, it raises the prospect of a longer mine-life and additional low-cost ounces. A full NI 43-101 technical report, with a restated Life of Mine Plan and a new reserve estimate, is due within 45 days and will convert some of these resources into economically mineable reserves.

explainer:
These are Greatland's first full-year results covering 12 months of owning the Telfer gold-copper operation in Western Australia, which it acquired in December 2024. Because the prior year (FY25) only captured roughly seven months of ownership, the announcement does not print like-for-like prior-year comparatives, so year-on-year percentage moves are not directly available — the figures reflect a maiden full-year benefiting from strong gold prices (an average $6,223/oz realised).

The company generated $862m of net profit and $737m of free cash flow, leaving it with net cash of about $1.3bn. That balance sheet strength underpins a heavy reinvestment programme rather than large returns to shareholders: FY27 is explicitly an investment year.

On guidance, FY27 gold production of 260-300koz is lower than the ~329koz produced in FY26, and unit costs (AISC) step up materially to $2,900-$3,330/oz from $2,179/oz. Management attributes this to open-pit mine scheduling, a planned 15-day process plant shutdown in Q1, and second-half weighting — not a deterioration in the asset. Alongside, Greatland has taken a final investment decision on the Havieron project (first gold expected FY29), funded partly by $500m of new bank debt, marking the start of a multi-year growth phase in the Paterson region.

Note figures are reported in dollars as printed in the announcement; Havieron study economics are quoted separately in Australian dollars (e.g. A$4,500/oz long-term gold base case).

• S&U plc trading update for Q2 2026/27 (1 May–5 August): group capital receivables at a record £616m vs £512m last year, a 20% increase.
  • Motor finance arm Advantage: year-to-date deal numbers up 50%, advances of £105m for the half-year despite a 3% fall in the UK car finance market; capital receivables now £408m.
  • Advantage debt quality: up-to-date receivables at 73% of the book vs 69% last year; collections against due 92% vs 90%, with bad debt/write-offs down nearly a fifth.
  • Property lender Aspen: capital receivables £208m, almost a third higher, but slower growth and longer loan terms weigh on near-term profitability; late/beyond-term customers steady at 7% of the book.
  • Group borrowings £285m against £330m of facilities; a major refinancing and securitisation project is to be unveiled at the 29 September half-year results.
  • Chairman Anthony Coombs cautiously optimistic; notes FCA broker commission redress scheme is under judicial review, with minimal expected financial impact on Advantage.
headline: S&U reports record group capital receivables of £616m, up 20% year on year, with half-year results and a securitisation refinancing due 29 September.
priority_reason: Quarterly trading update from a listed lender with record receivables and a pending refinancing/securitisation announcement.

guidance.commentary: No numeric guidance figures given; management notes Advantage's growth will be more significantly reflected in profitability in H2 and 2027/28, and flags a refinancing/securitisation to be unveiled on 29 September.

explainer:
S&U is a specialist lender with two arms: Advantage (motor finance) and Aspen (property/bridging finance). "Capital receivables" is the value of loans outstanding to customers — the closest thing to a top-line for a lender — so the record £616m group figure, up 20%, signals continued balance-sheet growth rather than a profit number. The company has not reported profit or EPS in this update; those come with the half-year results on 29 September.

The quality metrics matter as much as growth for a lender. Advantage's up-to-date receivables rising to 73% (from 69%) and collections at 92% of amounts due (from 90%) indicate the loan book is performing slightly better than a year ago, with bad debt and write-offs down nearly a fifth. Aspen is the softer spot: receivables are up sharply but slower repayments and a shift to longer loan terms delay income, and the prior-year comparison is flattered by a large one-off recovery in July 2025.

On funding, group borrowings of £285m sit below the £330m of existing facilities, but management says growth requires larger, cheaper and more flexible funding — hence a securitisation and refinancing project due to be announced with the September results. That is the key forward catalyst to watch.

There is no formal guidance change here. The FCA's motor-finance broker commission redress scheme is under judicial review, but S&U states the expected financial impact on Advantage is minimal.

• Revenue up 62% to $844.4m (H1 2025: $520.0m); adjusted EBITDA up 119% to $491.5m (H1 2025: $224.5m).
  • Profit before tax of $365.8m (H1 2025: $109.3m); basic EPS of $0.37 (H1 2025: $0.12).
  • Moved to net cash of $51.1m at 30 June 2026 (31 Dec 2025: net debt of $20.0m); interim dividend raised to 4.0 cents/share (H1 2025: 1.0 cent).
  • Attributable production of 151,830 gold-equivalent ounces, down from 165,176 a year earlier on budgeted lower grades at Inmaculada and San Jose.
  • Full-year AISC guidance raised to $2,380–$2,500/oz (previously $2,157–$2,320) on higher prices, taxes, profit-sharing and stronger local currencies; production target of 300,000–328,000 GEO and capex of $210–225m reiterated.

headline: Hochschild H1 2026 revenue up 62% to $844.4m and adjusted EBITDA up 119% to $491.5m on higher precious-metal prices, though full-year cost guidance raised.
priority_reason: Half-year results from an LSE-listed precious metals producer, with a cost-guidance revision and a raised interim dividend.

guidance.previous: Operations attributable AISC of $2,157–$2,320 per gold equivalent ounce
guidance.current: Operations attributable AISC of $2,380–$2,500 per gold equivalent ounce; production target reiterated at 300,000–328,000 GEO; sustaining and development capex reiterated at approximately $210–225m
guidance.commentary: The cost outlook has deteriorated: full-year AISC guidance was revised upward by roughly $200–225/oz, driven by higher precious-metal prices lifting royalties, workers' profit sharing and selling/export costs (notably in Argentina), stronger-than-expected local currencies across all three jurisdictions and continued Argentine cost inflation. Production and capex guidance were both left unchanged.

explainer:
Hochschild's headline gains are almost entirely price-driven rather than volume-driven. Revenue rose 62% and adjusted EBITDA more than doubled even though attributable production actually fell (151,830 gold-equivalent ounces versus 165,176 a year earlier), because record gold and silver prices lifted the value of each ounce sold. The lower output was planned, reflecting budgeted lower ore grades at the Inmaculada and San Jose mines. Adjusted EBITDA is a non-IFRS measure that strips out finance costs, tax, FX and non-cash items, so it flatters the operating picture relative to statutory profit.

The cost figures cut the other way. All-in sustaining costs (AISC) — the industry's fuller measure of what it costs to produce an ounce, including sustaining capital — jumped to $2,448/oz from $1,873/oz. Ironically, part of this is a side-effect of the strong prices: higher metal values increase price-linked charges such as royalties, workers' profit sharing and Argentine export taxes, while stronger local currencies raise dollar-denominated costs.

On guidance, the practical change is that the full-year AISC target has been raised to $2,380–$2,500/oz from $2,157–$2,320/oz — a negative revision, meaning costs will run higher than first budgeted. Crucially, the full-year production target (300,000–328,000 GEO) and the $210–225m capital spending plan were both reiterated, so the change is about margins per ounce rather than volumes.

Balance-sheet strength improved materially: the group swung to net cash of $51.1m from net debt of $20.0m at the year-end, and lifted the interim dividend fourfold to 4.0 cents per share. A fatality at Inmaculada in June is a serious operational and safety event, and management flags an ongoing investigation.

explainer:
This is a pre-close trading update: the FY26 numbers (year to 31 July 2026) are unaudited estimates the company is flagging ahead of full results on around 16 November 2026. Both revenue (up 50% to £160m) and adjusted EBITDA (up 40% to about £43.3m) are said to be ahead of the market consensus the company itself compiles and publishes. Importantly, the EBITDA figure excludes any contribution from the Nutrablend trade and assets acquired in June, so the underlying business is driving the beat.

Adjusted EBITDA strips out items such as interest, tax, depreciation, amortisation and one-off adjustments, so it is a proxy for operating cash profitability rather than statutory profit. Net cash of £15.9m is lower than it might otherwise have been because the period included the Nutrablend acquisition, capital spending on a production extension and extra working capital to fund growth.

On guidance, the company has introduced FY27 targets that are above consensus: roughly £205m revenue and about £49m adjusted EBITDA (+13%). The catch is margin: FY27 EBITDA margin is expected to dip slightly versus FY26. That reflects a bigger share of sales coming from the lower-margin US market and from whey-based products, plus significantly higher whey protein input costs, partly a consequence of the successful Critical Whey relaunch.

explainer:
This is a seven-month trading update (to 31 July 2026), not audited results — figures are unaudited and compared either with the same period a year earlier (7M 2025) or with the full 2025 year-end. Note that revenue and collections are quoted in US dollars, and cash collections (up 13%) differ from revenue (up 10%) because collections reflect take-or-pay provisions and the timing of receipts, whereas revenue tracks recognised sales.

Operationally the key positives are Uquo 13 reaching first gas and the Stubb Creek oil expansion lifting production 29% year-on-year. Group production of 16.3 Kboepd for the seven months sits below the 18.8 Kboepd full-year 2025 average, but that is a period-versus-year comparison; with Uquo 13 on stream, the company expects output above 20 Kboepd for the rest of the year.

On guidance, Savannah frames FY 2026 group production at 18-20 Kboepd. The balance sheet improved on cash (up to US$62.0m) though net debt edged higher to US$672.0m; management stresses only 8% of gross debt is recourse to the parent. The 22% fall in trade receivables signals better cash conversion in Nigeria, a stated focus area.

Investors should also weigh the ongoing overhangs: AIM trading remains suspended until the delayed FY 2025 Annual Report (due September 2026), the board's review of Savannah's AIM listing continues, and large Chad/Cameroon arbitration claims (over US$775m plus a ~US$330m COTCo claim, against which Chad has filed counterclaims) are expected to conclude in H2 2026.

• Operating Capital Generation of £96m, up 79% (HY25: £54m), of which £51m is acquisition-related, £33m from business-unit surplus emergence and £12m from Group Centre capital optimisation.
  • Interim dividend raised 6% to 8.16p per share, including a one-off 3% step-up; extends Chesnara's dividend-increase run to 21 years — payable 16 October 2026, ex-div 3 September 2026.
  • Cash Remittances of £73m, up 31% (HY25: £56m); Adjusted Operating Profit of £31m, up 46% (HY25: £21m); Own Funds of £976m, up 14% (FY25: £859m).
  • Solvency Coverage Ratio of 185% (FY25: 257%), reflecting completion of the HSBC Life (UK) deal — now Chesnara Life UK — and well above the 140-160% operating range; AuA of £21bn, up 38%.
  • Chesnara Life UK (largest deal to date) completed January 2026; proposed acquisition of Scottish Widows Europe SA expected to complete around end-2026, adding ~€1.7bn AuA, ~46,000 policies and €250m lifetime cash generation.
  • Total New Business Contribution of £12m, up 152% (HY25: £5m), driven by UK onshore bond demand across Countrywide Assured and Chesnara Life UK.
headline: Chesnara posts strong H1 2026 with Operating Capital Generation up 79% to £96m and a 6% rise in the interim dividend to 8.16p.
priority_reason: Half-year results from a FTSE 250 life insurer, with OCG up 79%, a dividend increase and M&A progress.

figures.note: HY26 vs FY25; 5ppts above c.180% FY25 proforma

figures.basis: reported, incl. proforma second Canada Life portfolio

guidance.previous: 6% increase in interim dividend guided at the time of the HSBC Life (UK) acquisition announcement
guidance.current: Interim dividend increased 6% to 8.16p per share, in line with prior guidance; Solvency Coverage Ratio expected to remain above the upper end of the 140-160% operating range after the Scottish Widows Europe SA acquisition completes
guidance.commentary: The dividend rise delivers exactly the 6% (including a one-off 3% step-up) previously guided at the HSBC Life (UK) deal. Chesnara reaffirms solvency will stay above its operating range post the Scottish Widows Europe acquisition, expected around end-2026.

explainer:
Chesnara is a life and pensions consolidator, so its headline measures are cash- and capital-based rather than the usual revenue/profit lines. Operating Capital Generation (OCG) — the Solvency II capital produced by the business — jumped 79% to £96m, but £51m of that came from the newly acquired Chesnara Life UK (the former HSBC Life (UK)), meaning about £45m was underlying (£33m surplus emergence plus £12m of Group Centre optimisation). Cash Remittances of £73m are the cash the operating units actually paid up to the parent, up 31%.

The Solvency Coverage Ratio fell to 185% from 257% at FY25, which sounds alarming but simply reflects paying for the HSBC Life (UK) deal and the extra capital it requires; management partly offset this with mass-lapse reinsurance and FX hedging. At 185% the ratio is still comfortably above the 140-160% target range and 5 percentage points ahead of the c.180% proforma the group flagged at year-end, leaving headroom for further M&A.

AuA of £21bn (up 38%) includes £5bn from Chesnara Life UK plus a proforma allowance for the second Canada Life portfolio and strong Swedish markets, so growth is largely acquisition- and market-driven rather than organic. New business nearly tripled to £12m, helped by demand for UK onshore bonds.

On guidance, the 6% dividend increase to 8.16p — with a one-off 3% step-up — is exactly what was promised when the HSBC Life (UK) deal was announced, so the position is maintained rather than upgraded. Chesnara also reiterated that solvency will stay above the top of its operating range even after the Scottish Widows Europe SA acquisition, which is expected to complete around the end of 2026 subject to regulatory Change in Control approval.

body:
• Hunting PLC cut its 2026 EBITDA guidance to $138-141m, slightly below previous guidance, after the Kuwait Oil Company (KOC) OCTG tender delay knocks c.$10m off 2026 EBITDA.
  • H1 2026 revenue fell 6% to $497.0m (H1 2025: $528.6m); EBITDA down 12% to $62.1m (H1 2025: $70.2m), reflecting the non-recurrence of prior-year KOC orders and slower Advanced Manufacturing activity.
  • Adjusted profit before tax of $34.5m (H1 2025: $43.7m); adjusted diluted EPS 15.2c (H1 2025: 19.6c); IFRS profit before tax up to $34.2m from $30.6m.
  • Interim dividend raised 13% to 7.0c per share (H1 2025: 6.2c); Directors project 13% per annum dividend growth through to end-decade; $40m second buyback underway.
  • Moved to net debt of $51.4m (H1 2025: net cash $44.7m) after a $58.0m working-capital outflow; free cash flow -$27.8m; management expects working capital to unwind in H2.
  • Strong Subsea and Perforating Systems performance; $63.5m titanium stress joint orders secured for ExxonMobil in Guyana; CEO Jim Johnson to retire, search underway.
headline: Hunting posts a 6% H1 revenue fall to $497.0m and trims 2026 EBITDA guidance to $138-141m after a Kuwait tender delay.
priority_reason: Half-year results accompanied by a lowered full-year EBITDA guidance range following a Middle East tender delay.

figures.note: moved from net cash to net debt

guidance.previous: Prior 2026 EBITDA guidance (not quoted as a figure in this announcement) and 2027 EBITDA consensus of $165m (Bloomberg, prior to release); year-end total cash and bank position guidance c.$50-60m.
guidance.current: Revised 2026 EBITDA guidance range of $138-141m, slightly below previous guidance; projected year-end total cash and bank position broadly unchanged at c.$50-60m. KOC tender could have a maximum adverse impact of c.$10m on current 2027 EBITDA consensus.
guidance.commentary: The KOC OCTG tender delay reduces 2026 EBITDA by c.$10m, prompting the trim to $138-141m. 2026 earnings remain H2-weighted; management still expects year-on-year growth into 2027, with the KOC outcome the key swing factor against the $165m 2027 consensus.

explainer:
Hunting reports in US dollars. Headline H1 revenue fell 6% to $497.0m and EBITDA fell 12% to $62.1m, but the decline is largely a comparative effect: the prior year (H1 2025) included large one-off orders for Kuwait Oil Company that did not repeat, plus slower Advanced Manufacturing work. Underneath that, the Subsea and Perforating Systems product groups grew organically, so the mix of earnings is shifting towards higher-margin, more durable lines.

The swing from net cash of $44.7m to net debt of $51.4m, and the negative free cash flow, are driven by a $58.0m working-capital outflow — chiefly forward material purchases and higher receivables in the Hunting Titan and Subsea segments. Management expects this to unwind in H2, hence the year-end cash guidance is broadly unchanged at c.$50-60m. This is a timing effect rather than a deterioration in profitability.

On guidance, the key change is 2026 EBITDA. Kuwait Oil Company has indicated it will re-run its OCTG tender (originally issued April 2026), pushing any award into 2027 recognition. That c.$10m hit lowers the 2026 EBITDA range to $138-141m, described as slightly below the previous range. For 2027, the same tender uncertainty represents a maximum c.$10m adverse impact against the pre-announcement Bloomberg consensus of $165m.

The adjusted figures strip out one-off items agreed by the Audit and Risk Committee; note IFRS profit before tax actually rose (to $34.2m from $30.6m) because the prior period carried $13.1m of adjusting items versus just $0.3m this half. The 13% dividend increase and the ongoing $40m buyback signal continued confidence in cash returns despite the softer near-term earnings.

• Aberdeen New India Investment Trust PLC update on its performance-related conditional tender offer, measured to 31 July 2026.
  • Adjusted NAV per share total return of 24.2% over the assessment period, versus 20.4% from the MSCI India Index (sterling adjusted) benchmark — 3.8% ahead.
  • Unaudited NAV per share 812.3p; unaudited Adjusted NAV per share 866.3p (Adjusted NAV adds back Indian capital gains tax for a like-for-like comparison).
  • The five-year assessment period runs 1 April 2022 to 31 March 2027; if Adjusted NAV total return fails to match the benchmark, the Board will propose a tender for 25% of issued share capital at 98% of NAV.
  • On current performance the tender condition is not triggered; no impact on trading.
headline: Aberdeen New India's Adjusted NAV total return of 24.2% is 3.8% ahead of its MSCI India benchmark at 31 July 2026, keeping the conditional tender offer off the table.
priority_reason: Routine interim performance update on a conditional tender offer; the trust is currently ahead of benchmark so no tender is triggered.

figures.note: adds back Indian capital gains tax

explainer:
This is an interim scorecard on a shareholder-protection mechanism, not a set of results. The trust has committed that if, over the five years to 31 March 2027, its net asset value fails to keep pace with the MSCI India Index (in sterling), the board will offer to buy back a quarter of the shares at 98% of NAV. This update simply reports where that race stands at 31 July 2026.

The "Adjusted NAV" figure of 866.3p is higher than the reported NAV of 812.3p because it adds back Indian capital gains tax paid or accrued on investments. That adjustment is made so the trust is compared like-for-like with the benchmark index, which does not bear such tax.

At this point the trust is ahead: a 24.2% Adjusted NAV total return against 20.4% for the benchmark, an outperformance of 3.8%. On that basis the conditional tender offer would not be triggered, though the outcome is only settled at the end of the assessment period on 31 March 2027.

headline: Ashtead Technology warns FY26 revenue will be around 5% below consensus and Adjusted EBITA around 15% below, as Middle East and other project delays bite.
priority_reason: Profit warning: revenue and Adjusted EBITA now guided materially below market consensus.

figures.basis: net debt / LTM Adjusted Proforma EBITDA

guidance.previous: Delivery of full-year market expectations (revenue £214.2m, Adjusted EBITA £59.2m consensus) was contingent on easing of the Middle East conflict and no major changes to project scheduling (per 15 July 2026 update).
guidance.current: FY26 revenue around 5% below consensus and Adjusted EBITA around 15% below consensus; leverage around 1.3x at year end.
guidance.commentary: Guidance cut because the Middle East conflict has not eased and regional H2 projects have slipped into 2027, with further delays in Europe and the Americas. Deferred rental revenue hurts the revenue mix and, via operating leverage, disproportionately reduces profit — hence the larger EBITA downgrade than revenue downgrade.

explainer:
This is a profit warning. On 15 July Ashtead Technology said it could still hit full-year forecasts, but only if the Middle East conflict eased and project timings held. Neither happened: several second-half projects in the region have been pushed into 2027, and vessel-scheduling and broader economic uncertainty have delayed work in Europe and the Americas too.

The company benchmarks itself against a self-compiled analyst consensus of £214.2m revenue and £59.2m Adjusted EBITA for FY26. Revenue is now expected to land about 5% below that, but profit (Adjusted EBITA) about 15% below. The gap between the two is the key point: much of the deferred work is rental revenue, which is high-margin, so losing it hits profit far harder than sales — this is the operating leverage the Board refers to.

Despite the profit hit, the balance sheet is presented as sound, with net debt around 1.3x LTM Adjusted Proforma EBITDA at year end. The Board frames the delays as timing rather than lost demand, pointing to energy-security tailwinds and a strong customer backlog.

  • UK improved (organic -0.2%, LFL +0.8%) on strong football replica kit and Outdoor; Europe organic -0.4%, LFL -2.7%; Asia Pacific organic +10.2%.

headline: JD Sports cuts FY27 pre-tax profit guidance to £700m-£800m from £750m-£850m after tough Q2 trading, with North America hardest hit.
priority_reason: Q2 trading statement with a cut to FY27 profit guidance — a de facto profit warning.

guidance.previous: FY27 profit before tax and adjusting items of £750m to £850m; free cash flow of £460m to £520m
guidance.current: FY27 profit before tax and adjusting items of £700m to £800m; free cash flow unchanged at £460m to £520m
guidance.commentary: JD cut its FY27 PBT (pre-adjusting items) guidance by £50m at both ends of the range, reflecting soft H1 sales trends and a promotional market it expects may persist into H2. Free cash flow guidance was left unchanged, supported by cost, capital and working-capital discipline.

explainer:
This is a second-quarter trading statement, not full results — it reports sales momentum by region rather than audited profit. JD quotes 'organic' and 'like-for-like' (LFL) sales at constant exchange rates: LFL strips out new and closed stores to show underlying trading, while organic also captures space growth from existing operations. Group LFL of -3.1% means underlying volumes fell, partly masked by new selling space (+2.1% to H1 sales).

The key news is the guidance cut. JD now expects FY27 profit before tax and adjusting items of £700m-£800m, down from £750m-£850m — roughly a £50m reduction at each end. 'Adjusting items' are one-off costs (such as the Finish Line-to-JD conversion) excluded from this underlying profit measure. North America, JD's largest region at 35% of sales, drove the downgrade, hurt by a cautious core consumer, a weaker quarter for 'high-heat' (hyped, limited-release) footwear, and 'back-to-school' spending slipping from July into August.

Importantly, free cash flow guidance of £460m-£520m is unchanged, and JD moved into a net cash position (before lease liabilities), versus net debt a year earlier. It also began the second £100m tranche of its £200m annual buyback on 3 August, signalling balance-sheet confidence despite the softer profit outlook.

Half-year results, which will confirm the actual H1 profit figures behind these sales trends, are scheduled for 23 September 2026.

priority_reason: First-half results with upgraded FY 2026 dividend guidance, reduced opex guidance and a record production quarter.

figures.note: Q2 record of 131 kboe/d; FY guidance 120-130 kboe/d

guidance.previous: FY 2026 dividend guidance of $470-520m; net operating cost guidance $820-860m; Rosebank net capital cost guidance $280-320m (all as provided 19 March 2026)
guidance.current: FY 2026 dividend guidance upgraded to $500-530m (30% post-tax CFFO); net operating cost guidance reduced to $800-840m; Rosebank net capital cost guidance reduced to $250-280m; production reaffirmed at 120-130 kboe/d; producing asset capex, decommissioning and cash tax guidance all reaffirmed
guidance.commentary: Dividend outlook was raised on strong H1 cash generation, while operating cost and Rosebank capex guidance were cut, the latter reflecting deferral of ~$35m of drilling activity into 2027. Production, decommissioning and cash tax guidance were left unchanged.

explainer:
These are half-year figures for the six months to 30 June 2026, reported in US dollars. Headline production and cash generation held up well: Ithaca averaged 128 kboe/d in the half (up from 124 a year earlier) and hit a record 131 kboe/d in the second quarter, giving management confidence to reaffirm the full-year range of 120-130 kboe/d. Adjusted EBITDAX and operating cash flow were both broadly flat year-on-year at about $1.1bn and $1.0bn respectively.

The swing from a $217m loss in H1 2025 to a $127m profit this year is flattered by the prior-year comparison: the 2025 period carried a one-off, non-cash deferred tax charge of $327.6m tied to the extension of the Energy Profits Levy. On a cleaner basis, adjusted net income was essentially unchanged at $128m versus $129m. Realised prices were $83/boe before hedging but only $69/boe after hedging losses, so a strong price environment was partly given back through the hedge book.

The key change is guidance. The FY 2026 dividend target has been raised to $500-530m from $470-520m (still pegged to 30% of post-tax operating cash flow), and a first interim dividend of $255m was declared. At the same time, full-year net operating cost guidance was trimmed to $800-840m and Rosebank capex guidance cut to $250-280m — the latter mainly a timing effect, with roughly $35m of drilling spend rephased from 2026 into 2027 rather than a genuine cost saving. Production, producing-asset capex, decommissioning and cash tax guidance were all left unchanged.

For context, Rosebank is the major growth project: the FPSO is now moored on station and first production has been narrowed to H1 2027, ramping to plateau over summer 2027, subject to regulatory approval. The balance sheet strengthened over the half, with adjusted net debt falling to $1.0bn (0.49x leverage) and liquidity of $1.9bn helped by a €155m bond tap.

headline: Kenmare's H1 output fell sharply on weak markets and slow WCP A commissioning, and it trimmed 2026 ilmenite production guidance to about 800,000 tonnes.
priority_reason: Half-yearly results with a moderated 2026 production guidance figure and a sharp fall in output and realised prices.

figures.note: boosted by conversion of 102,200t tailings stockpile

guidance.previous: Ilmenite production of more than 800,000 tonnes in 2026; shipments of at least 1.1 million tonnes
guidance.current: Ilmenite production of approximately 800,000 tonnes in 2026; shipments guidance of at least 1.1 million tonnes maintained; annual operating and capital cost guidance expected to be achieved
guidance.commentary: Softer-than-expected ilmenite production in H1 led Kenmare to moderate its 2026 ilmenite production guidance from 'more than 800,000 tonnes' to 'approximately 800,000 tonnes'. Shipments guidance — the company's key metric for the year — was maintained, with output said to have improved in July and early August.

explainer:
Kenmare mines heavy mineral concentrate (HMC) at Moma in Mozambique and processes it into finished titanium products — mainly ilmenite, plus zircon and rutile — and a newer concentrates product, ZrTi. The H1 figures are compared year-on-year against H1 2025. Production of nearly every product fell heavily: ilmenite was down 39%, largely because the ageing WCP A plant hit lower ore grades as it reaches the end of its current mine path, and because the plant's upgrade commissioning has run slower than planned, averaging 2,800 tonnes per hour against a 3,500 tph design.

The headline guidance change is that 2026 ilmenite production is now expected to be 'approximately 800,000 tonnes' rather than 'more than 800,000 tonnes' — a modest downgrade reflecting the weak first half. Crucially, the company kept its full-year shipments guidance of at least 1.1 million tonnes, which it calls its key metric; it has been meeting shipments partly by drawing down high product stockpiles (finished-product stock fell from 344,000 tonnes at end-2025 to 233,500 tonnes).

Prices are the other pressure point: the average realised price fell 26% to $242 a tonne as Chinese ilmenite supply kept the titanium feedstock market soft. Against that, the zircon market strengthened through H1 with higher Q2 prices, and demand for the new ZrTi concentrate has run well ahead of the company's initial expectations, which is why concentrates 'production' jumped 599% — largely a one-off conversion of a 102,200-tonne tailings stockpile rather than underlying growth.

Note the scraped text contains no revenue, profit, earnings or dividend figures and is cut off mid-sentence at the end, so this summary reflects only the operational and guidance detail actually present.

guidance.previous: Consensus for FY27: revenue £509.3m and adjusted PBT £77.1m (ranges £498.0m–£514.0m and £75.0m–£84.0m)

explainer:

The key benchmark it cites is a company-compiled consensus — an average of sell-side analyst forecasts that Kainos itself has gathered — of £509.3m of revenue and £77.1m of adjusted pre-tax profit (PBT). The upgrade is underpinned by contract wins in the Digital Services division and a large multi-year contracted backlog, which gives visibility on future revenue. • BHP Group Limited FY26 (year to 30 June 2026): Underlying EBITDA ~US$33bn (up ~US$7bn), with Copper contributing a record >US$18bn — 54% of group EBITDA and the first year the majority of earnings came from copper.
  • Underlying attributable profit US$13.2bn, up 30% on FY25; Attributable profit ~US$10bn (up 9%), after a US$2.3bn Jansen impairment and US$1.1bn Samarco charge.
  • Final dividend of 99 US cents per share (US$5.0bn), the largest in four years; total FY26 cash returns of US$8.7bn (US$1.72/share, fully franked).
  • Net debt US$8.7bn (FY25: US$12.9bn), below the US$10-20bn target range; net debt/EBITDA 0.3x, gearing 13.4%; free cash flow up 83% to US$9.8bn.
  • Record iron ore production at WAIO and ~2 Mt of copper for a second year; unit costs 6.1% lower across major assets; ROCE 26.1%.
  • Growth pipeline advancing: Escondida US$0.5bn pre-commitment for a new concentrator, Jansen Stage 1 84% complete (first production mid-CY27), and a potential Vicuña Stage 1 FID as early as end-CY26.
headline: BHP posts ~US$33bn Underlying EBITDA and US$13.2bn Underlying attributable profit for FY26, with copper contributing over half of group earnings for the first time.
priority_reason: Full-year results from a FTSE 100 mega-cap with record earnings, a large dividend and capital-return update.

guidance.previous: Capital and exploration expenditure guidance ~US$11bn in FY27
guidance.current: Capital and exploration expenditure ~US$11bn in FY27, now also ~US$11bn in FY28 and on average each year FY29-FY31; FY27 adjusted effective tax rate 35-40%
guidance.commentary: FY27 capex guidance is unchanged at ~US$11bn. The FY28 and FY29-FY31 average figures reflect the higher cost of completing Jansen Stage 2 and adverse FX, partly offset by capital efficiency. Group copper-equivalent production is guided to a 3-4% CAGR between FY27 and FY35.

explainer:
This is BHP's full-year result for the 12 months to 30 June 2026. Headline earnings are quoted in US dollars because that is BHP's reporting currency. 'Underlying' profit strips out exceptional items — here a US$2.3bn impairment on the Jansen potash project and US$1.1bn related to the Samarco dam failure — so Underlying attributable profit (US$13.2bn, +30%) is much higher than the statutory Attributable profit (~US$10bn, +9%). The gap is the one-off charges, not trading performance.

The standout structural change is that copper generated more than half of group EBITDA (54%) for the first time, overtaking iron ore. Higher realised prices for copper, iron ore and coal, plus lower unit costs (down 6.1% across major assets despite ~4% inflation), drove EBITDA up around US$7bn to ~US$33bn. Escondida cut unit costs 10% and Copper SA 73%, the latter helped by gold and silver by-product credits.

The balance sheet strengthened sharply: net debt fell to US$8.7bn from US$12.9bn, below the bottom of the US$10-20bn target range, aided by the US$4.3bn Antamina silver-streaming proceeds and asset sales. That, plus 83% higher free cash flow of US$9.8bn, funded a 99 US-cent final dividend — the largest in four years — and total shareholder returns of US$1.72 per share.

On guidance, capital and exploration spend is essentially held flat at ~US$11bn a year: FY27 is unchanged, while the new FY28 and FY29-FY31 figures reflect the added cost of Jansen Stage 2 and higher FX, offset by efficiencies. Production guidance is for 3-4% copper-equivalent growth CAGR to FY35, so this is a 'maintained' capex outlook rather than an upgrade or cut.

• SAFFRON Phase III trial met its endpoints: Tagrisso (osimertinib) plus Orpathys (savolitinib) delivered statistically significant, clinically meaningful improvements in progression-free survival and overall survival versus doublet platinum-based chemotherapy.

priority_reason: Positive Phase III trial data on a major franchise drug (Tagrisso) addressing resistance in EGFR-mutated lung cancer, supporting global registrations.

  • FY27 adjusted PBT phasing weighted 15%/85% H1/H2 (vs c.25%/75% last year); net debt to adjusted EBITDA expected to peak at c.1.5x.

priority_reason: AGM trading statement with a full-year guidance reiteration and detailed early trading momentum, directly relevant to the shares.

first four months of FY27 vs H2 FY26
first four months of FY27; FY27 target 50,000

guidance.previous: Adjusted profit before tax of £80m to £90m for FY27 (as set at 23 June 2026 strategy update)
guidance.current: Adjusted profit before tax of £80m to £90m for FY27, reiterated
guidance.commentary: Full-year adjusted PBT guidance is unchanged. The company reconfirmed the heavier H2 profit weighting (c.15%/85% H1/H2 vs c.25%/75% last year) reflecting phasing of the five-year investment programme, and net debt to adjusted EBITDA peaking at c.1.5x in FY27.

explainer:
This is an AGM trading update covering the first four months of the new financial year (FY27, April to July 2026), the opening period of the five-year growth plan announced on 23 June 2026. It is a narrative statement rather than full accounts, so most metrics are operational (customer growth, Partner numbers, cross-selling) rather than audited financials.

The key headline metric is multiservice customer growth, which is running slightly ahead of the 10% full-year target and more than 2.5 times the 3.9% rate delivered in FY26. Partner numbers — the self-employed distributors who sell Utility Warehouse services — are at record levels on both activity (c.4.9k monthly active, up from c.4.2k) and total headcount (over 85k, up from c.77k), which management links directly to the improved customer proposition.

On guidance, nothing has changed at the full-year level: adjusted profit before tax of £80m-£90m for FY27 is reiterated. What is worth noting is the phasing — because the investment programme is front-loaded, profit is skewed even more heavily to the second half (c.15%/85% split versus c.25%/75% last year), so a soft-looking H1 in November should not be read as a downgrade. Net debt to adjusted EBITDA is expected to peak at around 1.5x this year before falling to about 1x over the plan.

Separately, the £40m buyback is roughly half complete (c.2.44m shares at an average 818.66p, £20m still to deploy), the 12p FY26 final dividend is paid on 28 August, and the company flagged an interim dividend and likely buyback extension alongside November's half-year results.

body:
• GBG now expects FY27 total group revenue growth of 1-3%, down from previous guidance of mid-single digit, citing higher than expected volume attrition on a few material Americas Identity customers.
  • Q2 growth has not improved and the attrition impact is unlikely to be mitigated within the current financial year given the normal sales cycle; Q1 was in line with Board expectations, supported by strong EMEA Identity trading and GBG Go momentum.
  • FY27 adjusted operating profit margin guided to approximately 21%, with cost control offsetting the headwind; the one-off £6 million investment in GBG Go announced in June continues.
  • Tom Schutz (Chief Revenue Officer, Americas) has left the business; COO James Gothard assumes interim responsibility for the Americas.
  • Q1 Americas Identity revenue was only marginally below plan, but the sales pipeline remains described as strong.
headline: GBG cuts FY27 group revenue growth guidance to 1-3% (from mid-single digit) after higher-than-expected customer attrition in its Americas Identity business.
priority_reason: Guidance cut on weaker Americas Identity trading plus a senior departure — a profit-warning-style update from a FTSE 250 name.

guidance.previous: Mid-single digit total group revenue growth for FY27
guidance.current: FY27 total group revenue growth of 1-3%; FY27 adjusted operating profit margin of approximately 21%
guidance.commentary: GBG has cut its full-year revenue growth outlook because a small number of material Americas Identity customers reduced volumes more than expected, and the shortfall cannot be recovered this year given the length of the sales cycle. Management is holding margin near 21% through cost control while pressing ahead with the £6m GBG Go investment.

explainer:
This is a mid-year trading update, not full results. GBG had told the market at its 21 July AGM that Q1 was in line with expectations, helped by strong Identity trading in EMEA. The change here is that the Americas Identity business has deteriorated in Q2, with several sizeable customers cutting usage volumes by more than the company planned for.

The key figure is the downgrade to guidance: group revenue growth for the year to March 2027 is now expected at 1-3%, versus the 'mid-single digit' (broadly 4-6%) previously indicated. Because GBG recognises revenue over a normal sales cycle, new pipeline wins take time to convert, so the lost volume cannot be made up before the financial year ends.

On profitability, GBG still expects an adjusted operating margin of about 21%, protected by cost control, and is keeping the separate one-off £6m investment in its AI-powered GBG Go platform that it announced in June. 'Adjusted' means before certain one-off or non-cash items, so the reported margin could differ.

Alongside the numbers, the head of the Americas revenue function, Tom Schutz, has departed, with COO James Gothard stepping in on an interim basis — a leadership change directly tied to the region under pressure.

• Touchstone Exploration Inc. (AIM/TSX: TXP) posted Q2 2026 net income of $2.34m ($0.01 per basic and diluted share), reversing the Q1 2026 loss of $2.38m; all figures in US dollars.
  • Funds flow from operations rose to $7.13m from $1.85m in Q1 2026, and petroleum and natural gas sales climbed 39% sequentially to $17.47m on higher realised pricing across all streams.
  • Operating netback improved 77% quarter-on-quarter to $24.37/boe; realised crude and liquids averaged $70.13/bbl and natural gas $4.93/Mcf.
  • Production dipped 5% sequentially to 4,433 boe/d on planned third-party maintenance at Atlantic LNG Train 4; the Cascadura booster compressor entered service on 9 July 2026 at ~16.5 MMcf/d gross.
  • Net debt cut 10% sequentially to $68.71m; post-quarter the $8.4m debenture was repaid and converted into equity via a Purebond share subscription of 89,765,000 shares.
  • The interim accounts include a material uncertainty / going-concern note, with a $28.7m working capital deficit, a covenant waiver secured for 2026, and $14.2m of bank debt repayments due over the next 12 months.
headline: Touchstone returned to profit in Q2 2026 with net income of $2.34m as funds flow more than tripled to $7.13m on stronger pricing.
priority_reason: Quarterly results with a return to profit, but the accounts carry a material going-concern uncertainty.

guidance.commentary: No formal production or financial guidance figures provided; management flags near-term production optimisation opportunities as pipeline constraints normalise after the Atlantic Train 4 outage.

explainer:
Touchstone reports in US dollars, and its headline highlights compare Q2 2026 against the prior quarter (Q1 2026), whereas the results table compares against Q2 2025 a year earlier. The sequential comparison is the more flattering one: Q1 2026 was a weak, loss-making quarter, so the jump in funds flow (to $7.13m from $1.85m) and the 77% rise in operating netback largely reflect a recovery in realised oil and gas prices rather than higher volumes. Production actually fell 5% quarter-on-quarter to 4,433 boe/d because planned maintenance at the third-party Atlantic LNG Train 4 facility constrained gas output.

The return to profit — net income of $2.34m, or $0.01 a share — reverses the $2.38m loss booked in Q1 2026. Higher realised gas pricing was helped by redirecting Central block volumes to Atlantic LNG Trains 2/3, which carry a structurally higher price formula, during the Train 4 outage.

The most important caveat is the balance sheet. The interim statements carry a material-uncertainty note casting significant doubt on Touchstone's ability to continue as a going concern. The company reported a $28.7m working capital deficit, has $14.2m of bank debt repayments due over the next 12 months, and is chasing $11.1m of VAT receivables. It secured a waiver of its 2026 debt-service-coverage covenant and, after quarter-end, repaid an $8.4m short-term debenture by converting it into equity via a Purebond share subscription, which reduces near-term debt but dilutes shareholders. No formal forward guidance figures were given.

priority_reason: Quarterly and interim results from a major listed retailer, with a clear profit inflection despite falling revenue.

figures.metric: Net income attributable to ordinary shareholders
Non-GAAP net income attributable to ordinary shareholders

guidance.commentary: The announcement gives qualitative outlook comments but no numerical guidance for future periods.

explainer:
JD.com's second-quarter revenue dipped 2.9% year-on-year, which the company attributes largely to a 'high base effect' — Q2 2025 was unusually strong, so the comparison flatters the decline rather than signalling a collapse in demand. Product sales (goods JD buys and resells) fell 5.4%, while higher-margin service revenue (marketplace commissions and advertising) grew 6.8%, shifting the revenue mix toward more profitable activity.

Despite the softer top line, profitability improved sharply. The business swung from an operating loss of RMB0.9bn a year ago to a RMB4.5bn profit, driven by record peak-season margins at the core JD Retail unit, a 24.8% cut in marketing spend, and narrower losses in the New Businesses segment — chiefly reduced losses at JD Food Delivery. Note the gap between the RMB5.01 reported EPS per ADS and the RMB6.29 non-GAAP figure: the non-GAAP number strips out items like share-based compensation and acquisition amortisation, so it is management's preferred, flattering measure.

The company issued no numerical guidance; comments about 'a healthy financial trajectory' are directional only. Investors should also weigh the RMB1.0bn of H1 buybacks (about 2.5% of shares) as a supportive factor for per-share metrics, with a further US$1.0bn still available under the programme through August 2027.

Figures are in Chinese renminbi (RMB) with US dollar conversions provided by the company; there is no sterling figure in the announcement.

body:
• Ofwat's 2026 Cost Change Draft Decision supports the substantial majority of UUW's first AMP8 re-opener submission.
  • Draft Decision includes allowances of c.£975 million, keeping UUW on track to deliver approximately £2.5 billion of investment via the annualised AMP8 re-opener mechanism.
  • Financial framework reiterated: c.£11.5 billion capital investment, RCV growth of ~10% per annum to ~£25 billion by 2030, target regulatory returns of 10-11%, dividend growth in line with CPIH, target gearing 55-65%.
  • Ofwat has requested additional evidence on a limited number of projects; UUW will respond by 24 September 2026 ahead of the Final Decision in December 2026.
  • CEO Louise Beardmore said the in-period mechanism is working well to fund infrastructure supporting North West economic growth.
headline: United Utilities Water welcomes Ofwat's 2026 Cost Change Draft Decision, with c.£975m allowances keeping it on track for c.£2.5bn of annualised AMP8 re-opener investment.
priority_reason: Ofwat draft decision backs the substantial majority of UUW's re-opener submission and reaffirms the AMP8 financial framework, but changes no existing guidance.

guidance.previous: c.£11.5bn AMP8 capital investment; RCV growing ~10% p.a. to ~£25bn by 2030; regulatory returns 10-11%; dividend growth in line with CPIH; target gearing 55-65%
guidance.current: Financial framework unchanged: c.£11.5bn capital investment; RCV growth ~10% p.a. to ~£25bn by 2030; returns 10-11%; CPIH dividend growth; gearing 55-65%
guidance.commentary: The draft decision reaffirms rather than changes UUW's existing AMP8 financial framework. The c.£975m of supported allowances underpins the previously flagged c.£2.5bn annualised re-opener investment programme.

explainer:
This is a regulatory milestone rather than a results release. Under Ofwat's price control for 2025-2030 (AMP8), water companies can apply through a 'cost change re-opener' for extra allowances when new investment needs emerge mid-period. United Utilities Water submitted a bid and Ofwat has now published a draft decision backing most of it, worth c.£975m of allowances and underpinning roughly £2.5bn of investment on an annualised basis.

The key figures — c.£11.5bn of AMP8 capex, regulatory capital value (RCV) growing about 10% a year to ~£25bn by 2030, and target returns of 10-11% — are reiterated, not new. RCV is the regulated asset base on which the company earns a return, so its growth is central to the investment case. The return figures assume ~3% average inflation over AMP8.

Ofwat has asked for further evidence on a small number of projects. UUW will respond by 24 September 2026, with a Final Decision due in December 2026 — so the allowances quoted here are provisional and could still move at the final determination.

• Savills plc H1 to 30 June 2026: Group revenue up 9% (same in constant currency) to £1,225.5m (H1 25: £1,127.8m), with growth across all segments.
  • Group underlying profit before tax up 47% (49% constant currency) to £34.3m (H1 25: £23.3m), margin up to 2.8% from 2.1%; but reported PBT fell to £7.0m (H1 25: £15.8m) on one-off Eastdil Secured acquisition costs.
  • Interim dividend raised 5% to 7.8p (H1 25: 7.4p).
  • Transactional business revenue up 14% to £449.6m, underlying loss cut to £2.4m (H1 25: £7.8m loss); Less Transactional revenue up 6%, underlying PBT up 27%.
  • Acquisition of Eastdil Secured (US real estate investment banking) completed 31 July 2026; it delivered H1 revenue of US$302m (£225m) and EBITDA of US$51m (£38m), with a 5-month contribution to be consolidated in FY26.
  • Board's expectations for the enlarged Group for 2026 are unchanged; strong pipelines but macro volatility makes timing of Transactional conversion hard to predict.
headline: Savills H1 revenue rose 9% to £1,225.5m and underlying pre-tax profit jumped 47% to £34.3m, with 2026 expectations for the enlarged Group unchanged.
priority_reason: Half-year results with a 47% jump in underlying profit, dividend increase and a transformational US acquisition.

figures.note: impacted by one-off Eastdil acquisition costs

guidance.previous: not stated
guidance.current: the Board's expectations for the enlarged Group for 2026 are unchanged
guidance.commentary: Guidance for the enlarged Group (including Eastdil Secured) for 2026 is reaffirmed despite market uncertainty. The Board flags that transactional pipelines are strong but macro volatility, notably Middle East conflict and UK political change, makes the timing of pipeline conversion difficult to predict.

explainer:
Savills reports two profit measures. 'Underlying' profit before tax, which strips out one-off items, rose 47% to £34.3m — the number that best reflects trading. 'Reported' profit before tax fell to £7.0m because it includes sizeable one-off costs tied to buying Eastdil Secured, so the two figures moving in opposite directions is a timing/accounting effect rather than a deterioration in the core business.

Revenue growth of 9% was the same in constant currency, meaning exchange-rate movements had a negligible effect — the growth is real, not a currency artefact. The business splits into Transactional work (buying, selling and leasing property, which is cyclical and made a small loss in the seasonally weaker first half) and Less Transactional work (consultancy and property management, which is steadier). Both grew, and prior restructuring is now feeding through to better profitability.

• Ofwat has published its Draft Determination on Pennon's Cost Change submissions made in May 2026, confirming £190m of additional investment for FY27/28 through to the end of AMP 8.
  • The draft determinations reflect the core business cases proposed and, per Pennon, the strength of its submissions.
  • Pennon will review the determinations in detail and respond with representations by the due date of 24 September 2026.

headline: Ofwat's draft determination allows Pennon £190m of additional investment for FY27/28 through to the end of AMP 8.
priority_reason: Ofwat draft determination confirms a material uplift in allowed investment for Pennon, directly affecting the regulated capital programme.
explainer:
Ofwat is the economic regulator for the water sector in England and Wales. Water companies operate within five-year price control periods known as Asset Management Plans (AMP); AMP 8 covers 2025–2030. A 'Cost Change' submission is a mechanism for a company to request an adjustment to its allowed spending within the period, which Ofwat assesses and rules on via a Draft Determination.

The £190m figure is additional investment Ofwat is proposing to allow Pennon to make from FY27/28 to the end of AMP 8. In regulated water, allowed investment (totex) feeds the regulatory capital value on which the company earns a return, so a larger allowance can support future revenue and returns — though the announcement does not translate the £190m into any earnings or dividend figure.

This is a draft, not final. Pennon will submit representations by 24 September 2026 before Ofwat issues its final determination, so the number could still change. No trading guidance was issued or altered in this announcement.

figures.basis: order book plus preferred bidder book

guidance.current: FY 26 revenue, operating profit and margin unchanged and in line with the Board's expectations; FY 26 year-end net cash approximately £170m; step change in financial performance expected in FY 27 and beyond

explainer:
Costain reports both statutory ("reported") and "adjusted" figures. In H1 26 the two are almost identical because there were no adjusting items in the period, versus £0.4m in H1 25 — that is why reported profit growth (+5.5%) looks a little faster than adjusted growth (+3.0%), rather than reflecting any change in the underlying business. Revenue growth of 3.4% is on a reported basis, with Transportation down 3.2% (tough prior-year comparatives on road frameworks) offset by Natural Resources up 13.3% as the water sector moves into the construction-heavy AMP8 cycle.

On guidance, the key message is continuity: FY 26 revenue, operating profit and margin expectations are left unchanged, and the company points to 91% of both FY 26 and FY 27 consensus revenue already covered by its record £7.0bn forward work. Because construction earnings are second-half weighted, management expects H2 26 revenue and free cash flow to be stronger than H1.

The standout capital-return change is the dividend. After a January 2026 pension agreement removed a "dividend parity" constraint, the Board lowered its target dividend cover to 2.5x adjusted earnings (from 3x), split roughly one-third in H1 and two-thirds in H2. This mechanically allows the interim dividend to double to 2.0p even though earnings rose only modestly. Year-end net cash is guided to fall to about £170m (from £189.3m at FY 25) as working-capital benefits partly unwind and cash is returned via the £20m buyback and higher dividends.

• Hill & Smith PLC raised FY26 guidance: underlying operating profit now expected modestly ahead of previous expectations, with a small full-year margin progression versus 2025.
  • Group organic constant currency (OCC) revenue up 5%, with overall constant currency revenue and underlying operating profit both up 7%; Group now reports in US dollars.
  • US businesses grew 14% OCC, delivering 66% of Group revenue and 84% of underlying operating profit; US Engineered Solutions revenue up 18% and profit up 20% in constant currency.
  • UK & India Engineered Solutions OCC revenue fell 13%, margins down to 5.3% (2025: 9.6%); UK permanent steel road barrier business disposed in May 2026 for $7.1m (£5.3m).
  • Group underlying operating margin flat at 17.0%; interim dividend up 7% to 25.0c (2025: 23.4c); ROIC 26.7% and covenant leverage low at 0.4x.
  • £58.6m of the £100m share buyback completed as at 10 August 2026; Freeberg and Hentech acquired for combined $45.8m and performing well.
headline: Hill & Smith raised FY26 underlying operating profit expectations after H1 organic revenue grew 5%, driven by 14% US growth.
priority_reason: Half-year results accompanied by a raised FY26 profit outlook.

figures.note: working capital build; expected to reverse in H2

guidance.previous: Previous FY26 expectations for underlying operating profit (level not quantified in the announcement).
guidance.current: FY26 underlying operating profit now expected to be modestly ahead of previous expectations, with a small FY margin progression compared to 2025.
guidance.commentary: The upgrade follows a strong first half and sustained momentum in the US businesses. Management retains confidence in the medium-term outlook and its 18%+ margin target over time.

explainer:
Hill & Smith reports these results in US dollars for the first time, having switched its reporting currency in 2026, so the prior-year comparatives have been restated into dollars. The headline growth numbers are quoted on an organic constant currency (OCC) basis, which strips out both currency movements and the effect of acquisitions and disposals — so the 5% group figure reflects underlying demand rather than the boost from the Freeberg and Hentech deals or currency swings.

The story is a two-speed group. US operations grew OCC revenue 14% on strong infrastructure demand — power transmission and distribution, data centres and galvanizing — and now generate the bulk of group profit. Against that, UK & India Engineered Solutions saw OCC revenue fall 13% as UK roads, industrial and residential markets stayed weak, and the prior year had benefited from one-off UK transport project work, so the division's margin more than halved to 5.3%.

Cash conversion dropped to 50% from 85%, but this is presented as timing rather than deterioration: working capital was built up to support fast-growing US businesses and is expected to unwind in the second half, with the group still targeting 80%+ over time.

On guidance, the key change is that FY26 underlying operating profit is now expected to be modestly ahead of what the company previously guided, thanks to the strong first half and continued US momentum. The company does not put a specific number on either the old or new expectation, so the upgrade is directional rather than quantified.

priority_reason: Half-year results with an upgraded full-year outlook, higher dividend and continuing buyback.

explainer:
Balfour Beatty splits its performance into 'earnings-based businesses' (Construction Services and Support Services) and Infrastructure Investments. The headline 42% growth in profit from operations (PFO) applies to those earnings-based businesses, driven by strong Support Services (UK power transmission) and a swing to profit in US Construction as Buildings volumes rose and US Civils losses shrank. UK Construction's underlying profit grew 17% once you strip out a £10m insurance recovery that flattered the 2025 comparative — a reminder that year-on-year moves here include a one-off in the base.

Group underlying PFO of £119m sits below the £153m earnings-based figure because it includes a £9m loss in Infrastructure Investments, largely legal and monitor costs tied to US military housing that ceased in June. Separately, statutory profit is dragged by an £8m after-tax non-underlying charge, mainly a higher Building Safety Act provision — versus a £28m non-underlying gain a year earlier — so reported and underlying numbers diverge this period.

On guidance, the key change is direction: full-year earnings-based PFO growth is now expected to be 'slightly ahead' of what the company previously flagged, and average net cash guidance has been raised by £200m to a £1.5–£1.7bn range, with net finance income of £35–£40m to match. The dividend was raised 12% to 4.7p and the £200m 2026 buyback is on track to complete by year-end, both signalling management confidence in cash generation.

  • Board now expects 2026 full-year EPS of 4.6-5.5p, following the earnings pressure flagged in the 4 August 2026 trading update.
headline: CLS Holdings swung to a first-half statutory loss of £69.6m on £84.2m of property writedowns, scrapped its interim dividend and guided to 2026 EPS of 4.6-5.5p.
priority_reason: Half-year results with a statutory loss, scrapped interim dividend and a fresh full-year EPS guidance range.

guidance.previous: Not stated in this announcement; earnings pressure was flagged in the Trading Update on 4 August 2026
guidance.current: Board now expects 2026 full-year EPS in the range of 4.6 to 5.5 pence per share
guidance.commentary: The company reiterated the downgrade set out in its 4 August trading update, citing pressure from asset sales and the departure of its largest tenant. It also expects around £100m of disposals for the year and 89% of 2026 refinancing completed or agreed.

explainer:
CLS is an office landlord with a £1.6bn portfolio in the UK, Germany and France, so its results are dominated by property valuations. The £69.6m statutory loss is largely non-cash: it reflects an £84.2m markdown in the value of its buildings as property yields expanded (up 27bps) and estimated rental values (ERVs) slipped 1.8%. The underlying cash-generating measure, EPRA earnings, was still positive at £10.9m but fell a third as rent was lost to disposals and tenant departures.

The two 'per share' asset measures — EPRA NTA (177.7p) and statutory NAV (164.2p) — are compared with the year-end (31 December 2025) rather than the prior half, and both fell about 11-12%, chiefly on the valuation declines plus a small currency drag from a stronger pound against the euro. LTV rose to 51.6% not because debt increased (net debt actually fell £44.2m) but because the property value it is measured against fell faster.

The dividend has effectively been paused: no interim payout (versus 1.30p last year), with the Board deferring any decision to a single final dividend once full-year earnings are known, prioritising deleveraging and refinancing.

On guidance, CLS confirmed the downgrade first signalled in its 4 August trading update, now framing 2026 full-year EPS as 4.6-5.5p. The drivers are lower income from around £100m of planned asset sales and the loss of its largest tenant. Management stresses it has completed or agreed 89% of this year's refinancing and kept disposals at book value, positioning the business for when market conditions improve.
