IHG runs an asset-light, fee-based hotel franchising and management model, so the headline profit metric is operating profit from 'reportable segments' ($665m, +10%) rather than the larger IFRS total revenue figure ($2,659m), which is inflated by 'System Fund' and reimbursable costs passed through on behalf of hotel owners. The 'underlying' percentages strip out currency movements, and here they are broadly in line with reported growth, meaning FX was not a major distorting factor at the segment level.

The standout divergence is IFRS basic EPS falling (6)% to 283.3¢ while adjusted EPS rose +13% to 274.7¢. This is almost entirely an accounting/FX artefact: the prior year benefited from $79m of foreign-exchange gains on intra-group balances, versus a $7m loss this year. explainer:
These are US-GAAP quarterly results from a Midland Basin (West Texas) oil and gas producer reported in US dollars, not sterling. The headline profit measure, net income of $82.3m ($0.59 per diluted share), is a bottom-line accounting figure, while EBITDAX of $147.6m is a non-GAAP cash-earnings proxy widely used in the sector that strips out interest, tax, depreciation and exploration costs. The announcement does not print prior-year comparatives for any of these numbers, so no year-on-year change can be stated with confidence from this text alone.

Realised pricing is shown two ways. The guidance ranges are not restated, so this is best read as favourable execution against an unchanged plan rather than a formal upgrade.

The most market-sensitive item is not a number: the company confirms its Board is running a strategic review that may result in a sale of the company, though it stresses no transaction is assured and any deal may not increase shareholder value.   • 2026 production guidance re-affirmed at 72,000-76,500oz, but cost guidance raised: on-mine costs to US$1,600-1,800/oz (from US$1,500-1,700) and AISC to US$2,500-2,700/oz (from US$2,100-2,300).
  • 2026 group capex cut to US$103.3m from US$178.9m, mainly on Bilboes timing (growth capex there reduced to US$48.0m from US$132.1m); company says no change to project scope, cost or timetable.

headline: Caledonia Q2 revenue up 16% to US$75.9m on a stronger gold price, with 2026 cost guidance raised, capex cut and production re-affirmed.
priority_reason: Half-year and Q2 results with revised cost, capex and dividend news for an AIM/NYSE gold miner.

figures.basis: excluding US$11.5m fair-value gain and prior-year US$8.5m solar-plant sale gain

figures.metric: Net cash generated from operating activities

guidance.previous: On-mine costs US$1,500-1,700/oz sold; AISC US$2,100-2,300/oz sold; 2026 group capex US$178.9m; Blanket production 72,000-76,500oz.
guidance.current: On-mine costs US$1,600-1,800/oz sold; AISC US$2,500-2,700/oz sold; 2026 group capex reduced to US$103.3m; Blanket production re-affirmed at 72,000-76,500oz.
guidance.commentary: Cost guidance was raised — most notably AISC by around US$400/oz — reflecting higher royalties, US$4m of preparation for possible Blanket oxide mining, treatment of Blanket employee-trust dividends as labour costs, and power-line spend. Production guidance was maintained and 2026 capex was cut sharply, chiefly because Bilboes long-lead-equipment deposit timing pushes spend out; the company stresses this is timing, not a change to Bilboes' scope, cost or schedule.

explainer:
The headline growth is largely price-driven: the average realised gold price jumped 34% year on year to US$4,259/oz, lifting revenue, gross profit and EBITDA by 16% even though the number of ounces sold was lower than the record Q2 2025 quarter. The sequential story is more operational — production rose 18% versus Q1 2026 as Blanket accessed higher-grade areas, and management expects further improvement in H2 2026.

Be careful comparing the profit lines. Reported EBITDA of US$45.8m includes an US$11.5m non-cash gain from revaluing derivatives, and last year's comparative included a one-off US$8.5m gain on selling a solar plant. Stripping both out, underlying profit after tax rose 23% to US$18.5m — a cleaner measure of the trading performance.

On guidance, costs are heading higher: AISC guidance rose about US$400/oz to US$2,500-2,700/oz and on-mine costs to US$1,600-1,800/oz. Some of this is presentational — dividends to the Blanket employee ownership trust (which holds 10%) are now booked as labour costs — but there is also real spend on royalties, oxide-mining preparation and power infrastructure. Production guidance for 2026 is unchanged at 72,000-76,500oz.

The 2026 capex cut, from US$178.9m to US$103.3m, looks large but is mostly deferred Bilboes growth spend (down to US$48.0m from US$132.1m) driven by the timing of equipment deposits rather than any reduction in the project. Net cash of US$167.8m, up from just US$8.2m a year ago after the US$130m convertible note issue, gives Caledonia flexibility to fund Bilboes, and a quarterly dividend of 14 US cents was maintained.

guidance.previous: FY 2026 revenue guidance as previously communicated (specific prior figure not stated in this announcement)

guidance.commentary: FY 2026 revenue guidance has been cut, driven by clients deferring or delaying selected programmes, a larger client changing its procurement strategy and approval pathway, and a 6-month delay to operational readiness at the Durham, NC site. Lower revenues also compress the FY 2026 EBITDA margin via reduced cost absorption; medium and long-term ambitions are reiterated unchanged.

explainer:
Oxford Biomedica is a contract manufacturer (a CDMO) for cell and gene therapies. Its revenue depends on clients placing and ramping up orders, so timing shifts in a handful of large programmes can move the full-year outturn materially. H1 revenue still grew about 9% to c.£80m, and the company stresses that demand indicators — 17 new clients, a c.£193m backlog and a pipeline up c.30% — remain strong. The issue is timing, not lost demand: some clients are taking a staged approach and taking longer to convert contracts into billed work.

The key change is the FY 2026 revenue guidance, now set at £180-200m. Management attributes the cut to deferred or delayed programmes, one larger client altering its procurement and approval route, and a six-month delay in getting the Durham, North Carolina site operational (now said to be back on track with its first GMP run underway).

Because a manufacturing business carries largely fixed operating costs, lower revenue means those costs are spread over a smaller base, so the FY 2026 EBITDA margin is guided to only mid-single-digit % excluding one-offs (low-single-digit % on a reported basis). This still represents progress on profitability, just less than previously expected.

Importantly, the medium and long-term targets are unchanged: FY 2027 revenue growth of 25-30% with at least double-digit EBITDA margins, and an ambition for around £500m of revenue by 2030 with margins trending toward c.30%. Full detail follows at the interim results on 22 September 2026.

Record GMV of $453.0m (+10%) alongside revenue of $129.6m (+8%) shows the platform is handling more goods while taking a broadly stable cut; the faster 17% rise in completed transactions points to more, smaller deals and growing buyer/seller adoption.

The growth is 'reported' year-on-year (Q3 FY26 vs Q3 FY25). Management stresses an asset-light model, where more goods are sold on consignment rather than bought and resold — this lifts margins but can make revenue grow more slowly than GMV.

The Q4 FY26 outlook is qualitative only: no dollar ranges, but ratio guidance implying consignment GMV in the mid-eighties percent of total, revenue at mid-twenties percent of GMV and segment direct profit at mid-fifties percent of revenue — a richer margin mix. Notably, the company expects sequentially lower GMV and revenue in Retail, cushioned by stronger Capital Assets Group project work. The supplied text omitted the GAAP/non-GAAP EPS and net income tables, so profit-per-share cannot be verified here.

body:
• Diageo Capital Markets Day sets out FY27 and medium-term (FY27–FY29) guidance alongside a c.$1 billion three-year cost-savings programme.
  • Savings split c.$850m from operating framework redesign (c.40% in FY27, balance FY28) and c.$150m from supply chain (c.25% in FY27); total restructuring costs c.$1.2bn, of which c.$752m was incurred in FY26.
  • FY27 guidance: broadly flat organic net sales (North America down mid-single-digit, assuming the market down c.3%), organic operating profit up low-to-mid-single-digit, and free cash flow of c.$2bn.
  • Medium-term (FY27–FY29) CAGR guidance: low-single-digit organic net sales growth, mid-single-digit organic operating profit growth, EPS growth ahead of profit growth, and cumulative free cash flow of c.$8bn.
  • Expects to end FY27 around the mid-point of its 2.5–3.0x net debt/EBITDA leverage range, assuming completion of the EABL and Royal Challengers Bengaluru transactions.
  • CEO Sir Dave Lewis flags North America as the key priority, targeting improved performance "without taking a step back in operating profit".
headline: Diageo unveils c.$1bn three-year savings plan and guides to broadly flat FY27 organic net sales with low-to-mid-single-digit operating profit growth.
priority_reason: Capital Markets Day sets out new FY27 and medium-term guidance, a c.$1bn cost-savings programme and leverage targets — all market-moving.

figures.note: includes c.40% of c.$850m operating framework savings

figures.basis: after c.$800m + c.$50m exceptional cash costs
c.$850m operating framework + c.$150m supply chain
assumes EABL and Royal Challengers Bengaluru transactions complete

guidance.previous: No formal FY27 or medium-term financial guidance previously quantified in this announcement; three strategic priorities set out at the half year.
guidance.current: FY27: broadly flat organic net sales, organic operating profit up low-to-mid-single-digit, free cash flow c.$2bn, leverage around mid-point of 2.5–3.0x. Medium term (FY27–FY29 CAGR): low-single-digit organic net sales growth, mid-single-digit organic operating profit growth, EPS growth ahead of operating profit (currency neutral), cumulative free cash flow c.$8bn.
guidance.commentary: Diageo introduces fresh quantified FY27 and three-year targets, underpinned by a c.$1bn cost-savings programme, while flagging continued weakness in North America (organic net sales down mid-single-digit in FY27) as the drag on group growth.

explainer:
This is guidance from Diageo's Capital Markets Day rather than a set of results, so the numbers are forward-looking targets, not reported figures. "Organic" growth strips out the effect of acquisitions, disposals and currency movements, giving a like-for-like view of the underlying business. On that basis Diageo expects FY27 (its financial year to 30 June 2027) group net sales to be broadly flat, held back by North America — its largest market — where it assumes the overall market shrinks about 3% but its own share performance improves.

The headline self-help measure is roughly $1bn of cost savings over three years: about $850m from redesigning the operating model and about $150m from the supply chain. Delivering these carries a cash cost — c.$1.2bn of restructuring, much of it (c.$752m) already booked in FY26 — which is why free cash flow guidance of c.$2bn in FY27 and c.$8bn cumulatively over FY27–FY29 is stated after those exceptional cash outflows.

The medium-term framework (FY27–FY29 compound annual growth rates) points to a gradual recovery: low-single-digit organic net sales growth accelerating as North America stabilises, mid-single-digit operating profit growth helped by the cost savings and better product mix, and EPS growing faster still on a currency-neutral basis. Leverage is targeted around the middle of the 2.5–3.0x net debt/EBITDA range by the end of FY27, conditional on completing the EABL and Royal Challengers Bengaluru disposals.

In short, Diageo is asking investors to accept a near-flat FY27 top line in exchange for margin-led profit growth from cost cutting, with the North American turnaround the key swing factor for whether the medium-term targets are met.

explainer:
Reported revenue growth of 10.4% (9.3% in constant currency) is flattered and depressed by two prior-year items. The year-ago quarter included a $16m one-off from copyright infringement settlements (the 'Copyright Settlement'), while the ongoing loss of the BMG distribution deal removed $10m of digital revenue this year. Stripping both out, the underlying comparison is stronger at +12.1% (11.0% cc). 'Constant currency' simply removes the effect of exchange-rate moves, giving a cleaner view of organic growth.

The eye-catching net income swing — $200m profit versus a $16m loss last year — is mostly non-operating. Last year's quarter was hit by large foreign-exchange losses on the company's Euro-denominated debt and intercompany loans, plus a $70m impairment tied to its EMP business; those did not recur. The better underlying-profit signal is Adjusted OIBDA (a music-industry cash earnings measure), up 16.1% to $433m with margin widening to 23.2%.

On guidance, nothing was raised or cut: the CFO reiterated WMG is 'on track to meet the high end' of its FY26 margin expansion targets, which counts as maintained/reaffirmed rather than an upgrade. Cash generation improved sharply, with Free Cash Flow of $114m against just $7m a year earlier, helped by stronger trading and lower capex.

Note WMG reports in US dollars and is NASDAQ-listed, so figures are in $, not £. The Board also declared its regular $0.20 quarterly dividend, unchanged and routine alongside the results.

priority_reason: Quarterly results with production, cost, cash-flow and guidance detail — market-moving for the stock.

guidance.previous: Gibraltar 110–115m lb; Florence Copper 30–35m lb for 2026
guidance.current: Gibraltar 110–115m lb; Florence Copper 30–35m lb for 2026 (unchanged)
guidance.commentary: Full-year 2026 production guidance is reaffirmed for both operations. Management flags margin upside now the US$5.40 copper collars have matured (June) and continued strong molybdenum by-product credits, partly offset by roughly US$0.15/lb higher H2 Gibraltar costs from elevated diesel prices.

explainer:
This is a quarterly (Q2 2026) operating and financial update from a copper producer whose main revenue comes from the Gibraltar mine, with the new Florence Copper in-situ recovery operation in Arizona now ramping up. Adjusted EBITDA (a non-GAAP measure of underlying cash earnings) of $125m and $183m of operating cash flow reflect record copper prices rather than a like-for-like comparative, which the announcement does not print — so no year-on-year change can be verified for those headline figures.

The standout comparative is consolidated copper production of 36m lb, up 80% on Q2 2025, split between steadier Gibraltar output and Florence Copper's first full production quarter (5.2m lb, up from 1.5m lb in the previous quarter). Note the Florence comparison is sequential (quarter-on-quarter), not year-on-year, because the plant only recently started up.

Unit costs improved markedly: C1 cash costs fell to US$2.41/lb from US$3.14/lb a year earlier, mainly because higher volumes and larger molybdenum by-product credits (moly is sold alongside copper and its revenue is netted off the copper cost) outweighed higher diesel and explosives prices linked to Middle East conflict.

Guidance is maintained: 2026 targets of 110–115m lb (Gibraltar) and 30–35m lb (Florence) are unchanged. The key forward signal is margin leverage — the US$5.40/lb copper price collars that had capped upside matured in June, so realisations should now track spot copper more fully, though H2 Gibraltar costs are expected to run about US$0.15/lb higher on diesel.

explainer:
Michael Page (formerly PageGroup) reports two versions of its top line: in reported currency revenue was flat (+0.1%) and gross profit fell 1.1%, but stripping out favourable currency moves ('constant currency') both were weaker — revenue down 1.9% and gross profit down 2.4%. For a recruiter, gross profit (net fee income) is the key measure of activity, so the underlying trend is still mildly negative even though the headline revenue looks flat.

Operating profit jumped from £2.1m to £9.7m, but the comparison is flattered by one-off costs: H1 2025 carried around £13m of exceptional charges, versus only about £2.5m of senior-exit costs this half. On an underlying basis the conversion rate (operating profit as a share of gross profit) actually fell from 3.8% a year ago to 2.5%, so profitability is lower once the distortions are removed. The company expects a similar c.£2.5m of one-off costs again in H2.

The most market-relevant decision is the dividend: the interim payout has been cut by roughly three-quarters, from 5.36p to 1.46p, as the Board prioritises balance-sheet strength and investment in growth areas while trading stays weak. The group has also swung from net cash of £10.8m to net debt of £7.2m, partly reflecting £10.0m of dividends paid in the period.

On guidance, nothing has changed: the Board still expects full-year 2026 operating profit of about £28m, in line with the consensus it compiles. Roughly half its markets returned to growth in H1 — led by Asia Pacific, the Americas and a Q2 recovery in Southern Europe — while France, Northern Europe and the UK remained difficult, and management stresses continued uncertainty for the rest of the year.

On guidance, the important change is the net-inflows target: Quilter has moved from a fixed 4-5%-through-the-cycle goal to an open-ended aim of continuing to beat peers, reflecting its recent share gains. • Wizz Air reported a net loss for Q1 F27 (three months to 30 June 2026), driven by a 21% rise in unit fuel costs.
  • Revenue €1,507.4m, up 5.5% YoY; passengers carried 21.2m, up 25.1% YoY; ASKs up 14.9%, seats up 25.4%.
  • RASK down 8% YoY reflecting rapid capacity growth; ex-fuel CASK down circa 2%.
  • Strong balance sheet: cash €2,212.2m (up 4.0% vs 31 March 2026), liquidity ratio 36.9%; net debt €5,134.5m, leverage 4.4x (vs 3.7x at F26 year-end).
  • Guidance: Q2 RASK down low single digits, Q2 ASKs up circa 20% YoY, Q2 fuel CASK up mid-to-high single digits.
  • Moody's cut the rating to Ba3 (from Ba2, stable); GTF-grounded aircraft down to 27 (from 41), expected 15-20 by end-F27 and zero by end-2027.
headline: Wizz Air posts a Q1 net loss as a 21% rise in unit fuel costs and 8% RASK decline offset 25% passenger growth to 21.2m.
priority_reason: Quarterly results showing a net loss, with near-term RASK and fuel cost guidance for Q2.

figures.note: Q1 F27, three months to 30 June 2026

figures.current: net loss (amount not stated in text)

guidance.current: Q2 ASKs up circa 20% YoY, seats up high twenties percent; Q2 RASK down low single digits (supported by stage length reduction); Q2 fuel CASK up mid-to-high single digits (based on current market prices).
guidance.commentary: Wizz Air issued near-term Q2 F27 guidance pointing to continued strong capacity growth but softer unit revenue and rising fuel unit costs. Current trading indicates Q2 RASK down low single digits, an improvement on Q1's 8% decline, helped by shorter average stage lengths.

explainer:
This is a first-quarter update covering the three months to 30 June 2026, Wizz Air's F27 financial year. The headline tension is that traffic is growing fast — passengers up 25% and seats up over 25% — but revenue only rose 5.5%, because RASK (revenue per available seat kilometre, a measure of how much each unit of capacity earns) fell around 8%. Adding lots of capacity into a volatile market dilutes yields, so revenue grows far more slowly than passenger numbers.

The reported net loss was driven mainly by fuel: unit fuel costs rose 21% year-on-year, reflecting higher jet-fuel prices and Middle East disruption. Encouragingly, ex-fuel CASK (cost per seat kilometre excluding fuel) fell about 2%, showing the underlying cost base is improving as airport and labour costs per unit come down with scale.

The balance sheet remains a strength: over €2.2bn of cash and a 36.9% liquidity ratio, among the strongest in the sector. However, net debt rose to €5.13bn and leverage climbed to 4.4x (from 3.7x) as ten new aircraft were delivered, and Moody's downgraded the rating one notch to Ba3 citing weaker FY2026 profitability and GTF-related inefficiencies.

On guidance, this is fresh near-term outlook rather than a change to a prior number. For Q2, Wizz expects capacity (ASKs) up around 20%, RASK down only low single digits — a smaller decline than Q1 — helped by shorter stage lengths as it shifts flying from the Middle East to European routes, while fuel unit costs are still expected to rise mid-to-high single digits.

That squeezes the current-period loss and expense ratios, but the hit is cushioned by larger prior-year reserve releases — money set aside for past claims that is no longer needed — which rose to 17.3% of premium from 12.6%.

The dividend cut looks dramatic (70.5p versus 115.0p) but reflects two things: lower earnings per share (the normal dividend is down 18%, in line with EPS), and a change in how Admiral returns cash. It has modestly lowered its UK Motor reserve prudence (93rd percentile versus 94th at year-end), a deliberate drift toward the middle of its stated 85th–95th corridor rather than a signal of weakening reserves.

priority_reason: Half-year results accompanied by lowered 2026 NIM and RoTE guidance and a CEO handover.

figures.note: H1 2026 vs H1 2025; down 3bps vs H2 2025 (226bps)
H1 2026 vs H1 2025; core admin expenses down 0.4%

guidance.previous: Prior 2026 NIM guidance above current range and 2026 RoTE guidance above c.12.5%; mid-teens RoTE aspiration for 2027
guidance.current: 2026 net interest margin now expected at 215-220bps; 2026 RoTE now c.12.5% (both assuming elevated cost of funds continue and excluding incoming-CEO costs); administrative expenses still c.£280m ex-CEO costs; net loan book growth guidance unchanged
guidance.commentary: OSB lowered its 2026 NIM and RoTE guidance because it now conservatively assumes that strong competition in retail savings and elevated retail funding costs will not ease. It also flagged a possible modest hit to its 2027 mid-teens RoTE aspiration if funding cost pressures persist, while reaffirming longer-term 2028-2029 aspirations and loan book growth guidance.

explainer:
OSB is a specialist lender funded largely by retail savings deposits. Its profitability hinges on the net interest margin — the gap between what it earns on mortgages and what it pays savers. In H1 2026 that margin narrowed to 223bps from 230bps a year earlier, because fierce competition for deposits pushed up funding costs faster than the yield on new lending, and older, higher-yielding mortgages continued to roll off the back book.

The headline of this update is the guidance cut. Management now expects full-year 2026 NIM of just 215-220bps and RoTE of about 12.5%, having previously guided higher. The key word is 'conservative': OSB is assuming these elevated funding costs will NOT ease for the rest of the year, so the downgrade reflects a cautious planning assumption rather than a confirmed deterioration. Cost guidance (c.£280m admin expenses) and net loan book growth guidance are unchanged.

Two other moving parts are worth noting. The impairment charge leapt to £15.8m from just £2.0m a year ago — a rise from a very low base that lifted the loan loss ratio to 12bps, still modest in absolute terms. And core administrative expenses actually fell 0.4%; the reported rise in total costs is driven by continued spending on the transformation programme.

Separately, this is Andy Golding's final results as CEO after 14 years; Enrique Alvarez Labiano takes over on 1 September 2026. The dividend was still raised 5% to 11.8p, signalling board confidence despite the margin squeeze.

• Q2 2026 Adjusted EBITDA of US$125.1m (US$17.4m a year earlier); revenues US$330.6m vs US$116.1m, driven by record copper prices and higher volumes.
  • Consolidated production 36m lbs copper, up 80% year-on-year; Gibraltar produced 30.3m lbs at C1 cost of US$2.41/lb (down from US$3.14), Florence Copper added 5.2m lbs in its first full quarter.
  • Net income US$22.2m (US$0.06/share); Adjusted net income US$40.5m (US$0.11/share) vs a US$13.0m loss last year; operating cash flow US$183.4m.
  • Realised copper price US$6.10/lb; copper collars capped at US$5.40/lb matured in June, causing a US$24.2m derivative loss but freeing upside — Q3 ceilings now US$7.50–8.50/lb, no ceiling from Q4.
  • Production guidance unchanged: Gibraltar 110–115m lbs, Florence Copper 30–35m lbs for 2026.
  • Yellowhead permitting advanced: BC EAO issued a positive Readiness Decision and Notice of Decision to proceed to environmental assessment; liquidity US$342m including undrawn revolver, cash US$186m at 30 June.
headline: Trekor posts record Q2 with adjusted EBITDA of US$125m as revenues nearly triple to US$331m on record copper prices and 80% higher output.
priority_reason: Q2 results with record copper prices, an 80% production jump and new output from Florence Copper.

figures.note: Q2 2026, prior period was a loss

guidance.previous: Gibraltar 110 to 115 million pounds; Florence Copper 30 to 35 million pounds
guidance.current: Gibraltar 110 to 115 million pounds; Florence Copper 30 to 35 million pounds
guidance.commentary: Full-year 2026 copper production guidance for both Gibraltar and Florence Copper is unchanged. Gibraltar costs are expected to run roughly US$0.15/lb higher in H2 versus the prior year on elevated diesel prices.

explainer:
This is a second-quarter update from a copper miner reported in US dollars. The headline growth looks dramatic — revenues nearly tripling and Adjusted EBITDA rising from US$17m to US$125m — because it combines three tailwinds: record copper prices (a realised US$6.10/lb at Gibraltar), a large jump in output (consolidated production up 80% year-on-year), and first output from the new Florence Copper operation. Adjusted EBITDA and adjusted net income are non-GAAP measures that strip out depletion, amortisation and one-off items, which is why adjusted profit (US$40.5m) is much larger than reported net income (US$22.2m).

Reported net income was almost flat year-on-year (US$22.2m vs US$21.9m) despite the revenue surge, largely because the prior-year quarter included favourable items and this quarter carried a US$24.2m derivative loss. That loss came from copper 'collar' hedges that capped the price the company could realise at US$5.40/lb; with copper trading well above that, the cap cost money as it matured in June. The important forward point is that these caps have now expired — Q3 ceilings rise to US$7.50–8.50/lb and there is no ceiling from Q4 — so the company keeps more upside if copper prices stay high.

On costs, Gibraltar's C1 unit cost fell to US$2.41/lb from US$3.14/lb, helped by higher production and stronger molybdenum by-product credits (US$0.65/lb), partly offset by higher diesel and explosives costs linked to Middle East conflict. Management flags that diesel could add roughly US$0.15/lb to H2 costs versus last year.

Guidance is maintained, not changed: full-year production targets of 110–115m lbs at Gibraltar and 30–35m lbs at Florence Copper are unchanged. The growth story from here rests on ramping up Florence Copper's wellfield and advancing permitting at the Yellowhead project, which cleared an early BC regulatory milestone.

WPP reports on a like-for-like (LFL) basis, which strips out currency movements and the effect of acquisitions and disposals to show underlying trading. On that basis H1 revenue fell 3.2%, a smaller drop than the 4.4% reported (sterling) decline. The company's preferred profitability measure is 'revenue less pass-through costs' — net revenue after billed-through media and production costs — which fell 4.7% LFL to £4,745m. The key story is sequential improvement: the Q2 net-revenue decline of 2.8% LFL was better than Q1, helped by easing prior-year comparisons and a smaller drag from lost accounts, particularly at WPP Media.

Margins moved in opposite directions depending on the measure. The 'headline' margin (which excludes items like severance and impairments) edged up 0.2 points to 8.4% on lower staff and severance costs. Reported operating profit jumped 18.1% to £261m, but that was largely because the prior period carried much heavier impairment charges rather than a genuine trading gain.

On guidance, nothing changed: WPP reaffirmed a full-year headline operating margin of 12%-13% and cash flow before working capital of £800m-£900m. Management flagged that H2 margins could fall by up to around 200 basis points year-on-year as it phases in spending on growth initiatives and rebuilds employee incentives — so the full-year figure implies a stronger-margin first half offset by a heavier-investment second half.

The dividend was held flat at 7.5p interim (15.0p intended for the full year), signalling the board's confidence in cash generation despite falling revenue, while the Elevate28 restructuring targets £500m of gross annualised cost savings by 2028 and over £200m of disposal proceeds this year.

figures.note: H1 to 30 June 2026; includes $33.6m Zurich transaction costs

guidance.commentary: No explicit numeric earnings or premium guidance is quoted in this statement; management flags continued market softening and disciplined underwriting, with the Zurich acquisition expected to close before year-end.

explainer:
These are half-year results for the six months to 30 June 2026, reported in US dollars. The headline is a sharp fall in profit before tax, down 53% to $237.7m, driven by a 'softer' insurance market (falling premium rates, down 6.5% on average) and a return to a more active large-loss environment after several benign years. All the comparatives are versus the same period in 2025, on a reported basis, with no currency-adjusted or organic restatement given.

The combined ratio measures underwriting profitability — claims and costs as a percentage of premiums, so below 100% means an underwriting profit. Beazley's undiscounted combined ratio worsened from 84.9% to 93.3%, meaning underwriting is still profitable but markedly less so. The $33.6m of Zurich takeover costs sit outside the combined ratio (they are not underwriting costs), so they depress reported profit but not the underwriting metrics.

Premiums fell 4% partly by choice: Beazley says it is deliberately pulling back from lines where prices no longer reflect the risk, notably North American cyber and property. explainer:
This is not a results announcement but a material operational update. Ferrexpo mines and processes iron ore in Ukraine, and the war has repeatedly disrupted its ability to ship product out through Black Sea ports. Attacks in and around Ukrainian ports have now restricted export routes so severely that the company has chosen to halt production entirely rather than keep mining ore it cannot ship and burn through cash doing so.

The critical figure is the cash runway: management states that, without new funding, net accessible cash resources last only until mid-September 2026. That is a going-concern-style warning — the business needs an injection of working capital both to keep operating and to restart production. Restarting is explicitly conditional on that funding.

The vessel incident referenced from 28 July 2026 involves a third-party ship carrying Ferrexpo's DR-grade pellets; it has now been recovered from the war-risk zone and is being towed to port for inspection, so the cargo's condition is not yet known.

Several caveats compound the risk: iron ore price volatility, energy and operating costs, suspended VAT refunds in Ukraine, and ongoing legal proceedings involving Ferrexpo Poltava Mining. For now European customers can be served from existing stockpiles, but those inventories are finite while production is paused.

• Standard Chartered PLC reported record H1 2026 profit before tax of $4.8bn, up 9 per cent, with EPS up 17 per cent to 151.6 cents.
  • Record operating income of $11.6bn, up 6 per cent (up 8 per cent excluding the prior-year Solv India gain); Wealth Solutions up 38 per cent and Global Banking up 19 per cent.
  • New $1.0bn share buyback commencing imminently (after the $1.5bn buyback done in H1); interim dividend up 66 per cent to 20.4 cents per share ($448m).
  • Upgraded 2026 income guidance: operating income growth now seen around the middle of the 5-7 per cent range at constant currency; expenses ex-notables around $13.3bn.
  • CET1 ratio of 14.2 per cent (up 77bps q/q); RoTE broadly flat at 17.9 per cent in Q2; credit impairment of $446m including a $234m Middle East management overlay.
  • CEO Bill Winters cited a "record first half" and "confidence in the business"; comparisons stated on a constant-currency basis unless noted.
headline: Standard Chartered posted record H1 pre-tax profit of $4.8bn, up 9%, lifted income guidance and launched a new $1.0bn share buyback.
priority_reason: Half-year results with a record profit, upgraded income guidance and a new $1.0bn buyback — market-moving for the shares.

figures.basis: 26bps annualised loss rate; incl. $234m Middle East overlay

figures.metric: Tangible net asset value per share

guidance.previous: Prior 2026 income guidance not restated in this text (income growth range referenced as 5-7 per cent).
guidance.current: Operating income growth year-on-year to be around the middle of the 5-7 per cent range at constant currency, excluding material notables; within which NII expected to show low single-digit percentage growth; expenses excluding notables around $13.3bn at constant currency.
guidance.commentary: Management describes the income guidance as 'upgraded'/'revised', now pointing to the middle of the 5-7% range, reflecting momentum in Wealth Solutions and Global Banking. The new $1.0bn buyback signals confidence alongside the guidance change.

explainer:
These are half-year figures for the six months to 30 June 2026, reported in US dollars. Standard Chartered presents growth on a constant-currency basis — stripping out exchange-rate moves — so the headline percentage changes reflect underlying business trends rather than currency swings. Several comparisons are also shown 'excluding the Solv India transaction', a $238m one-off gain booked in Q2 2025; excluding it, underlying income growth looks stronger (8% for the half rather than 6%), because the prior-year base was flattered by that disposal gain.

On guidance, the bank says it has upgraded its 2026 income outlook: it now expects operating income growth around the middle of the 5-7% range at constant currency (excluding material notable items), driven by Wealth Solutions (up 38%) and Global Banking (up 19%). Net interest income — earnings from lending margins — is guided to only low single-digit growth, as lower interest rates offset higher volumes, so the growth story is increasingly fee-led. Costs excluding notables are guided to about $13.3bn.

The $446m credit impairment charge includes a $234m 'management overlay' for Middle East-related exposures — a precautionary provision set aside against potential future losses from the regional conflict, not actual defaults incurred. Capital returns step up: the interim dividend rises 66% and a new $1.0bn buyback follows the $1.5bn already completed in H1, funded by strong profit generation and a CET1 ratio of 14.2%.

explainer:
These are unaudited interim results for the six months to 30 June 2026. 'System sales' is the total sales generated by franchise partners across the network, from which the Group earns an average management service fee of about 15%; statutory revenue is the Group's own recognised income. Note that the prior-year system sales figure was restated upward from £209.4m to £214.9m because certain Pirtek directly-operated (DLO) operations had not previously been counted, so the 6.7% growth is measured against the restated base.

The gap between adjusted and statutory numbers is significant. Adjusted profit before tax (£12.6m) strips out amortisation of acquired intangibles, share-based payments and non-recurring items, and rose a modest 7.8%. Statutory PBT (£8.4m) jumped 42%, and basic EPS 45%, largely because those below-the-line charges were smaller than a year earlier, flattering the reported growth rate versus the underlying adjusted trend.

Deleveraging is a key theme: adjusted net debt fell £9.2m to £52.9m, cutting leverage to 1.5x from 1.8x, helped by strong cash conversion (81%) and a lower interest charge. The dividend was raised 9% to 1.25p, reflecting the cash-generative franchise model.

On guidance, the Group maintained its outlook: full-year performance is expected in line with market expectations, defined as FY26 adjusted EBITDA of £35.9m to £38.0m. Management is deliberately cautious, assuming no improvement in market conditions in H2, so confidence rests on self-help measures — the One Franchise Brands platform, cost control and the essential nature of the services — rather than any macro recovery.

headline: Shaftesbury Capital's H1 portfolio valuation rose 3.4% like-for-like to £5.6bn, with underlying earnings up 8% and the interim dividend raised 16%.
priority_reason: Half-year results from a FTSE-250 REIT, showing valuation, earnings and dividend progression.

guidance.current: Remains confident in achieving medium-term targets
guidance.commentary: No numerical change to guidance; management reiterated confidence in its medium-term targets, supported by a strong leasing pipeline, high occupancy and a robust balance sheet.

explainer:
This is a half-year (six months to 30 June 2026) results statement from a central London mixed-use REIT. The headline valuation and rental figures are quoted 'like-for-like', meaning they strip out the effect of acquisitions and disposals so the underlying portfolio's movement can be compared cleanly with the prior period. Property-level figures such as the £5.6bn valuation and £281m ERV are stated at 100% of the portfolio under management; the Group's own share is lower because the Covent Garden estate has been 75%-owned since the NBIM partnership was established on 1 April 2025, with NBIM's 25% shown as a non-controlling interest under IFRS.

ERV (estimated rental value) is the market rent the portfolio could achieve; the company notes that ERV is 28% above current passing rent, indicating scope to lift income as leases are renewed. New leasing completing 18% ahead of previous passing rents and 5% ahead of December 2025 ERV shows the company is capturing that reversion. EPRA NTA (net tangible assets) of 223p is the industry-standard measure of a REIT's underlying net asset value per share, up 8p on the back of the valuation uplift.

On guidance, there is no change to the numbers: the company reiterates confidence in its unchanged medium-term targets. The 16% dividend increase and 8% rise in underlying earnings reflect rental growth and cost efficiencies (the cost ratio fell to 32% from 33%), rather than any reset of the outlook.

figures.note: H1; beyond Investec W&I integration phase

guidance.previous: Q4 operating margin target of 30.0%
guidance.current: Q4 operating margin target revised to 28.7%
guidance.commentary: The target was cut by 1.3 percentage points because Rathbones will stop charging fees on the cash element of client portfolios — an action arising from the FCA Skilled Person Review — reducing H2 income and operating profit by c.£9m. The Group says it remains on track to hit the revised target, subject to FUMA growth, inflation and interest-rate conditions, and its progressive dividend policy is unchanged.

explainer:
The headline profit growth is on an 'underlying' basis, an alternative performance measure that strips out one-off and non-recurring items. Underlying PBT rose 14.4% to £123.2m, but statutory (reported) PBT was much lower at £72.1m because it includes £19.0m of costs tied to the FCA Skilled Person Review and £9.5m of acquisition/integration costs from the earlier Investec Wealth & Investment deal. Those integration costs are falling as expected and are due to cease during 2027.

FUMA (funds under management and administration) grew 10.7% year on year to £120.7bn, but net client flows were weak: the group saw £0.9bn of net outflows over the half. Wealth Management turned positive in Q2 (net inflows of £0.4bn) after Q1 outflows, leaving it broadly neutral for the half, while Asset Management kept losing money to industry-wide pressure on active equity funds.

The key guidance change is the Q4 operating margin target being lowered from 30.0% to 28.7%. This is a direct consequence of the remediation following the FCA Skilled Person Review: Rathbones will stop charging fees on the cash held in client portfolios, which it expects to reduce income and operating profit by about £9m in the second half, trimming the H2 underlying margin by 1.3 percentage points. Lower technology costs after the Salesforce rollout completes are expected to partly cushion H2.

Despite the margin cut, shareholder returns were increased: the interim dividend was raised 3.2% to 32.0p, and a £20m buyback (following an earlier £50m programme) concluded on 13 July 2026.

These are half-year figures for the six months to 30 June 2026, compared with the same period in 2025. headline: Greatland beat FY26 production and cost guidance, producing 328,987oz gold at AISC $2,179/oz and closing the year debt-free with $1,289m cash.
priority_reason: Quarterly production report with FY26 guidance beat, a large reserve upgrade and new FY27 guidance — all price-sensitive inside information.

guidance.current: FY27 guidance: 260,000–300,000oz Au at AISC A$2,900–3,330/oz
guidance.commentary: FY26 outcomes beat both production and cost guidance. Newly issued FY27 guidance points to lower volumes and materially higher unit costs, primarily due to a greater share of lower-grade stockpiles in the ore feed and a heavy year of growth investment at Havieron and Telfer's West Dome Underground.

explainer:
This is Greatland's June quarter (Q4) report, which also closes out its FY26 financial year to 30 June 2026. The company beat both its production and cost guidance: it produced 328,987oz of gold for the year against a 260,000–310,000oz target, and did so at an all-in sustaining cost (AISC) of $2,179/oz, below the $2,400–2,800/oz guided range. AISC is the industry's broad per-ounce cost measure, here shown net of copper by-product credits — Telfer is a gold-copper mine, so copper sales offset gold costs.

The balance sheet is the standout: strong gold and copper prices, better-than-budgeted recoveries and a better realised copper price lifted cash to $1,289m at year-end, up from $1,208m a quarter earlier, with no drawn debt. Greatland added $714m of cash over the year. Note the reporting currency is dollars; the FY27 AISC guidance is explicitly quoted in Australian dollars (A$2,900–3,330/oz).

FY27 guidance is deliberately lower and more expensive: 260,000–300,000oz at AISC A$2,900–3,330/oz. This is not a deterioration in the asset — the company is feeding a higher proportion of lower-grade stockpiles while it invests heavily in future high-grade ore sources. Costs rise partly because grade falls and partly because FY27 is a peak growth-spend year (Havieron pre-production capital, West Dome Underground early works, fleet renewal and tailings expansion).

Two resource items add strategic weight: the Telfer reserve was upgraded 150% to 1.8Moz, taking group reserves to 5.0Moz and underpinning a multi-year mine life, and high-grade Pinnacles drilling extended the West Dome structure. First gold is targeted at West Dome Underground in FY28 and at Havieron in FY29, framing FY27 as an investment year ahead of production growth. The dominant event is corporate rather than operational: IPF is being taken private by Bidco (linked to BasePoint Capital) at 235p per share via a court-sanctioned scheme. Regulatory approvals are now in place, the Sanction Hearing is on 31 July 2026, and the deal is expected to complete on 4 August 2026. Because of this, no interim dividend was paid; instead shareholders are due a 15p special dividend conditional on the court sanctioning the offer.

priority_reason: Q2 results with a major new 3-year cost-savings programme, R&D acceleration and reaffirmed FY guidance from a FTSE 100 pharma major.

figures.note: driven by impairments (camlipixant £1.3bn) and CCL charges

guidance.previous: FY 2026 at CER: turnover +3% to +5%; Core operating profit +7% to +9%; Core EPS +7% to +9%
guidance.current: FY 2026 reaffirmed at CER: turnover +3% to +5% (upper half of range); Core operating profit +7% to +9% (upper half); Core EPS +7% to +9% (lower half). Royalty income now expected at £850-900m; interest charges around £800m (including Nuvalent acquisition); tax rate rising to around 17.5%
guidance.commentary: Headline ranges are unchanged but GSK added specificity: turnover and Core OP now guided to the upper half of their ranges, while Core EPS is at the lower half owing to higher interest charges (including the Nuvalent deal) and a rising tax rate, partly offset by the buyback. R&D is now expected to grow significantly ahead of sales.

explainer:
GSK reports two sets of numbers. 'Total' (IFRS) results include one-off items, so the -75% operating profit and -69% EPS mainly reflect a £1.3bn write-down on the failed camlipixant lung/kidney-cancer asset plus contingent consideration (CCL) charges — not a deterioration in the underlying business. 'Core' results strip those items out, and on that basis operating profit rose 7% and EPS 9%, which is the figure management and analysts focus on.

Growth is quoted at constant exchange rates (CER), which removes currency moves. Because sterling strengthened against the US dollar, the reported (AER) figures are lower than CER for the year to date; for Q2 the two happened to match at +5%. GSK flags that if July exchange rates held, full-year sterling turnover growth would be about 2 percentage points lower and Core operating profit growth about 4 points lower than the CER guidance.

On guidance, the headline full-year ranges are unchanged (turnover +3-5%, Core OP and Core EPS both +7-9% at CER), so this is a reaffirmation rather than an upgrade. GSK did, however, sharpen the picture: turnover and Core operating profit are now expected in the upper half of their ranges, but Core EPS sits at the lower half because of roughly £800m of interest costs (including the Nuvalent acquisition) and a tax rate rising to about 17.5%, only partly cushioned by the completed £2bn buyback.

The strategic news is a new 3-year 'Accelerate Growth' restructuring programme targeting £1.9bn of annual savings by 2029 at a cost of £2.4bn, most of it reinvested into a late-stage pipeline (20+ phase III starts planned in 2026 versus 10 previously). Management frames this as protecting margins through the 2028-2030 patent expiry of HIV drug dolutegravir and underpinning its target of more than £40bn of sales by 2031.

explainer:
Unite is a student-accommodation REIT, so its results split into two very different stories. The 'adjusted' earnings measure — which strips out one-off costs and follows EPRA property-industry conventions — held up: adjusted EPS of 27.1p was only 8% lower, mainly because January's Empiric acquisition added both interest costs and extra shares before the promised cost savings arrive. The headline £417.1m IFRS loss is almost entirely a paper revaluation, not a cash loss. Rising property yields (investors demanding a higher return, which pushes valuations down) cut the value of Unite's portfolio by 6.4% on a like-for-like basis, and that write-down flows straight through the IFRS accounts. The same effect drove net asset value (EPRA NTA) down 9% to 865p and produced a negative total accounting return of 7.5% for the half.

Guidance was maintained rather than changed. Unite reaffirmed its FY2026 adjusted EPS target of 41.5-43.0p and its £300-400m disposal programme. Note that 2026/27 operational guidance points to a clear slowdown: rental growth of just 1-2% against 4.0% achieved in 2025/26, and occupancy of 94-96% versus 95.2%, reflecting a 'less certain' market even as reservations run ahead of last year.

The strategic message is a portfolio reshaping: selling 15,000-20,000 beds to concentrate on around 20 cities and the UK's strongest universities, funding development and buybacks. Higher leverage (net debt:EBITDA up to 7.5x, LTV up to 36%) largely reflects the lower asset values and the Empiric deal, and is expected to ease as disposals complete.

headline: Coats reports H1 revenue of $837m with market outperformance, maintained margins and reaffirms confidence in FY results in line with expectations.
priority_reason: Half-year results from a FTSE 250 company, with divisional detail, cash flow, net debt and reaffirmed full-year guidance.

guidance.previous: FY results in line with market expectations
guidance.current: Reaffirm confidence to deliver FY results in line with market expectations

explainer:
The headline revenue jump from $705m to $837m is flattered by acquisitions (OrthoLite and Viz Reflectives) and currency. Stripping those out, underlying 'organic' revenue grew just 1% at constant exchange rates — but that was still ahead of core apparel and footwear markets, which Coats estimates shrank by a mid-single-digit percentage as brands ran down inventory. In other words, the growth is share gain rather than a rising market.

Adjusted EBIT rose in reported terms to $166m but was actually 2% lower on an organic basis, because Coats spent more on growth and technology initiatives. The key resilience signal is the margin: adjusted EBIT margin held at 19.8%, helped by the higher-margin OrthoLite business, showing pricing and cost discipline offset inflation from the Middle East disruption.

Net debt edged up to $842m (from $815m at end-2025) mainly because the 2025 final dividend was paid in the period. Leverage of 2.3x is expected to fall to 2.0x by year end as working capital unwinds — a normal second-half seasonal cash inflow for Coats.

On guidance, nothing has changed: management reaffirms it expects full-year results in line with market expectations. The tone is cautiously confident — de-stocking has been prolonged, but Coats argues customer inventories are now lean, which could support a demand pick-up beyond what its own in-year outlook assumes.

• Ferrexpo plc reports a vessel carrying its high-grade DR-grade pellets (FDP) was struck by Russian drones in Ukrainian Black Sea waters; one crew member died and the cargo and vessel integrity are unknown.
  • Group does not expect to load additional vessels via this export route for the foreseeable future, as shipowners have cancelled vessel fixtures amid ongoing port attacks.
  • Approximately 189,000 tonnes of pellets await shipment — 55,000 tonnes of FDP on the stricken vessel and ~90,000 tonnes of FDP in stockpiles — with production/delivery cost of ~US$20 million.
  • Material negative impact on liquidity: Group now forecasts sufficient net accessible cash to operate only until end-August 2026.
  • Board continues to work towards an equity capital raise of a minimum US$100 million (the 'Intended Fundraise') to support working capital; terms to follow.
  • Forecast remains subject to iron ore pricing, energy costs, suspended VAT refunds and ongoing legal proceedings involving Ferrexpo Poltava Mining.
headline: Ferrexpo warns liquidity is materially hit after a drone strike sank an FDP-laden vessel and shut its Black Sea export route, leaving cash only to end-August 2026.
priority_reason: Vessel loss and blocked export route materially hit liquidity, with cash runway now only to end-August 2026 and a US$100m raise pending.

guidance.previous: Group had forecast increased FDP sales for export from Black Sea ports in H2 2026 (per 15 July 2026 Production Report & Trading Update)
guidance.current: Black Sea export route not available for the foreseeable future; net accessible cash forecast to last only until end-August 2026
guidance.commentary: The vessel incident and resulting fixture cancellations have removed the planned H2 2026 FDP export route, causing a material deterioration in liquidity and shortening the cash runway to end-August 2026. Management is evaluating mitigation scenarios and progressing a minimum US$100m equity raise.

explainer:
Ferrexpo mines iron ore in Ukraine and had been shifting its output towards its highest-quality 'DR-grade' pellets (FDP) for Middle East customers, exporting them through Black Sea ports. A vessel carrying about 55,000 tonnes of that product was hit by drones and one crew member was killed; the cargo may be lost and the route is now effectively closed because shipowners are cancelling bookings.

The key financial point is liquidity, not profit. Because the planned second-half FDP exports cannot ship, the company is left holding roughly 189,000 tonnes of inventory it cannot easily sell, and it now says its accessible cash only lasts until the end of August 2026 — a very short runway that signals acute funding stress.

This is why the company is pushing to launch an equity capital raise of at least US$100 million to shore up working capital. That raise is not yet live; its terms would come in a separate announcement, and the cash forecast still depends on iron ore prices, energy costs, suspended VAT refunds and unresolved legal proceedings in Ukraine. No prior-year comparative figures are given, so this is a liquidity warning rather than a full trading statement.

Constant-currency growth was 9.8%, meaning a stronger dollar/euro translation would have flattered the number; foreign exchange actually knocked 0.8% off reported revenue. Growth was organic and spread across all three regions, supported by both higher volumes and pricing.

Profitability is more nuanced. Adjusted operating margin nudged up to 10.9%, but gross margin slipped 60bps to 43.0% because of one-off Americas disruption — the transfer of manufacturing from Costa Rica to Mexico and lagging price recovery. Management expects gross margin to rebuild in H2 as Q2 pricing actions take full effect. EPS growth of 21.3% is quoted on a constant-currency basis, so the reported uplift will differ.

On guidance, the key point is that FY26 expectations are unchanged — no upgrade or downgrade despite the strong first half — because the Group is deliberately reinvesting and rebuilding variable (bonus) compensation, leaving full-year margins broadly flat even as underlying performance improves. The genuinely new item is a 2028 target of 14% adjusted operating margin, a milestone towards the existing 18% medium-term ambition. Management stresses this rests on self-help (pricing discipline, procurement, cost cuts, IT rationalisation worth c.£6-8m of cash benefit and c.150bps of margin) rather than any assumed improvement in end-markets.

headline: Yellow Cake's estimated NAV rose 0.2% to **£6.34/share** as uranium holdings grew towards **24.4m lb**, with a US$10m buyback completed post-quarter.
priority_reason: Quarterly operating update from a uranium holding company, covering NAV, holdings and market conditions.

figures.note: at 30 June 2026; rising to 24,374,996 lb after Kazatomprom delivery
24 July 2026, adjusted for Kazatomprom payment and completed buyback

explainer:
Yellow Cake is not an operating miner: it buys and holds physical uranium (U3O8) as a long-term store of value, so its NAV moves almost entirely with the uranium spot price, the size of its stockpile and the sterling/dollar rate. The figures here are quarter-on-quarter comparatives (30 June 2026 vs 31 March 2026), not year-on-year, and the uranium value is stated in US dollars while the per-share NAV is converted to sterling.

The modest 0.2% rise in NAV per share reflects three offsetting forces: a slightly higher uranium value (from an extra 100,000 lb bought and a small spot-price gain to US$84.85/lb), the accretive effect of buying back shares below NAV, and a partial drag from sterling strengthening against the dollar, which reduces the sterling value of dollar-priced uranium.

The most notable market signal is the divergence between a stable spot price (mid-US$80s/lb) and firmer long-term prices — the Ux Long-Term Price reached US$94.00/lb, up nearly 10% in the first half of 2026 — suggesting utilities are increasingly paying up to lock in future supply even as near-term trading stays subdued.

No formal earnings guidance applies to this type of vehicle; the pro forma NAV of £6.42 per share at 24 July 2026 simply reflects the completed US$10m buyback and the US$100m Kazatomprom purchase commitment already factored in.

explainer:
This is a first-quarter trading update, so Vodafone reports revenue and profit growth but does not give a full profit-and-loss comparison with prior-year figures for every line. Reported growth (e.g. total revenue +9.7%) includes the effect of consolidating Three UK following the May 2025 merger and adverse foreign-exchange movements, whereas organic growth (service revenue +5.2%) strips out acquisitions, disposals and currency to show the underlying trading trend. Türkiye figures are quoted excluding hyperinflation accounting adjustments.

The standout structural change is the Safaricom transaction, completed on 30 June 2026, which lifted the Group's effective stake to 55% and means Safaricom will be fully consolidated from 1 July 2026. The €2.9bn jump in operating profit to €3.9bn is largely a one-off gain from completing this deal rather than an improvement in underlying trading.

On guidance, the change is a re-basing rather than a straightforward upgrade: the FY27 ranges (Adjusted EBITDAaL €13.0–€13.3bn, Adjusted free cash flow €2.6–€2.9bn) now include Safaricom, which adds roughly €1.1bn of EBITDAaL over nine months but no free cash flow this year. • Q3 FY26 headline PBT of £85 million, impacted by the Middle East conflict and its effect on fuel prices and booking trends; strong late-booking demand continued but was insufficient to fully offset weaker post-conflict trends.
  • Fuel costs a £105 million headwind versus prior year on higher prices on the unhedged portion, with fuel peaking at approximately $1,800 per metric tonne in April; Q3 CASK ex fuel up 3% YoY.

  • Capacity: 29.0m seats flown (Q3 FY25: 28.7m); load factor 88.9% (90.2%); passengers broadly flat at 25.8m (25.9m). On-time performance 78% (+2ppt); airline customer satisfaction 84% (+3ppt).

headline: easyJet posts **Q3 FY26 headline PBT of £85m**, dented by the **Middle East conflict** hitting fuel prices and bookings, though late demand stayed strong.
priority_reason: Quarterly trading update from a FTSE airline, with a stated Q3 headline PBT figure, fuel/demand impact and a management board change.

figures.basis: cost per available seat km, ex fuel

guidance.current: The final outcome for FY26 remains dependent on the important remaining bookings, as well as fuel prices, which continue to be volatile.
guidance.commentary: No numeric FY26 guidance was issued or changed; management framed the outlook as dependent on peak-summer bookings and volatile fuel prices, while reiterating self-help initiatives aimed at medium-term margin and profit improvement.

explainer:
This is a Q3 trading update covering the three months to 30 June 2026, the third quarter of easyJet's financial year, which ends 30 September. It is not full results, so the company gives selected headline figures rather than a complete statutory income statement. The unaudited profit numbers are formally designated 'profit estimates' under Rule 28 of the UK Takeover Code, meaning the board has confirmed they were properly compiled — a technicality that does not imply a bid is in play.

The headline story is that group headline PBT was £85 million, held back by the Middle East conflict that began in March: it pushed up fuel prices and initially dampened bookings. Fuel alone was a £105 million year-on-year headwind, largely because the portion of fuel not hedged was exposed to prices that spiked to around $1,800 per tonne in April. Encouragingly, customers booked late and in strength, and the holidays arm proved resilient — its PBT slipped from £86m to £84m as reported, but rose 7% once adverse currency movements are stripped out, so the underlying trend was positive.

On operating metrics, easyJet flew slightly more seats (29.0m vs 28.7m) but load factor fell to 88.9% from 90.2%, meaning planes ran a little emptier as demand normalised after the conflict — passenger numbers were essentially flat. Comparisons such as CASK ex fuel (+3%) are flattered or hindered by prior-year one-offs; management notes last year benefited from a credit on buying aircraft back, so the underlying cost performance was better than the raw 3% suggests.

On guidance: there is no numeric target here to raise or cut. The outlook is deliberately cautious, hinging on the crucial peak-summer bookings still to come and on volatile fuel prices, with management pointing to self-help initiatives (new loyalty scheme in FY27, premiumisation, the Expedia hotels tie-up) as the medium-term profit drivers rather than any near-term figure.

priority_reason: Trading update guiding full-year profit 10-15% below last year — effectively a profit warning.

guidance.previous: not stated
guidance.current: Sales marginally below the 2025 comparative; profit approximately 10-15% below that of last year
guidance.commentary: First indication of FY26 outturn ahead of September results, signalling a profit decline of 10-15% driven by Iran-conflict input-cost surcharges the Company partly absorbed and soft LVT demand in Europe and Australia, despite UK market-share gains and strong Middle East and South Africa growth.

explainer:
This is a pre-close trading update: James Halstead is flagging how the year to 30 June 2026 has gone before it reports full audited results in late September. Its guidance is that sales will be a touch below last year, but profit will fall more sharply — roughly 10-15% lower — because margins were squeezed.

The main driver is cost, not demand collapse. Following the Iran conflict, suppliers imposed sudden surcharges on raw materials. Rather than pass all of this to contractors on committed projects, the Company chose to absorb part of it, protecting customers in fragile refurbishment markets. That decision cushions revenue but compresses profit margins, which is why profit falls faster than sales.

Demand was mixed by product and region. Resilient sheet flooring held up, but luxury vinyl tile (LVT) was weak in Europe and Australia. The UK, its biggest market, grew modestly, with an especially strong June — though management cautions some of that was customers buying ahead of July price rises, so it may partly borrow from future sales. Overseas, the Middle East (+54%) and South Africa (+25%) were standout gains versus the prior year.

The balance sheet remains ungeared (no net debt) with strong cash and reserves, and the Board says medium-term prospects are solid. The percentage figures quoted are year-on-year comparisons against FY25; the Company has not yet printed absolute revenue or profit numbers.

explainer:
Tractor Supply's headline net sales still grew 2.3% because it keeps opening stores, but the more telling number is comparable store sales — sales at existing stores — which fell 1.5%. That swing was driven almost entirely by a weak May, when shoppers pulled back on big-ticket seasonal and discretionary items; April and June were positive. Its 'consumable, usable and edible' staples held up, while the companion-animal (pet) business lagged.

The gap between reported and adjusted profit matters here. Reported operating income fell 19.2% and reported EPS fell to $0.69, but those figures are dragged down by one-off charges: a $65.8m impairment and restructuring hit tied to closing around 75 Petsense pet stores, plus $9.5m of costs for buying VIP Petcare. Strip those out and adjusted EPS was $0.81 — flat versus last year — and adjusted operating income fell a milder 5.1%. Gross margin actually edged up to 37.1%, helped by cost control and tariff benefits.

On guidance, the key event is that management cut its fiscal 2026 outlook and, more significantly, withdrew the multi-year financial targets it set at its December 2024 Investor Day. It plans to issue a new long-term framework alongside its Q4 2026 results. This release does not print the exact revised 2026 sales/margin/EPS numbers, so the precise new targets are not available from this text alone.

explainer:
This is a quarterly production report, not a full financial result — it reports tonnes and carats mined rather than revenue or profit. The percentage changes are versus the same quarter a year earlier, so some large swings (diamonds +88%, manganese +22%) mainly reflect a weak prior-year comparative period (Orapa maintenance and an Australian cyclone) rather than a step-change in current demand.

The most market-relevant change is the cut to copper unit cost guidance, from c.172 c/lb to c.145 c/lb for the year. That is driven by two external tailwinds — higher credits from by-products such as molybdenum, and favourable currency moves (a weaker Chilean peso and Peruvian sol against the dollar) — rather than by producing more copper, since production guidance is unchanged. Lower unit costs support margins at current copper prices.

Note the flagged warning that underlying EBITDA from De Beers and steelmaking coal is expected to be negative in H1 2026, reflecting weak diamond markets and coal conditions; both businesses are being sold or streamlined. Copper and iron ore output is weighted to the second half of 2026, so first-half volumes look softer by design.

Corporate context matters here: the Teck merger (completion window September 2026 to March 2027, awaiting Chinese anti-trust clearance) and the $3.875bn steelmaking coal disposal to Dhilmar are reshaping the group into a copper-focused business, so period-on-period comparisons will become less like-for-like over time.

explainer:

Because liquids (oil condensate) are priced against Brent crude, more liquids output means a larger slice of Energean's revenue moves with the Brent oil price rather than with gas contracts.

Guidance is therefore maintained, not raised. The H2 range already factors in planned shutdowns for Katlan tie-in work and maintenance, so investors should read the higher second-half figure as expected ramp-up rather than a fresh upgrade.

  • On track to meet 2026 attributable production target of 300,000-328,000 GEO; Inmaculada, San Jose and Mara Rosa all guided to hit full-year targets.
  • Attributable all-in sustaining costs currently running 5-10% above the guided $2,157-$2,320 per GEO, on higher prices lifting royalties/profit-share, stronger local currencies and Argentine cost inflation; any cost guidance revision at H1 results in August.
  • Swung to net cash of ~$51m at 30 June 2026 from net debt of $22.7m at end-2025; total cash and short-term investments ~$309m ($317.0m at 31 Dec 2025).
  • Fatality at Inmaculada in June — death of a contractor shift supervisor — prompting a full investigation; affected development area temporarily suspended.
  • Growth pipeline advancing: revised Royropata EIA to be submitted to the Peruvian government shortly; Monte Do Carmo investment decision expected in H2 2026.
headline: Hochschild produced 151,830 attributable gold-equivalent ounces in H1 2026, on track for full-year output guidance, but all-in sustaining costs are running 5-10% above the guided range.
priority_reason: Half-year production report with full-year guidance reaffirmed but a flagged cost overrun and possible cost-guidance revision in August.

guidance.previous: 2026 attributable production target of 300,000-328,000 gold equivalent ounces; AISC guided range $2,157-$2,320 per GEO
guidance.current: Production target of 300,000-328,000 GEO reaffirmed; AISC currently running ~5-10% above the guided range
guidance.commentary: Production guidance is unchanged and the group remains on track. Cost guidance is under pressure — AISC is tracking 5-10% above the guided range due to higher metal prices lifting royalties, workers' profit-share and selling expenses, stronger local currencies and Argentine inflation. Any revision to annual cost guidance will be communicated at the H1 2026 results in August.

explainer:
This is a quarterly production (operational) report, not full financial results — it reports ounces mined and sold rather than profit. Figures are quoted on an 'attributable' basis, meaning 100% of Inmaculada and Mara Rosa plus Hochschild's 51% share of the San Jose joint venture; the report also shows higher 'total' figures that include the JV partner's share. Gold equivalent ounces (GEO) convert silver output into a gold-equivalent using a price ratio, so the whole business can be measured on one number.

H1 attributable production of 151,830 GEO is down about 8% year on year, largely because Inmaculada processed lower grades. Despite that, the group says it remains on track for its full-year target of 300,000-328,000 GEO, helped by San Jose growing half-on-half and Mara Rosa's turnaround gradually improving.

Production guidance is unchanged, but cost guidance is the key watch item: all-in sustaining costs (the full cash cost of producing an ounce, including sustaining capital) are running 5-10% above the guided $2,157-$2,320 per GEO. Much of this is a side-effect of sharply higher gold and silver prices — realised gold averaged $4,167/oz versus $2,832 a year earlier — which mechanically increase royalties and profit-share; stronger local currencies and Argentine inflation add to it. Management will decide whether to formally revise cost guidance at the H1 results in August.

The balance sheet strengthened materially: the group moved from $22.7m net debt at end-2025 to roughly $51m net cash, driven by strong operating cash flow at high metal prices, even after paying dividends and a working-capital outflow of about $90m tied to 2025 tax and bonuses.

On a like-for-like basis it climbed 2.2 percentage points to 79.2% since the March year-end — a normal seasonal spring/summer pick-up — but is fractionally (0.2ppts) below a year ago. Net achieved rent of £36.45 per sq ft, up 2%, is the actual rate collected after discounts, so revenue growth is being driven by a mix of modestly higher rates and more space let.

On costs, the company has effectively issued new guidance: like-for-like store operating expenditure is expected to rise 4% in the first half and 3% for the full year, with the H1 skew reflecting when efficiency measures (automation-driven headcount reduction, solar/energy savings and a leaner marketing plan) take effect. These savings are meant to partly offset higher business rates from the 2026 Rating Revaluation.

The development pipeline is the growth story: 12 planned stores are projected to add £35m of net operating income at a 16.5% return on £212m of cost to complete, part-funded by the £38.4m Harrow disposal. Management struck a cautious tone on the wider environment, citing fiscal and budgetary uncertainty unlikely to clear until the autumn.

body:
• DFS Furniture plc expects FY26 underlying PBT (PBTu(A)) of around £45m, within its previously upgraded £43-50m guidance and up around +£15m year on year, despite weaker H2 market demand.
  • Profit underpinned by 2.7% revenue growth, gross margin expansion and cost discipline.
  • Net bank debt cut to c£69m at 28 June (from £107m in FY25), with leverage down to 0.9x (FY25: 1.4x).
  • Group order intake softened from +2.3% YoY in H1 to -4.4% YoY in H2, leaving full-year intake at -1.0% — broadly in line with the market; management cites weaker consumer confidence, housing transactions and the Iran War.
  • CEO Tim Stacey reiterated medium-term ambitions of £1.4bn revenue and an 8% PBT margin.
  • Full-year results due 24 September 2026.
headline: DFS expects FY26 underlying PBT of around £45m, within its previously upgraded £43-50m guidance and up about £15m year on year, despite softer H2 demand.
priority_reason: Full-year trading update with profit guidance and detailed financial metrics for a listed retailer.

figures.basis: underlying profit before tax and brand amortisation

guidance.previous: Previously upgraded guidance of £43-50m underlying PBT (PBTu(A))
guidance.current: Full year PBTu(A) expected to be around £45m, within the previously upgraded £43-50m range
guidance.commentary: DFS confirms it will deliver full-year profit within its previously upgraded range despite a notable softening in demand in H2, so this trading statement maintains rather than raises guidance.

explainer:
DFS's headline profit measure here is PBTu(A) — underlying profit before tax and brand amortisation — which strips out non-cash amortisation of acquired brands to show trading profitability. Around £45m is roughly £15m higher than the prior year and sits in the middle of the £43-50m range the company had already upgraded to earlier, so this is confirmation that it delivered on that upgraded target rather than a fresh increase.

The order-intake figures show the trading shape of the year: demand was positive in the first half (+2.3%) but turned negative in the second half (-4.4%), leaving the full year at -1.0%. The company attributes the H2 weakness to falling consumer confidence and fewer housing transactions, partly linked to the Iran War. The 'year-on-two-year' +9.1% is measured against two years ago and reflects large market-share gains booked in FY25, so it flatters the underlying trend rather than describing current momentum.

On the balance sheet, net bank debt fell from £107m to about £69m and leverage improved from 1.4x to 0.9x (on the banking covenant IAS17 definition), driven by strong free cash flow. Guidance is effectively maintained: profit lands within the range already set, and management keeps its medium-term goals of £1.4bn revenue and an 8% PBT margin unchanged.

• Foxtons Group plc expects H1 2026 adjusted operating profit of approximately £8.5m, down from £12.3m in H1 2025, against a strong prior-year comparator boosted by activity ahead of the March 2025 stamp duty deadline.
  • Full-year 2026 Group adjusted operating profit guided to a range of £17m-£19m, with profit expected to be H2-weighted on Lettings seasonality and a normalisation in tenancy terminations.
  • Lettings hit by short-term volatility after the Renters' Rights Act in May: elevated tenancy terminations, especially in student rentals, reversed approximately £3m of previously recognised revenue.
  • Sales market described as more challenging on weaker consumer confidence, higher-than-expected interest rates and Middle East conflict; further operational and organisational changes under consideration.
  • Financial Services delivered revenue growth on stronger refinance volumes and cross-sell; Group delivered £4.5m of annualised cost savings in H1 (£3.0m cost-reduction programme plus £1.5m from the January 2026 HQ relocation).
  • Half-year results due 30 July 2026.
headline: Foxtons expects H1 2026 adjusted operating profit of about £8.5m, down from £12.3m, and guides full-year profit to £17m-£19m.
priority_reason: Pre-close trading update flagging materially lower H1 profit and setting a full-year adjusted operating profit range.

guidance.previous: Not stated in this announcement
guidance.current: Full year 2026 Group adjusted operating profit expected in the range of £17m-£19m
guidance.commentary: The Group sets a full-year adjusted operating profit range of £17m-£19m, with profit skewed to H2 as Lettings revenues are seasonally stronger and tenancy termination levels normalise. The update strikes a cautious tone, citing a subdued sales market and short-term Renters' Rights Act disruption in lettings.

explainer:
This is a pre-close trading update ahead of Foxtons' half-year results on 30 July 2026. The headline profit fall — roughly £8.5m of adjusted operating profit versus £12.3m a year earlier — is flattered on the downside by an unusually strong H1 2025, when buyers rushed to complete before the March 2025 stamp duty change. So part of the decline reflects a tough comparative rather than a pure deterioration in the underlying business.

The £3m revenue reversal is a one-off consequence of the Renters' Rights Act, which came into force in May and abolished fixed tenancy terms. Because tenants could terminate early, contractually due revenue that Foxtons had already booked had to be unwound, hitting student rentals in particular. Management frames this as transitional volatility rather than a permanent loss, and argues the new rules should boost demand for professional lettings over the medium term.

On guidance, the Group has set full-year 2026 adjusted operating profit at £17m-£19m and stressed it will be H2-weighted. That skew matters: the weak first half does not scale simply to a full-year number, because lettings income is seasonally stronger later in the year and the tenancy-termination spike should fade. Against this, £4.5m of annualised cost savings is helping to offset National Insurance and inflation pressures, while the sales market is expected to stay subdued.
