headline: Dunelm reports FY26 sales up 3.1% to £1,825m with full-year PBT expected in line with previous guidance and £210m consensus.
priority_reason: Full-year trading update from a listed retailer with sales, margin, cash and PBT guidance detail.

figures.note: FX tailwind, partly offset by promotions

guidance.previous: Previous FY26 PBT guidance; company-compiled consensus of £210m
guidance.current: FY26 PBT expected to be in line with previous guidance and current consensus of £210m
guidance.commentary: Guidance is reaffirmed rather than changed: Dunelm expects full-year PBT in line with both its previous guidance and the £210m analyst consensus, with capex also held at the previously guided c.£40m.

explainer:
This is a full-year trading update ahead of Dunelm's audited Preliminary Results on 8 September 2026, so it gives sales, margin and cash figures but not a precise profit number. The key point for traders is that full-year pre-tax profit (PBT) is expected to be 'in line' with both prior guidance and the company-compiled consensus of £210m — meaning no upgrade or downgrade to profit expectations.

Sales grew 3.1% for the full year to £1,825m, with the fourth quarter up 2.9% to £428m. Management flags that Q4 was held back by two separate weeks of exceptionally warm weather that cut store footfall, one of which clashed with the start of the Summer Sale, so the underlying trend was described as solid rather than weak. Gross margin rose 10 basis points (0.1 percentage point) to 52.5%, helped by a favourable foreign-exchange (FX) tailwind but partly offset by more customers buying on promotion, especially in the second half.

Two items to note on the cost and cash lines: full-year costs include about £7m of insurance income relating to compensation for two stores temporarily closed after fires — a one-off benefit rather than trading performance. Cash generation remained strong, with roughly 70% of operating profit converted into free cash; after £40m of capex and £141m of dividends, the group still ended the year with a small net cash inflow.

Overall this is a 'no surprises' update that confirms guidance, with the bigger news — a strategic update from relatively new CEO Clo Moriarty — deferred to the September results.

• Frasers Group PLC FY26 (52 weeks to 26 April 2026): revenue up 8.7% to £5,325.9m, driven by 59.2% international revenue growth.
  • Adjusted profit before tax (APBT) down 4.0% to £538.0m, hit by a £259.5m rise in fixed-asset impairments and higher interest costs; reported PBT up 38.9% to £527.8m on non-repeat derivative fair-value losses.
  • Retail profit from trading up 22.1% to £912.5m; UK Sports profit up £83.6m (17.6%) to £559.4m; group gross margin +160bps.
  • Basic EPS 86.7p (+28.4%) but adjusted EPS 83.3p (-15.1%); net debt ex-securitisation rose to £1,168.1m (FY25: £847.5m).
  • No FY27 financial guidance provided given ongoing takeover offers of EUR€38.00/share for HUGO BOSS and AUD$0.65/share for Accent Group; to be reviewed at half year.
  • CEO Michael Murray flags tough trading, subdued consumer confidence and industry-wide excess inventory persisting into early FY27.
headline: Frasers Group FY26 revenue rose 8.7% to £5,325.9m and retail profit 22.1% to £912.5m, but adjusted profit fell 4% and no FY27 guidance was given.
priority_reason: Full-year results from a FTSE-listed retailer, with adjusted profit down, no FY27 guidance provided, and live takeover offers for HUGO BOSS and Accent Group.

figures.note: reflects capex, acquisitions and strategic investments

guidance.previous: Not applicable / not stated
guidance.current: The Board considers it is not appropriate to provide financial guidance for FY27 at this time; position to be reviewed at half year.
guidance.commentary: Frasers has declined to issue FY27 guidance because its voluntary takeover offer for HUGO BOSS and on-market offer for Accent Group are ongoing and could lead to a range of outcomes depending on acceptances. It will revisit at the half-year stage.

explainer:
Frasers reports two profit measures. Adjusted profit before tax (APBT), the metric management views as underlying, fell 4% to £538.0m — weighed down by a £259.5m jump in impairments of fixed assets, £34.7m of impairments on associates and £37.5m more in bank interest, only partly offset by disposal gains, provision releases and a bigger share of profit from associates such as HUGO BOSS. Reported PBT, by contrast, rose 38.9% to £527.8m, but that increase is largely mechanical: last year's figure was depressed by fair-value losses on equity derivatives linked to strategic investments, which did not repeat.

The same split explains the EPS numbers. Basic (reported) EPS climbed 28.4% to 86.7p, tracking reported PBT, while adjusted EPS fell 15.1% to 83.3p, reflecting the lower APBT and a higher effective tax rate driven by non-deductible goodwill impairments. Retail profit was flattered in part by international acquisitions adding £53.7m under IFRS 16, which strips rent costs out of that measure, so trading momentum is not quite as strong as the 22.1% headline implies.

On guidance, the key change is that Frasers has chosen not to give any FY27 financial targets. This is not a profit warning as such, but management explicitly cites tough trading, weak consumer confidence and excess industry inventory continuing into FY27, alongside uncertainty over the outcome of its live takeover bids for HUGO BOSS and Accent Group. Investors will have to wait until the half-year results for a clearer steer.

  • Full-year expectations unchanged; CEO Brian Cassin cites trusted data assets, scaled platforms and growing AI-enabled opportunities.
  • North America organic revenue up 7% (total 8%), led by Financial Services (Ascend, fraud, mortgage), Automotive (AutoCheck) and Health (Patient Access Curator).
  • Latin America organic revenue up 12%; Consumer Services there grew 22%, with Brazil's Limpa Nome performing strongly; closed idwall acquisition on 1 July.
  • UK and Ireland organic revenue up 5% (total constant currency 7%, aided by KYC360 acquisition); EMEA and Asia Pacific organic growth 1% against strong prior-year comparators.

headline: Experian posts strong Q1 FY27 with revenue up 10% at actual rates and 7% organically, reiterating unchanged full-year expectations.
priority_reason: Q1 trading update from a FTSE 100 company with revenue growth data and reaffirmed full-year guidance.

guidance.previous: Full-year (FY27) expectations
guidance.current: Full-year expectations unchanged
guidance.commentary: Experian reaffirmed its full-year FY27 expectations, with Q1 revenue growth in line with those expectations and no change to guidance.

explainer:
Experian reports revenue growth on three bases. 'Actual exchange rates' (+10%) is the headline reported figure including currency movements; 'constant currency' (+8%) strips out FX so you see underlying trading; and 'organic' (+7%) additionally excludes the effect of acquisitions and disposals, showing growth from the existing business alone. The gap between organic and total growth reflects recent deals such as idwall (Brazil), KYC360 (UK) and others.

The one soft spot is Consumer Services, where group organic revenue fell 2%. This was expected and is a one-off comparability effect: Experian is winding down two large, long-running mass data breach support contracts. Excluding those, Consumer Services actually grew 3%, so the decline reflects a lapping issue rather than deteriorating demand.

On guidance, nothing has changed. Management explicitly stated full-year expectations are unchanged, with Q1 tracking in line. This is a reassurance-style update rather than an upgrade or downgrade. Half-year results (six months to 30 September 2026) are scheduled for 18 November 2026.

headline: BHP delivered record iron ore production of 265 Mt and ~2 Mt of copper in FY26, with FY26 unit costs expected within guidance and net debt of ~US$9bn.
priority_reason: Full-year operational review with production records, FY26 cost/tax guidance, preliminary H2 financial items and net debt, plus FY27 production guidance.

guidance.previous: FY26 unit costs guidance ranges; adjusted effective tax rate guidance range 36–40%
guidance.current: FY26 unit costs at bottom end of ranges at Escondida, Spence and Copper SA, within range at WAIO, top end at BMA; adjusted effective tax rate in lower half of 36–40%. FY27 production: total copper 1,650–1,800 kt, Escondida 1,000–1,100 kt, Spence 210–230 kt, Copper SA 290–320 kt, Antamina copper 120–140 kt / zinc 35–55 kt, iron ore 260–272 Mt (WAIO 253–264 Mt), energy coal 7.5–8.0 Mt
guidance.commentary: FY26 costs are tracking well against guidance despite inflation and higher diesel prices, helped by by-product credits and favourable FX. New FY27 copper guidance is lower than FY26 output mainly because of the forecast grade decline at Escondida, while iron ore guidance points to broadly maintained record-level volumes.

explainer:
This is BHP's operational review for its financial year to 30 June 2026 — the production scorecard that precedes the audited results due on 18 August 2026. Production figures are actual tonnages; where the company only prints a percentage change (copper -3%, iron ore +1%) rather than the prior-year tonnage, the comparative is not stated here. 'Record' means the highest annual figure for that asset or commodity, not a market-wide record.

On costs, BHP guides to unit costs 'at guidance FX rates and by-product prices', meaning it standardises for currency (AUD/USD, USD/CLP) and for gold/uranium credits so cost performance is not flattered by favourable markets. FY26 unit costs landing at the bottom of ranges for most copper assets signals genuine cost control rather than a currency tailwind. The '~35% higher' copper price is a realised-price comparison versus a year earlier and flows into revenue, not costs.

The H2 FY26 items table is a preliminary heads-up on what will hit the income statement and balance sheet: a Jansen potash project impairment, continuing Samarco dam-failure costs and settlement payments, disposal gains (SolGold, Antamina silver streaming, Carajás), and an effective tax rate in the lower half of 36–40%. These are not yet finalised, so treat them as directional. Net debt of ~US$9bn is the flagged balance-sheet figure at year-end.

The FY27 guidance is new. Group copper of 1,650–1,800 kt is below FY26's 1,953 kt, driven mostly by a planned grade decline at Escondida (feed grade guided to ~0.70% versus 0.90% in FY26). Iron ore guidance of 260–272 Mt holds output near FY26's record. One-off operational risks are flagged separately, notably up to eight weeks of lost Carrapateena production after a conveyor failure.

guidance.commentary: The ilmenite production target has been trimmed because WCP A has not consistently reached its 3,500 tph nameplate capacity (averaging 2,800 tph in Q2) and dry mining at WCP B was temporarily stopped. Shipment and concentrates guidance were unaffected, with concentrates already exceeded on strong ZrTi demand.

explainer:
This is a quarterly production (operational) update rather than a full financial results statement, so most figures are tonnages compared with the same quarter a year earlier (year-on-year, or YoY). Production of heavy mineral concentrate (HMC) and finished products fell sharply — HMC down 37% and ilmenite down 40% — mainly because ore grades dropped as the main WCP A plant nears the end of its current Namalope mining area and because the plant's upgrade has not yet delivered its designed throughput.

The headline change for traders is the softening of full-year ilmenite guidance from "more than 800,000 tonnes" to "approximately 800,000 tonnes". That is a modest downgrade rather than a profit warning, and Kenmare expects a stronger second half as WCP A improves, WCP B recovers and a new SMO 2 unit commissions in Q4. Shipment guidance of at least 1.1 million tonnes is unchanged, helped by drawing down high product stockpiles.

The striking 770% jump in concentrates output is largely a one-off: 75,000 tonnes of historically stored tailings were converted into the new ZrTi by-product to meet demand, so it is not a repeatable run-rate — Kenmare guides to only 30,000-40,000 tonnes of ZrTi a year going forward.

On the balance sheet, net debt rose to $175.7m from $158.8m at the start of the year as cash was consumed, though the company secured a $30m increase to its revolving credit facility and covenant relief to add flexibility during weak titanium-feedstock markets. Zircon prices, by contrast, are recovering.

explainer:

Gross margin collapsed mostly on lower housing volume and mix rather than one-off items alone.

On guidance, Crest has not scrapped its FY26 range but signalled it now expects to land in the lower half of the £5m-£15m adjusted profit range, a de facto downgrade driven by weaker demand since April and a more cautious sales outlook.   • Net asset value of USD2,109.6m (GBP6.33 per share), up from USD1,414.4m (GBP5.05 per share) a year earlier.
  • Uranium (U3O8) holdings rose to 23.11 million lb (2025: 21.68 million lb), with the value of holdings up 39% to USD1,940.4m.
  • Spot U3O8 price closed at USD83.95/lb, up 30% from USD64.45/lb at 31 March 2025; term prices at highest since 2008.
  • Raised gross USD283.1m (GBP210.3m) via two placings (September 2025 and February 2026) to fund additional purchases, including exercise of the Kazatomprom options; debt-free structure maintained.

headline: Yellow Cake swung to a USD419.5m annual profit as net asset value rose to USD2,109.6m (GBP6.33/share) on a 30% jump in the uranium spot price.
priority_reason: Full-year annual results with a swing to profit and a sharp rise in net asset value.

figures.note: No dividend declared for the year

explainer:
Yellow Cake is not an operating miner but a holding vehicle: it buys and stores physical uranium (U3O8) so that its share price tracks the uranium spot price. Because of this, almost all of its reported profit or loss comes from marking its uranium inventory to the prevailing spot price rather than from trading revenue. This year's USD419.5m profit is essentially the USD434.3m uplift in the fair value of its holdings, and last year's large loss was the mirror image — a USD456.1m fair-value fall — so the swing reflects the uranium price direction, not a change in the underlying business.

Net asset value (NAV) per share is the key gauge for this type of company: it rose from GBP5.05 to GBP6.33, boosted both by the higher uranium price and by buying more physical material. The volume of uranium held grew from 21.68m to 23.11m lb, funded by USD283.1m raised through two equity placings during the year plus the exercise of purchase options with Kazatomprom. The company remains debt-free.

Note the currency mix: the uranium price and NAV are quoted in US dollars (uranium trades in USD/lb), while the per-share NAV and placing proceeds are also shown in sterling, so movements in the USD/GBP rate affect the sterling figures independently of the uranium price.

The company issued no formal financial guidance and, as is its policy, declared no dividend — it returns value through NAV growth rather than income. headline: Gore Street NAV fell to **74.9p** per share from **102.8p**, driven mainly by lower third-party merchant revenue forecasts, as revenue rose to **£36.27m**.
priority_reason: Audited full-year results with a sharp NAV decline, a new fixed distribution policy and an active asset-sale programme.

figures.basis: prior year restated for ownership adjustments (APM 6)

figures.note: in respect of FY to 31 March 2026

guidance.previous: Prior dividends declared of 4.00pps in respect of FY25; earlier policy not framed as a fixed distribution.
guidance.current: Fixed distribution of 7 pence per share per annum, paid quarterly, under the March 2026 revised strategy; KPI-linked with the continuation vote brought forward from 2028 if targets are missed.
guidance.commentary: The new Board has replaced the previous distribution approach with a higher, fixed 7p annual dividend funded by capital release from asset sales and augmentation, alongside cost cuts. The period under review predates the new strategy, which is expected to yield tangible shareholder results in the near term.

explainer:
The headline story is valuation, not trading. Gore Street's NAV per share fell from 102.8p to 74.9p over the year — a fund of this type marks its batteries to model, discounting projected future revenues. When independent forecasters cut their expected 'merchant' revenue curves (the prices batteries earn in wholesale and balancing markets), the value of those future cash flows falls. About two-thirds of the NAV decline came from these lower third-party curves (-17.2p), with a further -1.8p adjustment directed by the new Audit Committee to bring near-term projections closer to actual recent revenue.

Operationally the fund actually grew: revenue rose to £36.27m from £32.84m because far more capacity was online (643MW at year-end versus 417MW). But average revenue per MW/hr fell sharply to £7.32 from £9.56, as GB and Texas markets became oversupplied with battery capacity, suppressing prices. Because costs are largely fixed per MW, EBITDA was roughly flat despite the bigger fleet. Note the prior-year revenue and EBITDA figures were restated to reflect ownership percentages, so the year-on-year comparison is on a like-for-like basis per the company.

On distributions, the 7.19p declared for the year is flattered by 3.00p of special dividends and is not the new run-rate. The forward policy is a fixed 7p per share per annum paid quarterly — this is the 'new' guidance element, tied to the March 2026 strategy of selling selected assets (Cremzow, Irish and Middelton pre-construction sites) and reinvesting in augmentation (extending two GB assets from 1-hour to 2-hour duration). The Board has attached KPIs and warned it will pull the continuation vote forward from 2028 to 2026 if progress disappoints, so execution over the coming year is the key watch item.

guidance.current: Full-year copper production 650,000-700,000 tonnes; cash cost after by-product credits $1.15-1.35/lb; capital expenditure $3.4bn; cash cost before by-product credits now expected $2.40-2.60/lb
guidance.commentary: Headline production, net cash cost and capex guidance are all held unchanged, with output expected to rise sequentially in H2 on higher throughput and grades. The one moving part is the newly stated before-by-product cash cost range of $2.40-2.60/lb, reflecting fuel and consumable prices remaining above January 2026 levels; the after-credit range is preserved because higher by-product credits offset that inflation.

explainer:
This is a production report, not full financial results, so the key numbers are tonnes of metal and unit cash costs in US dollars per pound of copper, rather than revenue or profit. Antofagasta reports both quarter-on-quarter (Q2 versus Q1) and year-to-date year-on-year (H1 2026 versus H1 2025) comparisons; the year-on-year figures are weaker mainly because of lower grades and throughput at Los Pelambres and Centinela earlier in the mine plan.

Cash costs come in three layers. 'Before by-product credits' is the raw cost of producing copper; 'by-product credits' are the value of gold and molybdenum sold alongside the copper, which is netted off; and 'net cash costs' is the result after those credits. In H1, gross cash costs rose 23% year-on-year on diesel, sulphuric acid and a one-off Centinela labour settlement, but because by-product credits jumped 64% on higher gold and moly prices, net cash costs actually fell 8%. A roughly 7,000-tonne slug of copper processed at Los Pelambres in Q2 is being held in inventory and will only be booked as production in H2, flattering the second half.

On guidance, the practical message is 'no change' where it matters most: full-year copper of 650,000-700,000 tonnes, net cash cost of $1.15-1.35/lb and capex of $3.4bn are all reaffirmed, with management expecting a stronger H2 as grades and throughput improve. The only new number is a before-credit cash cost range of $2.40-2.60/lb, an acknowledgement that input-cost inflation is running above start-of-year assumptions, even though richer by-product credits keep the all-in net figure within the original range.

explainer:
This is a full-year trading update ahead of Barratt Redrow's annual results on 16 September 2026. The figures compare FY26 (52 weeks to 28 June 2026) against FY25. The group prints two FY25 comparatives — 'A' (as previously reported by Barratt on its own) and 'R' (restated to reflect the combined Barratt Redrow group after the merger) — so the more meaningful like-for-like comparison generally uses the 'R' numbers. Adjusted profit before tax is quoted before PPA (purchase price allocation) adjustments, which are non-cash accounting charges arising from the Redrow acquisition.

Completions rose 5% to 17,667, at the upper end of guidance, and profit came in line with market expectations — a 'solid' outcome in a weak market where cautious consumer sentiment, higher mortgage rates and elevated incentives have pressured margins. The higher total ASP of c. £352k is largely mix-driven (more higher-priced regions and larger homes); underlying price movement was under 1%, so the headline ASP rise overstates genuine pricing power.

The key news is the capital allocation change. With the shares trading at a 36% discount to tangible net asset value of 433.4p (versus c. 9% at the February interims), the Board is scrapping most ordinary dividends and returning capital via buybacks instead. It still targets returning 50% of adjusted net income, but this — plus additional capital — makes up a c. £400m FY27 return, of which c. £386m is a buyback starting today (completing by 2 July 2027) and just c. £14m is a nominal 1p dividend to satisfy income mandates.

FY27 guidance is mixed: completions are guided at 17,700–18,200 (slight growth), but average sales outlets have been cut from 425–435 to around 415 owing to faster outlet closures and slow planning. • Rio Tinto Q2/H1 2026 production update: group copper equivalent (CuEq) production up 3% year-on-year in the first half.
  • Highest first-half Pilbara iron ore production since the 2018 record, driven by its productivity improvement programme.
  • Copper: Oyu Tolgoi ramp-up on schedule, delivering more than 30% growth in the first half; aluminium business sustained strong performance.
  • Simandou: SimFer mine construction and port infrastructure both more than three-quarters complete, with full rail commissioning achieved in Q1.
  • Lithium: first production achieved ahead of plan at Sal de Vida and Fénix 1B; growth options advancing at Resolution and Winu.
  • Note: the scraped page lists the production data tables (copper, iron ore, LCE) as headers only — the actual quarterly volume figures did not render, so specific tonnages cannot be quoted here.
headline: Rio Tinto reports copper equivalent production up 3% in H1 2026, with its highest first-half Pilbara iron ore output since the 2018 record.
priority_reason: Quarterly production update from a major FTSE 100 miner, market-moving for the stock and the wider mining sector.

figures.basis: Rio Tinto share, long-term consensus prices

guidance.previous: 2026 sales guidance (100% basis): Simandou 5-10 Mt; IOC 15-18 Mt
guidance.current: 2026 sales guidance (100% basis): Simandou 5-10 Mt; IOC 15-18 Mt
guidance.commentary: Guidance is reiterated in the notes rather than changed. Pilbara iron ore guidance remains subject to the timing of approvals for planned mining areas and heritage clearances.

explainer:
This is a production (operational) update, not financial results — it reports how much metal and ore Rio Tinto dug up and shipped, not revenue or profit. The headline measure, copper equivalent (CuEq), rolls all of Rio's different products into a single number by converting each into its copper-price equivalent, so a '3% rise' means total output grew 3% once weighted by long-term consensus prices.

The iron ore comparison is against Rio's own history: this was the strongest first-half Pilbara output since it set a record in 2018, credited to productivity improvements rather than new mines. Growth elsewhere comes from the Oyu Tolgoi copper mine in Mongolia continuing its planned ramp-up (over 30% more copper), and from new lithium operations (Sal de Vida, Fénix 1B) starting production earlier than scheduled following the Arcadium acquisition.

On guidance, nothing has changed: the note simply restates existing 2026 sales targets of 5-10 Mt for the new Simandou iron ore project in Guinea and 15-18 Mt for the Iron Ore Company of Canada, with the usual caveat that Pilbara volumes depend on approvals and heritage clearances.

One caveat on this summary: the scraped article contained the production tables as headings only, with no numbers attached, so the specific quarterly tonnages could not be captured. The percentage moves above come from the CEO's commentary, which is the only place figures were legible.

• Ashmore Group plc reported AuM up US$3.3bn (7%) over the quarter to 30 June 2026, comprising positive investment performance of US$2.0bn and net inflows of US$1.3bn.
  • Net inflows spread across local currency, equities, blended and corporate debt; redemptions fell sharply versus the prior quarter, though a net outflow in external debt persisted on a few institutional redemptions.
  • EM fixed income indices rose 2%–5% and the large-cap equity index gained a notable 24%; proportion of AuM outperforming benchmarks broadly consistent with 31 December.
  • CEO Mark Coombs cited EM resilience after the Strait of Hormuz closure and oil-price spike, and a supportive forward macro backdrop for emerging markets.
  • Local currency AuM includes US$9.8bn in overlay/liquidity strategies (31 March 2026: US$8.9bn).
  • Full-year results for the year to 30 June 2026 due on 7 September 2026.
headline: Ashmore's AuM rose US$3.3bn (7%) in Q4 to reflect positive investment performance of US$2.0bn and net inflows of US$1.3bn.
priority_reason: Quarterly AuM trading statement with fund-flow and performance data ahead of full-year results.

figures.note: net outflow in external debt theme

explainer:
This is Ashmore's fourth-quarter assets under management (AuM) statement — a routine flows-and-performance update rather than full results. AuM is the pool of client money Ashmore manages and earns fees on, so growth here signals higher future revenue. The US$3.3bn rise splits into two parts: US$2.0bn of investment performance (markets going up) and US$1.3bn of net inflows (new client money in, minus withdrawals). Net inflows are the more telling figure because they reflect client demand rather than market moves.

The announcement notes flows were positive across most strategies but that the external debt theme still saw a net outflow due to a small number of institutional redemptions — a mixed but improving picture, as overall redemptions fell sharply versus the prior quarter.

Ashmore reports in US dollars because it is an emerging-markets manager, but as a UK-listed firm its accounts translate into sterling; the statement flags the GBP:USD rates used (1.3273 spot at 30 June, 1.3419 average for the year), which affect reported revenue and balance-sheet values. No profit or revenue figures are given here — those come with full-year results on 7 September 2026. The company issued no formal earnings guidance.

It is not a full financial results statement, so it does not give revenue, profit or EPS figures for the period — the numbers quoted are leasing metrics. 'Ahead of ERV' means rents agreed on new lettings are above the estimated rental value (the market rent the property owner's valuers expect), while 'ahead of previous passing rent' means the new rent beats what the previous tenant was paying — both signals of a strong rental market and rising income.

'Underlying' EPS strips out revaluation movements and one-off items to show recurring earnings from rent. Management says this is underpinned by like-for-like net rental growth running at the top end of its 3-5% range, plus expected 3-5% growth in ERV across the portfolio.

For a trader, the read is steady-as-she-goes: momentum from the prior year has carried into Q1, with high occupancy on retail parks and continued campus demand, and the guidance reaffirmation removes near-term earnings uncertainty. The CEO succession (Simon Carter to Joanne McNamara in September) is flagged but framed as an orderly handover.

• Watches of Switzerland Group PLC FY26: Group revenue £1,828m, +13% constant currency (+11% reported); excluding the 53rd week +11% cc (+8% reported).
  • US revenue £927m, +24% cc (+18% reported), now more than half of Group revenue and profit; UK revenue £901m, +5%.
  • Adjusted EBIT £155m, +6% cc (+3% reported); Adjusted EBIT margin 8.5%, -60bps (FY25: 9.1%), citing brand margin adjustments, US ecommerce investment and a one-off Roberto Coin debtor write-down.
  • Statutory PBT £133m (FY25: £76m), +76%, mainly lower exceptional costs; free cash flow £162m (FY25: £98m), conversion 80%.
  • Net debt cut to £57m (FY25: £96m) after the Deutsch & Deutsch acquisition; £25m buyback completed June 2025 (£13m purchased in FY26).
  • FY27 guidance unchanged from the Q4 update; encouraging first ten weeks' trading, targeting further strong revenue growth and a return to Adjusted EBIT margin expansion.
headline: Watches of Switzerland reports record FY26 revenue of £1.83bn, up 13% in constant currency, with statutory PBT up 76% and FY27 guidance confirmed.
priority_reason: Full-year results with record revenue and profit, ahead of previous guidance, plus FY27 outlook confirmed.

figures.note: now over half of Group revenue and profit

guidance.previous: FY27 guidance as provided in the Q4 trading update
guidance.current: FY27 guidance unchanged from the Q4 trading update; another year of strong revenue growth expected alongside a return to Adjusted EBIT margin expansion (52-week guidance provided on an organic pre-IFRS 16 basis and an IFRS 16 basis)
guidance.commentary: Guidance is confirmed rather than changed. Management points to encouraging trading in the first ten weeks, good US momentum and early signs of UK market improvement, though the specific numeric guidance tables were not reproduced in the scraped text.

explainer:
The headline growth is flattered by two effects worth separating. First, FY26 contained a 53rd week; stripping that out, constant-currency revenue growth falls from 13% to a more comparable 11% (8% reported). Second, 'constant currency' removes the drag from translating US sales back into a stronger pound — reported growth is lower (11% Group, 18% US) because the actual FY26 average rate was $1.34. The US is now the largest market, so sterling/dollar moves matter increasingly for reported numbers.

The 76% jump in statutory profit before tax (£133m from £76m) largely reflects a fall in exceptional (one-off) costs rather than a similar surge in underlying trading; the cleaner measure, Adjusted EBIT, rose a more modest 6% in constant currency. The Adjusted EBIT margin actually slipped 60bps to 8.5%, squeezed by US tariff-driven brand margin changes, investment in US ecommerce and marketing, and a one-off Roberto Coin department-store debtor write-down.

Cash performance was the standout: free cash flow rose to £162m with conversion jumping to 80% from 51%, helping cut net debt to £57m despite paying for the Deutsch & Deutsch acquisition.

On guidance, nothing has changed — FY27 targets are confirmed as set at the Q4 update, so this is a 'maintained' rather than upgraded outlook. Management flags encouraging early-year trading and, importantly, expects the Adjusted EBIT margin to start expanding again in FY27 after this year's decline.

  • Reported upstream production 2,170-2,220mboe/d (1Q: 2,339mboe/d), down on seasonal maintenance in the Gulf of America and Middle East disruption; oil 1,420-1,450mboe/d, gas & low carbon 750-770mboe/d.
  • Realisations to lift earnings vs 1Q: oil +$1.8 to 2.1bn, refining margins +$1.2 to 1.4bn, gas +$0.5 to 0.7bn; Brent averaged $103.85/bbl (1Q: $81.13), bp RIM $29.6/bbl (1Q: $16.9).
  • Net debt expected at $22-23bn (1Q: $25.3bn), after $2.9bn to redeem €2.5bn perpetual hybrids and $1.1bn Gulf of America settlement; total of net debt, hybrids and settlement liabilities down ~$6.3-7.3bn.
  • Exploration write-offs ~$(0.5)bn (Bay du Nord sale, Canada) and post-tax impairment adjusting items of ~$1.0bn in gas & low carbon transition businesses; underlying effective tax rate 33-37%.
  • Refining throughput 1,445-1,475mb/d (1Q: 1,527mb/d) on higher turnarounds and lower Whiting volumes after the April third-party event, now resolved.
headline: BP flags lower Q2 upstream production of 2,170-2,220mboe/d but sharply higher oil, gas and refining realisations, with net debt falling to $22-23bn.
priority_reason: Pre-results trading statement flagging quarter-on-quarter earnings drivers, net debt reduction and impairments ahead of Q2 results on 4 August 2026.

figures.metric: Henry Hub gas (first of month index)

figures.note: Q2 2026, primarily Bay du Nord sale
Q2 2026, gas & low carbon transition businesses

guidance.previous: 1Q 2026 group results (28 April 2026) guidance for Q2 and full-year 2026
guidance.current: 1Q26 guidance items continue to apply unless explicitly stated; hybrid reduction of $4.3bn by end 2027, divestment proceeds $9-10bn including ~$6bn from Castrol
guidance.commentary: BP reiterates that its full-year and Q2 guidance from the 1Q 2026 results still applies. It confirms progress on cutting hybrid debt (€2.5bn perpetual hybrids redeemed in June) and on the Castrol divestment, alongside expected lower turnaround and structural cost reductions.

explainer:
This is a pre-results trading statement, not the actual numbers. BP gives directional guidance on how underlying replacement cost (RC) profit — its preferred earnings measure that strips out inventory holding gains and losses — is likely to move from the first quarter to the second, but does not print a profit figure. Full Q2 results follow on 4 August 2026.

The key swing factors are prices and volumes. Production is seasonally lower because of maintenance in the Gulf of America and Middle East disruption, but this is more than offset by much stronger price 'realisations': Brent averaged $103.85 a barrel versus $81.13 in Q1, and refining margins (the bp RIM) nearly doubled. BP quantifies these as positive quarter-on-quarter earnings impacts of roughly $1.8-2.1bn in oil, $1.2-1.4bn in refining and $0.5-0.7bn in gas.

On the balance sheet, net debt is expected to fall to $22-23bn from $25.3bn, even after paying $2.9bn to redeem €2.5bn of perpetual hybrid bonds and $1.1bn towards Gulf of America (Deepwater Horizon) settlement liabilities. BP prefers investors to watch the combined total of net debt, hybrids and settlement liabilities, which it expects to drop by around $6.3-7.3bn.

Two one-off items sit outside underlying profit: ~$0.5bn of exploration write-offs tied to the sale of Bay du Nord in Canada, and ~$1.0bn of post-tax impairment charges on low-carbon 'transition' businesses. Guidance from the April results is reaffirmed rather than changed, including the plan to cut hybrids by $4.3bn by end-2027 and to raise $9-10bn from divestments (about $6bn from Castrol).

explainer:

Funds under direction (FUD) is the total client money on the Transact platform; the 23% year-on-year rise to £85.5bn reflects both market gains and continued net inflows. Because IntegraFin earns fees on assets held, the record average daily FUD of £82.8bn (up 24%) is the figure most directly tied to revenue over the quarter.

Net inflows of £1.0bn were slightly below the £1.2bn a year earlier. Management attributes this to the pre-tax-year-end period falling in the prior quarter, and stresses it is the sixth straight quarter above £1bn. Gross inflows (new money in, before withdrawals) were actually up 5%, so the softer net figure reflects timing and outflows rather than weakening demand.

On guidance, nothing has changed: the December 2025 cost outlook is reiterated, with underlying admin expense growth held to about 3% in both FY26 and FY27. The key nuance is timing — those savings will show up more clearly in the second half of FY26 as efficiency initiatives take effect, supporting margin expansion later in the year.

explainer:
This is a pre-AGM trading statement rather than a full results release, so it contains directional commentary but no hard numbers to compare against last year. GMV (gross merchandise value — the total value of goods sold across the platform) is said to be growing year on year, with higher margins and lower returns, but the company does not print the actual figures, so none can be quoted here.

The group, recently renamed from Boohoo to Debenhams Group, is mid-turnaround. It references two guidance upgrades in the past nine months but does not issue a fresh upgrade today; instead it reaffirms momentum and sets a net-debt target of below 1x Adjusted EBITDA by the financial year ending February 2027, aided by property disposals and possible brand licensing or business sales.

Management also flags that reported EBITDA and operating profit should convert much better from Adjusted EBITDA this year as the one-off transformation costs fall away — a point to watch in the H1 results due in September. Adjusted EBITDA strips out such exceptional items, so the gap between the two measures narrowing indicates the cost of the restructuring is largely behind the business.

• Rule 2.4 announcement: easyJet Board and Castlelake, L.P. have reached agreement in principle on the key financial terms of a recommended cash offer.
  • Under Castlelake's "Fifth Proposal" (submitted 4 July 2026), it would acquire the entire issued and to-be-issued share capital of easyJet not already held by Castlelake for £6.90 per share in cash, including a partial unlisted share alternative.
  • Offer price of 558.20p last close implies the £6.90 (690p) proposal is at a ~23.6% premium to the prior close.
  • Board concluded the terms are at a value it "would be minded to recommend" to shareholders if a firm Rule 2.7 offer is made on those terms, subject to agreement of all other terms including the partial unlisted share alternative.
  • Castlelake would agree to a "best endeavours" commitment to obtain required regulatory clearances and approvals.
  • Castlelake stated it has "tremendous respect for easyJet and its people, along with its intention to support its future growth and transformation to a stronger, more resilient European airline," and is "supportive of easyJet's fleet modernisation programme," which it regards as "central to the Company's long-term competitiveness, efficiency and sustainability objectives."
  • Proposal remains subject to satisfaction/waiver of customary pre-conditions, including completion of satisfactory due diligence and agreement of definitive transaction documentation.
  • PUSU deadline extended (with Panel consent) to 5.00pm on Monday, 3 August 2026, by which Castlelake must announce a firm intention to bid (Rule 2.7) or walk away (Rule 2.8).
  • Castlelake reserves the right to vary the mix of consideration, to bid on less favourable terms (e.g. with Board agreement, a lower rival bid, or a Rule 9 waiver/reverse takeover), and to reduce the price by any further dividend/distribution paid by easyJet.
  • This is the fifth proposal, indicating a series of prior rejected/escalated approaches.
  • No certainty a firm offer will be made; shareholders advised to take no action.

body:
• Recommended all-cash acquisition of Capricorn by Genel Energy (via Bidco, Genel Energy No.9 Ltd), effected by Scottish scheme of arrangement.
  • Total Acquisition Value of US$4.74 per share (≈357p at the announcement FX rate), split into US$3.75 cash + a US$0.99 special "Permitted Dividend."
  • Premium of ~34% to the 266p undisturbed close (10 March 2026) and ~48% to the 241p three-month VWAP.
  • Implies an equity value of ~US$360m / £271m on a fully diluted basis.
  • The Permitted Dividend represents an aggregate ~US$75m payout — described as substantially in excess of any dividend Capricorn could pay standalone while retaining working capital, and a significant portion of its US$129m cash balance (as at 31 May 2026).
  • Dividend paid in Sterling equivalent of US$0.99, within 14 days of the Effective Date; only payable if the Scheme becomes Effective, and its non-payment is flagged as a risk that could cause the Scheme to fall away.
  • Cash consideration expressed in US$ (reflecting Capricorn's US$-denominated business); a Sterling Foreign Exchange Facility election will be offered (indicative ~282p on the Acquisition Price alone, FX-dependent).
  • Irrevocable undertakings secured over ~39.3% of share capital — Palliser Capital 13.8%, Newtyn 12.2%, Kite Lake 8.0%, Madison Avenue 5.3%, plus CEO Randy Neely's 0.006%; shareholder irrevocables lapse only if a competing bid tops the deal by ≥6.5%.
  • Capricorn Directors intend to recommend unanimously; Canaccord Genuity (Rule 3 adviser) considers terms fair and reasonable.
  • Deal conditional on the "Egyptian Condition" (EGPC/Egyptian Government consent to the transfer of the Western Desert concessions) and an Egyptian Competition Authority merger clearance — Genel may seek Panel consent to invoke the Egyptian Condition if unsatisfied by the Long-stop Date (2 January 2027).
  • Financing via Bidco cash plus a US$125m unsecured bridge facility arranged by Mauritius Commercial Bank (3-month initial maturity), guaranteed by Genel; PJT satisfied funds are available for the Acquisition Price (but not the Permitted Dividend).
  • Enlarged Group would hold pro-forma 2P reserves of 117 mmboe and combined December 2025 exit production of 41,003 bopd, split roughly evenly between Kurdistan and Egypt, with further upside in Oman/Somaliland.
  • Scheme Document within 28 days; Scheme expected Effective in H2 2026.
  • Capricorn to be delisted and re-registered as a private company; deal is a reverse takeover for Genel, triggering a listing-category transfer (Jefferies as sponsor); Enlarged Group HQ to be London.
  • Genel expects a material reduction in Capricorn headcount (particularly corporate/support functions) and cost synergies via rationalisation of systems and contracts; non-executive Capricorn directors to resign on completion.
  • Context: Capricorn cited persistently low trading liquidity and non-operator/single-country (Egypt) concentration risk (reliance on timely EGPC collections) as key drivers; UK North Sea value-realisation efforts have not yet yielded an executable deal.
  • Neely (Capricorn CEO): "Capricorn requires greater scale to materially improve trading liquidity. We believe the transaction with Genel crystallises the value created by Capricorn while providing shareholders with a clear and efficient exit."
  • Weir (Genel CEO): "Today we announce a landmark transaction to acquire a leading oil and gas portfolio in Egypt - a move that delivers our strategic intent, reshapes our company's growth trajectory, diversifies our portfolio of oil and gas fields and begins our role as a partner in Egypt's energy future... we will work with the operator to accelerate production optimisation, replace reserves, reduce unit costs, and capture significant near-term cash flow while preserving optionality for future development."

body:
• Group Q3 revenue £5,304m, +3% actual / flat constant currency; YTD £14,774m, +1% actual / -1% constant currency.
  • Full-year outlook unchanged except for Sugar; Group adjusted operating profit and adjusted EPS still expected to be below last year.
  • Sugar guidance downgraded: now expects an adjusted operating loss of £25m to £60m in FY2026, driven by higher gas costs from the Middle East conflict, potential onerous contracts on the 2026/27 beet crop, possible Malawian kwacha devaluation, and Tanzania new factory ramp-up risk.
  • FY2027 Sugar result expected to deteriorate further from the £60m upper-end loss; European sugar market likely to remain in surplus despite reduced production due to high 2025 inventory carryover.
  • Management flagged further cost base action to come, particularly in European Sugar.
  • Sugar Q3 revenue £451m, -4% constant currency; lower European ASPs, Tanzania rain-related delays, South Africa hit by import surge from delayed tariff adjustments.
  • Primark Q3 sales +3% (new stores contributed 5%); like-for-like -2.2%.
  • Primark FY2026 adjusted operating margin guidance maintained at ~10%.
  • Primark UK: total sales +1%, LFL broadly flat (-0.1%); gained market share; weak April/May due to Middle East conflict impact on sentiment and unseasonal weather, improved in June.
  • Primark Europe (ex UK/Ireland): total sales -1%, LFL -3.6%; weak consumer confidence; new integrated marketing campaign launched in Spain.
  • Primark US: sales +16%, 3 new stores (41 total), including first Manhattan store opened in May; trading described as "mixed".
  • Grocery Q3 revenue +1% constant currency; Twinings strong in US/UK/Australia on wellness teas; US oils weak due to reduced Hispanic consumer spending; CMA approved Hovis acquisition, working towards completion.
  • Ingredients Q3 revenue +3% constant currency; AB Mauri and ABFI both solid; guidance unchanged.
  • Agriculture Q3 revenue -14% constant currency on lower compound feed sales; disposed of one of nine UK compound feed mills; guidance unchanged.
  • Retail/Food demerger on track to complete before end of 2027 calendar year (as announced 21 April 2026).
  • Lucy Slinger to join as Primark CFO in September (announced 11 June).
  • George Weston: "The Group delivered a resilient trading performance in the third quarter."
  • Weston on Sugar: "the duration and severity of the Middle East conflict have increased gas price expectations for next year, which has impacted our European profit outlook."

body:
• Board unanimously and unequivocally rejected Prologis's possible offer, stating it "falls a long way short of SEGRO's own views on value."
  • Proposal currently worth 881p per SEGRO share, reflecting a 5% decline since the offer period began (down from 925p on 23 June, driven by Prologis share price falling from $145.3 to $138.9).
  • SEGRO to publish a detailed growth strategy and value update in the week commencing 6 July, covering development pipeline and data centre strategy.
  • Key rejection arguments:
  • Inadequate: fails to reflect logistics development pipeline, data centre pipeline, portfolio scarcity, operating platform quality, or any change-of-control premium.
  • Opportunistic: timed to share price dislocation from the Middle East conflict; pre-conflict (27 Feb 2026) the proposal implied only a 6% headline premium (890p vs 841p share price).
  • One-sided: SEGRO holders would swap 100% exposure to SEGRO for only a c.10.5% stake in the combined group (based on 0.084 exchange ratio).
  • Board emphasises "Capital is not a constraint" to delivering the standalone growth strategy — balance sheet and platform sufficient without Prologis.
  • Chairman Andy Harrison: "Prologis is trying to acquire SEGRO on the cheap when our share price has been dislocated by the Middle East conflict and at a price that reflects none of the quality, scarcity and growth embedded in the business."
  • Harrison added: "We have unanimously rejected their Proposal because we continue to believe our compelling standalone investment case can deliver superior shareholder value."
  • SEGRO urges shareholders to take no action.
  • PUSU deadline: 5.00pm on 22 July 2026 — Prologis must either announce a firm Rule 2.7 offer or walk away (subject to Panel extension).
  • Rule 2.9: 1,353,927,858 ordinary shares in issue; no treasury shares.
  • Advisers: Evercore, Morgan Stanley (also joint corporate broker), UBS (also joint corporate broker); Slaughter and May as legal adviser; FTI Consulting for PR.

  • Covers up to 100% of school-certified cost of attendance; fixed and variable rate options; interest-only or P&I repayment choices; 0.25pp rate reduction for autopay.
  • Soft-pull prequalification available (no credit score impact); 100% U.S.-based support.
  • Extends existing suite alongside undergraduate, graduate, and career training loans (nursing, health, medical, aviation, law).
  • Patrick Freeman, SVP: "Families have different priorities when deciding how to pay for college; while many parents choose to cosign a student loan, others prefer to borrow in their own name to support their student's higher education goals."
  • Strategic read-through: product launch targets the Parent PLUS addressable market at a time of federal student lending reform, potentially expanding SLM's private origination TAM beyond its traditional cosigned undergraduate channel.

  • Open Lending Board unanimously recommends shareholders tender their shares.
  • Offer expires one minute after 11:59pm NYC time on 27 July 2026; Outside Date of 15 October 2026 (auto-extended to 15 December 2026 if HSR is sole outstanding condition).
  • Deal structured as Section 251(h) DGCL merger — no shareholder vote required post-tender.
  • Premium: ~78% to 90-day VWAP as of 15 June 2026; ~132% premium vs 13 February 2026 unaffected price; ~48% vs 11 June 2026 close of $2.13.
  • Supporting Stockholders (CEO Jessica Buss, Bregal Sagemount, Nebula Holdings) holding ~12.8% of shares have signed Tender and Support Agreements.
  • Termination fee: $13.58m (~3.5% of equity value) payable by Open Lending in specified scenarios; reduced from ANV's initial 4.5% proposal.
  • Financing: $100m equity commitment + $250m debt commitment; no financing condition.
  • Background highlights:
  • AmTrust (key insurance partner) made unsolicited approaches in 2025 at $2.00 (April), raised to $3.00 (May), both rejected; AmTrust paused in July 2025 and extended insurance partnership through 2033 in August 2025.
  • ANV (newly formed AmTrust/Blackstone MGA platform) approached December 2025; verbal offer escalated from $3.25 → $3.50 then cut to $3.00 in Feb 2026 citing "concerns regarding the Company's recent certified loan volume trends," before settling at $3.15.
  • Targeted market check of 8 parties (5 sponsors, 3 strategics) produced no competing offers.
  • Process paused late Feb–May 2026 while ANV restructured; ANV reaffirmed $3.15 on 26 May 2026.
  • Updated June 2026 Management Forecasts (provided to ANV) — Revenue: 2026E $118.6m, 2027E $185.0m, growing to $274.4m by 2030E; Adjusted EBITDA: 2026E $43.8m, scaling to $168.0m by 2030E.

  • Board noted Q1 2026 results led to decreased certified loan volume guidance but increased Adj EBITDA from improved profit share economics.
  • FT Partners DCF implied $2.68–$3.91/share; selected public companies $1.35–$2.80; precedent transactions $1.74–$2.42.
  • FT Partners fee: ~$8.7m total ($1m on opinion, remainder contingent on close).

body:
• Agreed to acquire Kayne Anderson Real Estate (KARE) for upfront enterprise value of ~$1,393m: $759m cash + ~189m newly issued Bridgepoint shares (~$634m equity), plus performance-based earn-out.
  • Vendor is Kayne Anderson Capital Advisors; KARE is a Boca Raton-based real estate platform with $22bn AUM across equity and debt strategies.
  • Combined Enlarged Group AUM ~$117bn across 5 verticals: PE $40bn, credit $21bn, infrastructure $30bn, real estate $22bn, secondaries $4bn.
  • Valuation: high single-digit multiple of 2027E EBITDA, falling to mid-single-digit by 2028; KARE 2027E EBITDA guided $130–190m.
  • EPS accretion: mid-single-digit % in 2027, >20% in 2028; FRE accretive from 2027.
  • Cash funded via existing balance sheet and credit facilities (incl. £400m bridge facility entered 5 June 2026 with Lloyds).
  • Expected to close end of 2026; subject to shareholder approval, regulatory approvals, fund consents. Shareholders representing ~36% have given irrevocable undertakings to vote in favour.
  • Earn-out: up to 102.5m additional Bridgepoint shares in 2030, tied to management fee revenue hurdles ($100m minimum / $150m target Earn-Out Revenue), measured at 31 Dec 2029.
  • KARE management (CEO Al Rabil, CIO David Selznick) to continue running business under new "Kayne Bridgepoint" brand; equity subject to staggered lock-ups to 2029.
  • Acquired perimeter: 100% of KARE FRE, 15% of carry in historic funds (KAREP VI/VII, KAROD II, KARED IV), 100% of KCRED economics, up to 35% of carry in future funds.
  • Pro forma mix shift: US-domiciled management fees rise from 28% → 42%; real assets rise from ~⅓ → ~45% of AUM; FRE/EBITDA rises from ~50% → ~60%; largest-fund concentration drops from ~20% → ~15%.
  • Adds >115 new institutional LP relationships with limited overlap (only 5 of Bridgepoint's top 50 LPs overlap with KARE).
  • KARE track record: ~20% AUM CAGR 2019–May 2026; KAREP VII closed oversubscribed at $5.12bn on 15 May 2026, nearly 2x predecessor.
  • KARE 2025 financials: $141m net management fees, $63.6m gross profit; gross assets $598.2m (predates KAREP VII final close).
  • KARE standalone medium-term guidance: $15bn fundraising expected over next 3 years at >1% blended fee rate; management fee growth 20–30% p.a.; FRE margin 60–70%; EBITDA margin ~65–70% in 2027, >70% medium-term; PRE 5–10% of income in 2027, 20–30% medium-term.
  • Incremental interest expense: ~£30m in 2027, ~£25m p.a. from 2028.
  • Updated Bridgepoint standalone guidance: 2027 EBITDA £390–460m; 2024–2026 fundraising guidance raised to €28bn.
  • Pro forma management fees rise from £435m to £540m for 2025; illustrative Enlarged Group EBITDA CAGR >30%, EBITDA margin trending above 60%.

body:
• Group Ore Reserve grew 62% to 5.0Moz Au (157Mt at 0.99g/t Au & 0.12% Cu) plus 196kt Cu, post 15 months of mining depletion vs December 2024 ORE.
  • Telfer Reserve +150% to 1.8Moz Au (119Mt at 0.46g/t Au & 0.06% Cu) plus 68kt Cu, after depletion — driven by just the first ~half of the FY26 240,000m drill program.
  • West Dome Open Pit Reserve +375% to 1.4Moz Au (90.6Mt at 0.46g/t Au); higher-grade component 70.8Mt at 0.53g/t for 1.2Moz.
  • Main Dome Underground maiden Reserve of 0.2Moz (3.6Mt at 1.33g/t Au & 0.31% Cu), confirming multi-year underground mine-life extension.
  • Stockpiles contribute 22.5Mt at 0.36g/t Au for 0.3Moz Au + 11kt Cu, providing processing flexibility.
  • Havieron Reserve unchanged at 3.3Moz Au & 128kt Cu (38.5Mt at 2.63g/t Au & 0.33% Cu).
  • West Dome Underground (WDU) and Vertical Stockwork Corridor (VSC) deliberately excluded from this ORE — both remain in Resource pending ongoing studies, flagged as the key future growth lever.
  • Telfer residual resources outside ORE: WDO 3.5Moz (244Mt at 0.45g/t), Underground 2.6Moz (53.9Mt at 1.53g/t Au & 0.37% Cu) across MDU/WDU/VSC.
  • Upside flagged: potential to convert 42% more gold from Inferred treated as waste in open pit shell, and 8% more in underground shapes; Inferred→Indicated conversion running at >85%.
  • Telfer March 2026 MRE update: ~15Mt converted from Inferred to Indicated at WDO; total WDO MRE now 336Mt at 0.45g/t Au for 4.9Moz Au & 148kt Cu.
  • Economic assumptions: Telfer medium-term prices A$4,000/oz Au and A$6.00/lb Cu; Havieron long-term A$2,500/oz Au and A$4.60/lb Cu — both well below spot (~A$5,930/oz Au, ~A$8.70/lb Cu), implying material reserve price leverage.
  • Financial close achieved on Facility B of the $500m corporate debt facility — a $225m undrawn 7-year RCF for working capital, general corporate purposes and Havieron development.

  • However, Board willing to grant limited commercial diligence access in the hope of eliciting a more attractive proposal.

With good sales growth, higher margins and an increased dividend, we are delivering improved shareholder returns alongside a more compelling customer proposition."

• Board unanimously and unequivocally rejected an unsolicited possible offer from Prologis, received on 16 June 2026, for the entire issued and to be issued share capital.
  • Proposal terms: 0.084 new Prologis shares per SEGRO share, implying 925 pence per SEGRO share based on Prologis' $145.3 close and 1.32 GBP:USD on 23 June 2026.

  • Board characterised the approach as "opportunistically timed", exploiting the dislocation between SEGRO's share price and underlying business value.
  • Cites major geopolitical issues adversely impacting UK/European real estate trading valuations relative to US REITs as accentuating the dislocation — a key strategic rationale for Prologis (US REIT) bidding for a UK peer.
  • Board reiterated confidence in standalone strategy, citing strong balance sheet, building occupational market momentum, large development pipeline, and "exceptional data centre platform."
  • PUSU deadline: 5.00pm London time on 22 July 2026 — Prologis must either announce a firm Rule 2.7 offer or walk away by then (extendable only with Panel consent).
  • Announcement made without Prologis' consent; no certainty of firm offer.

body:
• Board proposes managed wind-down and return of capital to shareholders, subject to investor approval; circular and general meeting (expected August 2026) to follow, requiring 50% of voting shareholders in favour.
  • Board concluded that continuation, corporate sale or thematic pivot would not meaningfully close the discount given structural shift to larger, more liquid UK equities.
  • Wind-down expected to take c.2–3 years to allow asset management initiatives to maximise realisation values.
  • Board states portfolio can be realised in the direct property market "at a value in excess of what is currently implied by the prevailing share price".
  • Underlying EPRA earnings (pre-exceptionals) €3.6m vs €3.9m prior year (-7.7%).
  • IFRS profit of €1.1m (vs €(0.1)m loss in H1 FY25).
  • NAV €151.3m / 115.1 cps, down from adjusted €154.2m / 117.3 cps at 30 Sept 2025 (-1.9% per share); driven by unrealised revaluation losses.
  • Prior period error of €2.5m identified (service charge misclassification 2021–2024), restating opening NAV down by 1.9 cps.
  • NAV total return +0.7% (H1 FY25: +0.3%).
  • Dividends declared 2.96 cps for the half, 93% covered by EPRA earnings; yield c.8.6% on 59.6p share price (19 June 2026).

  • Exchange ratio: 0.084 new Prologis shares per SEGRO share, implying 925p per SEGRO share and valuing SEGRO at ~£12.6bn.
  • Implied premia vs 23 June close: 24.6% to spot (742p), 26.7% to 1-month VWAP, 31.4% to 3-month VWAP.
  • Offer pitched at SEGRO's 31 Dec 2025 EPRA NTA of 925p (i.e. zero premium to NTA) — likely a key sticking point for the SEGRO Board.
  • SEGRO holders would own ~10.5% of the enlarged Prologis (market cap ~$140.9bn).
  • PUSU deadline: 5:00pm London on 22 July 2026 to either firm up under Rule 2.7 or walk away.
  • Prologis reserves right to lower terms with Board recommendation, on a competing bid below this value, or following a SEGRO Rule 9 waiver/reverse takeover; and to adjust for any SEGRO dividends.
  • Strategic rationale highlighted by Prologis:
  • SEGRO has traded at an average discount to EPRA NTA of 19% (2yr) and 17% (3yr), framed as a structural constraint.
  • Balance sheet gap: Prologis Net Debt/EV 22% vs SEGRO 37%; Net Debt/Adjusted EBITDA 4.8x vs 8.4x.
  • Claims superior capital access can accelerate monetisation of SEGRO's development, power and data centre pipeline.
  • TSR comparison: Prologis 3yr 37% / 5yr 39% vs SEGRO 3yr 19% / 5yr -20%.
  • Anticipates "significant synergies" (unquantified) from integration.
  • Advisers to Prologis: Rothschild & Co, J.P. Morgan, Eastdil Secured; Brunswick PR; Linklaters legal.
  • No financing details, cash alternative, or synergy quantification disclosed — pure stock deal as currently structured.

body:
• Board intends to present formal proposals to shareholders for a managed wind-down of the Company and return of capital, after reviewing options to address the persistent NAV discount.
  • Drivers cited: equity market disadvantage for sub-£100m market cap vehicles, institutional preference for larger vehicles with better liquidity/diversification/cost efficiencies, and macro uncertainty.
  • Alternatives considered and rejected: share buybacks and transition to thematic/sector-specific investments — not expected to materially close the discount.
  • Board view: portfolio can be realised in the direct property market at a value in excess of what is currently implied by the prevailing share price.
  • Portfolio comprises 14 assets across France, Germany and the Netherlands.
  • Wind-down expected to take approximately two to three years, allowing for targeted asset management and management of the French tax litigation.
  • Realisations via single or multi-asset disposals; proceeds to repay borrowings and return capital to shareholders.
  • Investment Manager (Schroders) in discussions on revised management terms during wind-down to align with maximising shareholder returns; details in forthcoming Circular.
  • Circular to be published in due course; general meeting to seek ordinary resolution modifying investment objective and policy.
  • Dividends to continue to maintain investment trust status, but level will decline as portfolio income reduces and capital is returned.
  • Over £80 million of dividend payments since IPO (December 2015) cited as track record.
  • Fund Manager Jeff O'Dwyer: "the ongoing discount to NAV has hindered our ability to scale and achieve our growth potential, particularly against the deteriorating market backdrop."
  • Chairman Phil Redding: "more recent interest rate and inflationary concerns" have exacerbated the persistent material discount to NAV.
  • Redding added: "a managed wind-down strategy and return of capital is in the best interests of the Company's shareholders."

body:
• Board unanimously rejected an unsolicited, indicative and conditional proposal from Castlelake, L.P. received 20 June 2026 to acquire all shares not already held by Castlelake at £6.25 per share in cash, with a partial alternative of unlisted, non-transferrable, non-voting shares in a Castlelake-structured vehicle.
  • Bidding vehicle would be 49% owned by Castlelake and 51% by EU nationals and potentially other undisclosed investors.
  • This is the third proposal — prior bids at £5.60 and £6.00 per share were also unanimously rejected.
  • Board called the bid "highly opportunistic", delivered against a "temporarily depressed share price" and said it "fundamentally undervalues easyJet and its prospects."
  • Board criticised Castlelake's analysis as relying on Middle East conflict-affected share prices, short-term earnings and analyst reports, with no adequate control premium.
  • Board flagged concerns over opaque ownership structure, elevated leverage and overall conditionality of the proposal.
  • Reaffirmed investment grade balance sheet with net cash position.
  • Cited 46% increase in pre-tax profit over the two financial years to September 2025, driven by easyJet Holidays growth and operational improvement.
  • Reiterated medium-term target of >£1bn profit before tax, despite current-year Middle East conflict disruption.
  • Fleet renewal: 17 A320neo/A321neo deliveries in FY26, a further 73 across FY27–FY28, with 79 older A319s retired on accelerated basis — driving upgauging and fuel efficiency gains.
  • easyJet Holidays: delivered prior £250m PBT target early; new target of £450m PBT by 2030 with no capital intensity.
  • Additional growth levers cited: route maturity gains from network rebalancing (incl. Milan Linate and Rome Fiumicino slot acquisitions), tech-driven cost efficiencies, and premiumisation (business traffic, loyalty, bag connectivity, partnerships).
  • Board concluded the proposal represents an opportunistic attempt to acquire easyJet "on the cheap".
  • Announcement made without Castlelake's consent; shareholders advised to take no action.

  • Possible Offer rejected by the IP Group Board (most recent proposal tabled on 16 June 2026).
  • Total indicative value: 69.7p per share (plus up to 5p CVR), comprising:
  • 59p cash per share ("Cash Offer")
  • ~10.7p per share representing pro rata value of IP Group's stake in Oxford Nanopore (ONT) at 116.5p ONT close
  • CVR of up to 5p linked to disposal of Istesso stake within 12 months: 3p if proceeds ≥£98m, additional 2p if >£200m
  • Cash Offer represents a 48% premium to IP Group's 25 March 2026 price (stripping out ONT stake and net cash) — 25 March being the date Saba Capital disclosed lifting its stake to 12.01%.
  • Railpen intends to roll over its entire existing 18.4% stake into the transaction (not cash out).
  • Strategic rationale: Railpen believes IP Group's "strategic aims would therefore be best served in the private markets," citing persistent NAV discount, difficulty raising equity, and mismatch between public market horizons and patient venture capital.
  • Plans to assemble a consortium of pension funds managing >£235bn collectively to back a scaled third-party venture/scale-up manager aligned with HMG's productive finance agenda.
  • Pre-conditions: (1) consortium formation; (2) satisfactory confirmatory due diligence; (3) unanimous unconditional board recommendation.
  • Istesso context: IP Group holds undiluted 56.5% stake, carried at £98m in 31 Dec 2025 NAV; described as developing oral regenerative medicines.
  • PUSU deadline: 5.00pm on 20 July 2026 for Railpen to announce firm intention or walk away.
  • Rothschild & Co acting as financial adviser to Railpen.
  • Railpen invites institutional shareholders to engage and pressure the board to enter discussions.

  • Marine: revenue +2% to £1,591.5m; underlying op loss £29.8m (Type 31 charge); ex-Type 31 margin 6.5% (+40bps).
  • Nuclear: revenue +14% to £2,070.4m; margin +70bps to 9.5%; Cavendish Nuclear +18%.
  • Land: revenue -3% to £1,084.4m (back to growth in H2); margin +110bps to 8.8%.

body:
• Castlelake has made a Rule 2.4 announcement disclosing three rejected non-binding indicative cash proposals for easyJet, going public after the Board declined to engage.
  • First Proposal: 560p cash (12 June) – rejected 16 June.
  • Second Proposal: 600p cash (17 June) – rejected 20 June.
  • Third Proposal: 625p cash per share (20 June) – rejected 21 June; now disclosed to shareholders ahead of the PUSU deadline of 5.00pm on 26 June 2026.
  • 625p represents a ~59% premium to the 394.20p undisturbed price (28 May 2026) and ~71% premium to the VWAP since the 16 April interim trading update (365.42p).
  • 35% premium to the 464.00p close on 27 February 2026 (pre US-Iran conflict) and ~39% to the 12-month VWAP of 449.50p.
  • Offer is above every closing price since 25 February 2022 and above all post-16 April 2026 analyst price targets (range 280p–570p; Morgan Stanley lowest, Barclays highest).
  • Implies a 16.5x P/E on 2027E EPS (37.9p FactSet).
  • Castlelake argues 625p compares favourably to the NPV of easyJet's share price even assuming the company achieves its >£1bn medium-term PBT aspiration (modelled for 2029) at 5–10yr average EV/EBITDA multiples of 3.2x–4.3x.
  • Partial equity alternative to be offered, allowing shareholders to roll into the private vehicle, subject to a cap and transfer restrictions.
  • Castlelake reserves right to reduce offer by any dividend/distribution declared post-announcement.
  • EU ownership compliance structure: EU national partners Peter Bellew and Mark Breen (ex-LCC executives) will hold a controlling stake via an EU-owned/controlled vehicle ("EU Partner"), mirroring structures used by other EU airlines.
  • Bellew acquired 50,000 easyJet shares (~0.007%) between 2 March and 20 May 2026 at a top price of 437.14p – under Rule 6, any firm offer cannot be below 437.14p.
  • Financing: fully funded via committed equity from Castlelake funds, co-investors and the EU Partner, with Goldman Sachs "highly confident" of arranging required debt.
  • Castlelake is strategically partnered with Brookfield (>$1tn AUM) and has invested >$24bn in aviation since 2005 across 200+ airline relationships; AUM ~$38bn.
  • Intends to implement via scheme of arrangement (with right to switch to contractual offer); pre-conditions include satisfactory due diligence and definitive documentation.
  • Post-acquisition, easyJet stated to remain "well-capitalised, with a robust capital structure and ample liquidity."
  • Castlelake quote on rationale: ambition to support easyJet as "a stronger, more resilient European airline under European control."
  • No certainty a firm Rule 2.7 offer will be made; next required announcement by 5pm 26 June 2026 unless Panel extends.

• Group adjusted revenue +25% to £1,716m; adjusted operating profit marginally lower at £219.4m (FY25: £222.8m), but +18% ex-DfT TOCs.
  • Adjusted EPS 20.3p vs 19.4p (+4.6%), aided by FY26 £50m buyback; basic EPS 21.4p (FY25: 21.3p).

  • Final dividend 5.0p; full-year 7.2p (+10.8% vs 6.5p); policy to move from c.3x cover toward 2.5x cover over time.
  • New £100m buyback announced, to complete over next 12 months (follows £50m completed in FY26); £89m total returned in FY26.
  • c.£400m free cash flow guided over next three years, including c.£90m cash inflow from DfT TOCs/Rail Services as GWR and WCP transition.
  • Adjusted net debt £137.7m (FY25: £86.9m); reported net debt £725.3m (FY25: £985.6m) post IFRS 16 lease run-off; £364.1m undrawn committed headroom; leverage policy <2.0x adjusted net debt:EBITDA.
  • Free cash flow £73.8m before acquisitions/returns (FY25: £113.5m); capex stepped up to c.£190m, mainly First Bus electrification.
  • First Bus revenue +33% to £1,443.6m; adjusted op profit +7% to £102.8m despite £26m fare-funding cut, c.£15m NIC headwind, and 3% volume decline (transition to £3 fare cap, weaker consumer confidence).
  • First Bus margin -180bps to 7.1% (lower-margin franchising mix); Regional Bus margin 8.8% (FY25: 9.7%), with NIC a 1.7pp drag.
  • First Bus London contributed £310m revenue, ahead of acquisition assumptions; 99% of FY27 contracted revenues secured, 77% for FY28.
  • Business & Coach revenue +28% to £230.1m; five coach acquisitions (3 in-year, 2 post period); Flixbus launched and extended.
  • Electrification: 26% of UK bus fleet zero emission (43% of London red buses); 4 fully + 17 substantially electrified depots; third-party charging at 15 depots; minority stake in Palmer Energy Technology for battery storage.
  • Fuel hedging: 88% of FY27 diesel hedged at 43p/litre, 54% of FY28 at 41p; electricity 77% FY27 at £74/MWh, 72% FY28 at £73/MWh.
  • First Rail adjusted revenue £272.4m (FY25: £288.8m); adjusted op profit £129.9m (FY25: £148.8m), hit by Stirling mobilisation costs of £6.3m, c.£2m higher Lumo infrastructure charge, SWR transfer, and normalised DfT TOC variable fees.
  • Open access revenue £109.3m (+3%); journeys +4% to 3.1m; H2 yields pressured by LNER East Coast capacity/price competition and weaker leisure demand; pence per seat mile flat at 11.1p.
  • London Overground contract started 3 May 2026: c.£300m annual revenue, 8-year term + 2-year option (c.£3bn total); TfL retains revenue risk.
  • On track to more than double open access capacity in 2-3 years: Lumo Glasgow extension and extra Hull Trains/Lumo paths from Dec 2025; Stirling-London fully operational July 2026; Carmarthen and Lumo 10-car from FY29; applications for c.1bn additional annual seat miles under ORR review.
  • DfT TOC transitions: SWR transferred May 2025; GWR to transfer 13 December 2026 (c.£15m op profit / c.£9m earnings reduction); WCP expected around end of FY27.
  • FY27 outlook: Group adjusted EPS to be maintained from higher-quality earnings base.
  • FY27 segment guidance: First Bus revenue just over £1.5bn with further op profit growth and c.£140m decarbonisation capex; open access revenue c.£130-150m with margin progressing to mid-teens post 2-yr Stirling/Carmarthen ramp; London Overground c.£300m.
  • First Bus capex to normalise to c.£80-100m p.a. from FY28; Stirling and Carmarthen routes each targeted at c.£50m annual revenue at mid-teens margin post 2-year ramp.
  • c.£9m Group cost savings delivered in FY26 from restructuring; central costs down to £13.3m (FY25: £22.0m).
  • Prior-year accounting restatements: £167.6m DfT levy reclassified from revenue deduction to expense (no profit impact); First Bus London PPA finalised.
  • CEO Graham Sutherland: "Our strong performance in FY 2026 against significant headwinds has reinforced our track record for delivery and shareholder returns."

  • First retailer globally to exceed 1m Trustpilot reviews at 4.9/5.
  • Mobile business now profitable; improved network commercial terms agreed in principle.
  • musicMagpie now run-rate profitable on annualised basis (from c.£6m loss-making at acquisition 15 months ago), aided by US exit, warehouse consolidation, and Timpson trade-in partnership (1,300+ stores).
  • Switch24 launched H2 FY26 (initial iPhone supply constraints); AO Mobile MVNO launched post year-end in friendly user trials, full launch in Q1 FY27.
  • Offshoring of inbound sales to South Africa delivered c.£2m savings (c.£4m annualised); majority of customer engagement to be offshore by end FY27.
  • SG&A +14.9% to £266.7m (21.1% of revenue vs 20.4%); advertising +20.4% driven by PPC +£8.4m, partly offset by -£4m Mobile acquisition spend; warehousing +21.1% on labour inflation and musicMagpie.
  • National Insurance/NMW changes added c.£8.5m to Group operating costs YoY; 80% of fuel hedged to March 2027, electricity fixed to October 2027.
  • FY27 capex/lease investment guided to c.£29m (vs lower current levels), including 360 new vehicles (c.£22m lease-funded), ERP, and recycling expansion.
  • ERP spend £3.8m in FY26 (vs £2.0m); WMS upgrade targeted for FY28 completion.

body:
• Update on the 12 May 2026 Rule 2.4 indicative all-share offer for Picton; confirmatory due diligence "advancing well" and documentation being finalised with a view to a Rule 2.7 firm offer announcement.
  • Proposed consideration unchanged: 0.190 LondonMetric shares + 0.881 SREIT shares per Picton share.
  • Based on 15 June 2026 prices (LMP 185.2p, SREIT 47.3p), offer values Picton at £396m / 76.9p per share, a 9.0% premium to Picton's 15 June close and split 46% LondonMetric / 54% SREIT.
  • Implied earnings accretion for Picton holders of 37.7% on a pro-forma basis (using FY26 for Picton/LMP and LTM Dec-25 for SREIT).
  • Dividend income uplift of 46.2% for Picton shareholders (vs Picton Q4 2026 declared dividend of 0.95p).
  • 5.8% discount to Picton GAV (EPRA NIY 4.7%) and 8.6% discount to EPRA NTA.
  • Joint statement from Andrew Jones (LMP CEO) and Nick Montgomery (SREIT FM): "Since announcing our proposal on 12th of May, we have made steady progress and are advancing towards a Rule 2.7 announcement… material and immediate uplift in dividend income for Picton shareholders, while allocating assets to the platforms that we believe are best positioned to unlock their full value".
  • Asset allocation aligned with Picton debt structure:
  • LondonMetric to take Canada Life-secured pool: 22 assets, £320m, 81% industrial / 12% office, NIY 4.7%; plus ~£24m of Picton net cash.
  • SREIT to take Aviva/NatWest/uncharged pool: 22 assets, £380m, 55% industrial / 29% office / 12% retail warehouse, NIY 4.7%.
  • Pro-forma SREIT net LTV ~32% (within 25–35% target range); sub-sector mix largely unchanged.
  • Deal is marginally earnings accretive for LondonMetric and earnings accretive for SREIT in year one.
  • SREIT manager fee concessions: 10bps IMA fee reduction across all tiers, revised tiering 50% NAV / 50% lower of NAV and market cap, plus 1-year IMA fee waiver (spread over 24 months) on Picton NAV share, lowering pro-forma EPRA cost ratio below both standalone levels.
  • Succession planning underway for Nick Montgomery as SREIT fund manager; he remains committed and will lead through transition, retaining oversight as Chair of Schroders' direct real estate Investment Committee; Bradley Biggins continues as Co-Fund Manager.
  • Shareholder support: letter of intent from TR Property Investment Trust (Picton's largest holder, 11.4%, 58.43m shares) to vote in favour; TR reiterated support in its 10 June 2026 final results.
  • Lender support: Canada Life (£129.0m facility) and Aviva (£79.0m facility) have indicated preliminary support and willingness to grant pre-emptive change-of-control waivers, subject to credit approval.
  • Permitted dividends: Picton's 0.95p Q4 dividend (period ending 31 March 2026) plus future ordinary-course dividends covered by cash earnings; any excess triggers consideration reduction or equalisation payment.
  • Pre-conditions to Rule 2.7: completion of due diligence, lender consents/waivers, LMP & SREIT board approvals, and unanimous Picton board recommendation.
  • Consortium not subject to Rule 2.6(a) 28-day PUSU deadline while participating in Picton's formal sale process (Panel dispensation).
  • Deal expected to be implemented via Guernsey scheme of arrangement; no LMP or SREIT shareholder vote required for new share issuance.
  • Track records cited: SREIT EPS CAGR 7.0% and DPS CAGR 5.2% (FY20–FY25); LondonMetric EPS CAGR 7.2% and DPS CAGR 7.6% (FY21–FY26), fully covered.
