body:
• CEO Duncan Wanblad said: "We've delivered a strong start to the year across both Copper and Premium Iron Ore, tracking well to our mine plans. In Copper, the reopening of the second plant at Los Bronces has provided incremental profitable production, Collahuasi continues to progress towards higher grade ore later this year and Quellaveco's recoveries improved, helping to partially offset the expected lower grades through the first half. In Premium Iron Ore, Kumba and Minas-Rio once again delivered stable operational performances. While the conflict in the Middle East is creating considerable volatility in the broader market, our resilient supply chain is currently supporting business continuity, and we are actively managing the situation to address potential adverse effects, including cost inflation.

"We are continuing to execute our portfolio optimisation. We have resumed normal operations at Moranbah North and the sale process for Steelmaking Coal is progressing well, with expectations for a sale to be agreed in the second quarter of 2026. We are progressing the sale process for De Beers and continue to assess further cost and capital preservation measures to minimise the impact from challenging diamond markets. In Nickel, we are working through the European Commission's anti-trust approval process.

"Our merger with Teck, to form a copper-focused global critical minerals champion, is on track for an expected September 2026 to March 2027 close. We were pleased to receive regulatory approval from South Korea in the quarter, with anti-trust approval from China now the final outstanding regulatory milestone, alongside other customary closing conditions. Although we both continue to operate separately until closing, the integration planning is progressing well, ensuring that once the transaction closes, we will be well positioned to begin delivering the exceptional value and expected synergies that we have identified."

  • Group “simplified portfolio” production: Copper 170.4kt (+1% YoY); Premium iron ore 15.2Mt (-2% YoY); Manganese ore (40% share) 759.1kt (+118% YoY).
  • “Exiting businesses” production: Diamonds 7.1Mct (+17% YoY); Steelmaking coal 1.5Mt (-31% YoY); Nickel 9.1kt (-7% YoY).
  • 2026 production and unit cost guidance unchanged for continuing businesses: Copper 700–760kt (unit cost ~172c/lb; Chile ~230c/lb, Peru ~100c/lb); Premium iron ore 55–59Mt (unit cost ~$41/t; Kumba ~$45/t, Minas-Rio ~$36/t).
  • Diamonds guidance unchanged (exiting business): 21–26Mct at unit cost ~$80/ct; De Beers output to be aligned to demand amid weak rough trading conditions.
  • Realised prices vs Q1 2025: Copper 572c/lb (+29%); Premium iron ore (FOB) $91/wmt (-5%); Diamonds $101/ct (-19%) and De Beers price index 68 (-17%); Hard coking coal $199/t (+16%); Nickel $6.71/lb (+7%).
  • Copper: Chile 97.0kt (+9% YoY) driven by throughput (Los Bronces +12% to 48.5kt after second plant restart; Collahuasi attributable +10% to 38.8kt on higher throughput and recoveries 71.8% vs 66.2%, despite lower grades 0.77% vs 0.86%).
  • Collahuasi: processing lower-grade stockpile ore continues until access to higher-grade ROM in Rosario pit “towards the end of the year”; desalination plant commissioning underway and “on track” to ramp up and be fully operational by mid-2026.
  • Peru (Quellaveco): 73.4kt (-8% YoY) on expected lower grades (0.68% vs 0.80%) partly offset by higher recoveries (85.5% vs 80.2%); production still weighted to H2 2026.
  • Copper sales volumes: 166.5kt (-4% YoY) and -5% vs Q4 2025.
  • Premium iron ore: Kumba production 8.8Mt (-2% YoY) with Sishen +5% (to 6.3Mt) offset by Kolomela -15% (to 2.6Mt) due to planned stock drawdown ahead of Q2 rail maintenance.
  • Kumba: sales 9.1Mt (+2% YoY) on improved port performance; finished stock 7.3Mt (vs 7.5Mt in Q4 2025) with mine stock down (4.7Mt from 5.7Mt) and port stock up (2.6Mt from 1.8Mt).
  • Kumba pricing: realised export basket $93/wmt (wet) stated as 8% above Fastmarkets 62% Fe benchmark; Fe content 63.7% (vs 64.2%), lump:fines 65:35 (vs 68:32).
  • Minas-Rio production 6.4Mt (broadly flat / -1% YoY) supported by higher plant utilisation in wet season; realised price $89/wmt stated as 5% above Fastmarkets 65% Fe benchmark.
  • Manganese ore (40% share): +118% YoY driven by easier comps after Cyclone Megan disruption in March 2024; current quarter still impacted by adverse weather incl. Cyclone Narelle.
  • De Beers: rough production 7.13Mct (+17% YoY), with Canada +163% (planned ore release at Gahcho Kué) and Venetia underground +53%; Namibia -12% (vessel maintenance + decommissioning impact).
  • De Beers trading: Q1 rough sales 7.7Mct (consolidated 6.4Mct) from two Sights; consolidated rough sales value $648m (+25% YoY), but average realised price $101/ct (-19%) on weaker price index and lower-value mix; “challenged” trading conditions cited (industry, geopolitical and tariff headwinds).
  • Steelmaking coal: production 1.545Mt (-31% YoY, -25% QoQ) due to Moranbah North post-incident and significant weather impacts at Dawson.
  • Moranbah North: regulator lifted final directives in Feb 2026; site transitioned to normal longwall operations and is ramping up.
  • Steelmaking coal pricing: realised hard coking coal $199/t vs benchmark $235/t; price realisation 85% (vs 93% in Q1 2025) due to lower premium HCC volumes from Moranbah North.
  • Grosvenor: re-entry/rectification “final stages”; longwall restart targeted late 2027 (subject to investment approval) after inspections confirmed limited infrastructure damage and undamaged next-panel longwall equipment.
  • Steelmaking Coal divestment: sale process “progressing well” with expectation for a sale to be agreed in Q2 2026.
  • Nickel: production 9.1kt (-7% YoY) on maintenance at Barro Alto and Codemin; output expected to increase gradually from Q2; sale to MMG Singapore Resources progressing through European Commission anti-trust approval.
  • Portfolio actions referenced during/around the period: delisting from SIX Swiss Exchange (23 Mar 2026); Woodsmith investment agreement with Mitsubishi (20 Feb 2026); FY25 results and final dividend notice (20 Feb 2026).

time_period: Year ended 31 December 2025 (with Q1 2026 update and 2026 guidance)
body:
• CEO Ian Perks: “delivered against a clear set of strategic priorities… [including] significant cost reductions… positioned the company strongly for the successful refinancing, which completed earlier this month… provides… financial foundation and flexibility required to deliver value for stakeholders.”
  • CEO Ian Perks: “A key milestone has been the agreement to purchase the TEN FPSO, a value-accretive acquisition that… eliminates lease costs… [and] capture operating cost savings… extending the Jubilee and TEN petroleum agreements to 2040, and higher oil prices have further strengthened our platform…”
  • Group WI production averaged 40.4 kboepd (2024: 51.5; -21.6%), reflecting portfolio change post-Gabon disposal.
  • Revenue $847m (2024: $1,287m; -34.2%), including hedge impact of $19m (2024: $74m).
  • Adjusted EBITDAX $586m (2024: $1,008m; -41.9%); gross profit $247m (2024: $635m; -61.1%).
  • Continuing operations loss after tax $129m (2024: $55m loss); total profit after tax $7m (2024: $55m; -87%), driven by discontinued ops profit $136m.
  • Free cash flow $99m (2024: $156m; -36.5%); management flags lower realised revenue late-year + delayed Kenya proceeds + delayed Ghana cash calls/gas payments as key drags.
  • Net debt $1,353m (2024: $1,452m; -6.8%); net debt/EBITDAX 2.3x (2024: 1.4x) on lower EBITDAX.
  • YE liquidity headroom $322m (2024: $715m; -54.9%); post-refinancing liquidity headroom stated as “in excess of $200m” (free cash + undrawn facilities).
  • Disposals: Gabon sale completed July for $307m net cash; Kenya sale completed September with $80m received (two tranches) and $40m contingent due no later than 30 June 2033 (oil-price-linked schedule). 2025 proceeds disclosed as $347m.
  • 2025 capex $166m (ex-Gabon; 2024: $179m ex-Gabon) + decommissioning cash/provisioning $17m (2024: $60m).
  • Q1 2026 production averaged 43.4 kboepd, supporting delivery at the higher end of prior 34–42 kboepd guidance (incl. ~6 kboepd gas).
  • Ghana terms strengthened: Jubilee & TEN Petroleum Agreement extensions to 2040 ratified Feb 2026; revised Jubilee gas price terms to end-2040 at an escalating $2.50/mmbtu + heads of terms for potential TEN gas supply + agreed gas payment security mechanism.
  • TEN FPSO acquisition: SPA signed 19 Feb 2026 to buy TEN FPSO for $205m gross / $125.6m net to Tullow, payable on completion end-Q1 2027; intended to remove lease cost and drive Jubilee/TEN operating synergies.
  • 2026 guidance uplift: pre-financing cash flow guidance increased to ~$260–365m at $70–100/bbl (citing YTD production outperformance, higher realised prices, and a higher oil-price assumption); FCF guidance $70–175m at $70–100/bbl.
  • Oil-price leverage disclosed: cash flow +~$40m moving from $70 → $80/bbl, then +~$30m per additional $10/bbl, non-linear due to hedges.
  • FCF guidance includes recovery of 2025 cash call receivables + ~$40m gas revenues from 2026 gas, but excludes $110m historical gas receivables and $50m TEN development debt receivable; GoG receivables at end-2025 stated as ~$225m net to Tullow (split: $65m cash calls, $110m gas, $50m TEN dev debt).
  • Refinancing completed 27 April 2026: Senior Secured Notes extended to 15 Nov 2028 (after $100m paydown; $1.185bn new notes issued + $25m fungible notes to Glencore) and Glencore facility extended to 15 May 2030 (with $21m accrued interest + $2m PIK fees added); new $100m cargo prepayment facility to 15 Nov 2028 (undrawn), with no maintenance covenants.
  • Refinancing structure includes a forward-looking cash sweep tied to maintaining rolling 15-month projected liquidity ≥ $100m; and a conditional maturity “springing” to 15 May 2028 if an M&A process (to commence before end-2026) does not reach a binding SPA within nine months.
  • Going concern assessment period stated to 30 April 2027; reverse stress test implies average oil price of ~$32/bbl over the period would be required to reduce headroom to zero.
  • Operations: average FPSO uptime 97% (Jubilee & TEN) in 2025; Jubilee J72-P onstream July 2025 (currently ~8 kbopd); J74-P onstream Jan 2026; J75-P onstream Mar 2026; total six Jubilee wells expected onstream in 2026 (5 producers + 1 injector), with next producers targeted June/July and injector September.
  • Reserves: audited 2P reserves 100.4 mmboe (2024: 164.5; -39.0%) driven by 2025 production (14.7 mmboe), Gabon disposal (36.0 mmboe) and Jubilee revision (11.8 mmboe); 2P NPV10 ~$1.27bn (price deck starts $62.29/bbl in 2026 rising to $66.24/bbl in 2030, then 2% inflation).
  • Disputes: Kenya Revenue Authority tax assessment ~$170m (VAT/CGT alleged on Kenya disposal) — company states assessment is “wholly without merit”, will contest, no expected cash outflow for objections/appeal and no provision recorded.
  • Governance: four new INEDs announced 8 April 2026 to satisfy refinancing requirements; Henry Steel effective immediately (also SID); Garrett Soden, Euan Shirlaw, James Peterkin effective 1 May 2026 (subject to AGM election in June).
  • Sustainability: routine flaring reduced 22% following FPSO process improvements/modifications in Ghana; reiterates Net Zero by 2030 commitment.

body:
• Q126 RoTE 13.5% (Q125: 14.0%); profit before tax £2.8bn (+3% YoY); attributable profit £1.9bn (+4% YoY); EPS 14.1p (+8% YoY).
  • CEO C. S. Venkatakrishnan: "Barclays delivered another solid quarter with a 13.5% RoTE in Q126, and double-digit returns in all our businesses. This was despite a one-off charge and impairments in the quarter. Top line income grew 6% year-on-year, driven by broad based divisional performance including in the Investment Bank, where we generated over £4bn quarterly income for the first time. The cost: income ratio improved to 56% and earnings per share (EPS) grew by 8% to 14.1p. Our capital position remains robust with a 14.1% common equity tier 1 (CET1) ratio and we are announcing a £500m buyback today. The breadth and quality of our businesses mean we remain confident in delivering all our financial targets across a range of environments. This includes greater than 12% RoTE in 2026 and greater than 14% RoTE in 2028."
  • Announced intention to initiate a share buyback of up to £500m, to start after completion of the ongoing £1.0bn buyback announced at FY25 results.
  • Reiterated all 2026 and 2028 targets (incl. >12% RoTE in 2026 and >14% RoTE in 2028; CET1 target range 13–14%; 2024–26 capital returns ≥£10bn with quarterly buybacks; planned £2bn dividend for 2026; 2025–28 income >5% CAGR; cost:income high-50s in 2026 / low-50s in 2028 with c.£2bn gross efficiency savings in 2026–28).
  • Group income £8.2bn (+6% YoY); investment bank income £4.0bn (+4% YoY) with over £4bn quarterly income for the first time.
  • Group cost:income ratio improved to 56% (Q125: 57%); delivered c.£150m gross cost efficiency savings in Q126; total operating expenses £4.5bn (+4% YoY).
  • Credit impairment charges £0.8bn (Q125: £0.6bn); loan loss rate 74bps (Q125: 61bps) including a £0.2bn single-name impairment in the Investment Bank (c. 20bps impact on Group LLR).
  • FY26 impairment guidance: Group LLR expected around the top end of the 50–60bps through-the-cycle range (explicitly linked to the Q126 single-name charge).
  • Capital: CET1 ratio 14.1% (Dec-25: 14.3%); RWAs £364.5bn (Dec-25: £356.8bn). Pro-forma for the new £500m buyback, CET1 would be 13.9% (top end of 13–14% target range).
  • CET1 bridge highlights: +53bps from attributable profit; -41bps from shareholder distributions (incl. FY25 £1.0bn buyback + FY26 dividend accrual); RWAs +£7.7bn (incl. £5.5bn ex-FX, mainly UK lending growth + higher Global Markets activity).
  • UK leverage ratio 4.8% (Dec-25: 5.1%) as leverage exposure rose £74.0bn to £1,321.3bn, mainly higher Global Markets activity.
  • Liquidity: liquidity pool £326.1bn (down £11.7bn vs Dec-25); average LCR 165.4% (Dec-25: 170.0%); average NSFR 135.4% (Dec-25: 135.2%); deposits £587.6bn (slightly up vs Dec-25) driven by IB International Corporate Bank deposit growth.
  • MREL: issued £3.0bn equivalent of MREL instruments in Q126; MREL ratio 35.4% vs requirement 30.5% (ex-PRA buffer).
  • Barclays UK: RoTE 19.7% (Q125: 17.4%); income £2.26bn (+9%); NII £2.0bn (+9%); NIM 3.72% (+17bps); PBT £863m (+14%). Loans £217.8bn (+£1.3bn vs Dec-25, mortgage-led); deposits £243.9bn (-£0.7bn, seasonal).
  • UK Corporate Bank: RoTE 19.9% (Q125: 17.1%); income £530m (+10%); NII £394m (+15%); PBT £273m (+32%); impairments £3m (Q125: £19m).
  • Private Bank & Wealth Mgmt: RoTE 25.5% (Q125: 34.5%); income £347m (flat); costs +9%; PBT £92m (-25%); net new assets under management £1.5bn (Q125: £1.0bn); client assets & liabilities £223.8bn (-£3.8bn vs Dec-25, negative markets partly offset by inflows/FX).
  • Investment Bank: RoTE 15.0% (Q125: 16.2%); income £4.03bn (+4%); Global Markets £2.83bn (+6%) driven by Equities +16%; Banking fees & underwriting £754m (+17%) with Advisory +78% and ECM +31% (DCM -6%). PBT £1.62bn (-5%) as impairments rose to £279m (incl. £228m single-name).
  • US Consumer Bank: RoTE 18.8% (Q125: 4.5%); income £983m (+14%); NII £823m (+21%) and NIM 12.76% (Q125: 10.53%); PBT £236m (Q125: £55m). Impairments £367m (down vs £399m); card arrears ticked up (30/90 day 3.1%/1.7%).
  • UK motor finance redress (CFSL): FCA final rules published March 2026; Barclays increased provision by £105m in Q126 to £430m (Dec-25: £325m). Barclays: "has decided not to challenge the FCA's final rules in the interests of enabling a swift resolution for customers. However, Barclays strongly disagrees with aspects which require financial redress even where customers suffered no demonstrable financial harm."
  • USCB portfolio changes (Q226): exited American Airlines co-branded partnership on 24 April 2026, releasing c.$5bn RWAs and estimated gain on sale c.$300m; expects to complete Best Egg acquisition around 1 May 2026 for $800m (expected c.$500m goodwill & intangibles). Estimated net impact of both transactions expected to marginally increase Group CET1 in Q226.
  • FX impact: 7% YoY appreciation of average GBP vs USD reduced income/profits (and reduced reported opex/impairments), cited as a material headwind across Group/IB/USCB.
  • Structural hedge: gross structural hedge contribution £1,660m (Q125: £1,335m); structural hedge notional £241.8bn (Dec-25: £236.1bn); average structural hedge duration c.3.5 years.

• Leeds local planning committee passed a resolution to approve a planning application from Harworth and MSFT MCIO Ltd (a Microsoft subsidiary) at Skelton Grange.
  • Application covers a data centre campus (with associated infrastructure) plus outline planning for a warehouse building.
  • Proposed development: 500,000 sq ft across three data centre halls and auxiliary buildings.
  • Additional scope includes 160,000 sq ft of industrial & logistics space and EV charging on Harworth’s adjoining 16-acre plot.
  • Phase 1 of the Microsoft transaction completed in June 2024: GBP51.2m for 27 acres; Harworth continues remediation and enabling works for Microsoft.
  • Phase 2 covers 21 acres; Harworth expects a further GBP53.2m on completion of the sale to Microsoft.
  • CEO Lynda Shillaw said: “Obtaining the resolution to grant planning consent is demonstrable progress towards the completion of the Plot 2 sale and reflects our close and effective collaboration with Microsoft,”
  • Shillaw added: “This transaction has driven group level value growth and facilitates investment in the region, catalysing economic growth, with Skelton Grange estimated to deliver GBP4 billion of inward investment when the development completes.”

time_period: Broker reaction to FY results; outlook/forecast changes covering FY2026–FY2028
body:
• Shares fell 3.0% to 334.10p on Monday morning after two broker downgrades.
  • Goldman Sachs double-downgraded the stock to ‘sell’ from ‘buy’; Citigroup downgraded to ‘neutral’ from ‘buy’.
  • Goldman said FY2026 Ebit and free cash flow were in line with its expectations, but: “the outlook from here is likely to be more challenging”.
  • Goldman’s macro rationale: UK household consumption growth expected at 0.6% YoY in 2026 (its lowest since 2009 excluding Covid) and April’s GfK survey showing higher intentions to save rather than spend.
  • Goldman now forecasts another year of flat retail Ebit, assuming still-elevated price inflation and grocery Ebit growth offset by FY2027 Argos like-for-like sales -2% and an Ebit decline amid a “demanding macro outlook, and growing competitive intensity”.
  • Goldman flagged the recently launched Chinese marketplace Joybuy as a competitive threat, noting 300,000 active users in March.
  • Goldman cut FY2027/FY2028 Ebit forecasts by 4% and 6%, and lowered its price target to 335p (from 390p).
  • Goldman rationale for the rating shift: “With our new [target price] implying 3% downside versus sector average 14% upside, we move to a sell rating on the shares (from buy),” the bank said.
  • Citigroup cut FY2027/FY2028 EPS forecasts by 10% and 12% to reflect weaker guidance for the current financial year.
  • Citi reduced FY2027 Ebit forecast by 7% to GBP1.05bn, citing “continued headwinds from wage inflation and price investment amid a competitive market backdrop.”
  • Citi kept FY2027 grocery sales growth forecast at 4.3% (vs consensus 4.5%), assuming ongoing volume momentum, but expects Sainsbury to “under-inflate the market” via price investment to defend improved relative price positioning.
  • Citi lowered its price target to 335p (from 377p), maintaining valuation at ~13x FY2027 P/E (in line with long-run sector average).

time_period: Quarter ended 31 March 2026 (plus post-period updates to 24 April 2026)
body:
• Uranium spot market volatility during the quarter: near-term trading range from mid-US$80s/lb to just above US$100/lb, with activity driven in part by financial buying.
  • Term market strengthened: reported term prices US$90–93/lb; increased contracting activity expected to influence spot purchasing patterns and may add upward pressure.
  • U3O8 holdings at 31 March 2026: 23,114,230 lb (stored in Canada and France).
  • Holdings increased by 1,431,912 lb (+6.6%) vs 31 Dec 2025 (21,682,318 lb), reflecting: (i) 1,331,912 lb delivery from Kazatomprom (16 March 2026) and (ii) 100,000 lb spot purchase delivered 20 March 2026 (Orano, France).
  • Equity raise: completed an oversubscribed placing of ~13m shares on 17 Feb 2026, raising gross proceeds of ~£80.6m (≈US$110m).
  • 2026 Kazatomprom option: elected to purchase 1,160,766 lb at US$86.15/lb (aggregate US$100.0m); delivery expected H2 2026.
  • 2025 Kazatomprom option (settled in-quarter): option exercised Sept 2025 to buy 1,331,912 lb at US$75.08/lb (aggregate US$100.0m); delivered 16 March 2026; funded by Sept 2025 placing (gross ~£129.6m / ~US$175m).
  • Post quarter-end: bought an additional 100,000 lb spot, delivered 20 April 2026.
  • Pro-forma holdings (after H2 Kazatomprom delivery + April spot purchase): expected to rise to 24,374,996 lb.
  • Uranium holdings value increased 9.7% over the quarter to US$1,940.4m (from US$1,768.2m), driven by higher lbs held and spot price moving from US$81.55/lb (31 Dec 2025) to US$83.95/lb (31 Mar 2026) (+2.9%).
  • Estimated NAV per share increased 5.0% to £6.33 (from £6.03), aided by higher uranium value and GBP depreciation vs USD.
  • Estimated pro-forma NAV on 24 April 2026: £6.34/share (US$ 2,167.9m), assuming 24.37m lb valued at US$86.45/lb, and adjusting for the US$100.0m Kazatomprom commitment plus US$8.5m paid for the post-period 100,000 lb spot purchase.
  • CEO Andre Liebenberg said: **"The first quarter of 2026 marked a transition from policy ambition to large-scale implementation, accentuated by the conflict in the Middle East once again highlighting the importance of energy security. With 39 nations now committed to tripling nuclear capacity, the World Nuclear Association projects global capacity could reach 1,446 GWe by 2050, surpassing the targets launched at COP28 in 2023. This momentum is evidenced by China elevating its 2030 target to 110 GWe, near double its current capacity, and the U.S. 'UPRISE' initiative, which fast-tracks reactor uprates to power the AI and data centre revolution.

"While we welcome the progress of long-dated supply projects like NexGen Energy's Rook I and Denison's Phoenix, the market remains structurally tight today. We see utilities increasingly prioritising security of supply, driving term prices higher as they compete for limited available material.

"Against this backdrop, Yellow Cake continues to deliver tangible value for shareholders. Our oversubscribed US$110 million placing and the exercise of our Kazatomprom option have grown our holdings to 23.1 million pounds, with committed purchases expected to increase holdings to approximately 24.4 million pounds."**

body:

  • Application seeks full planning permission for a hyperscale data centre campus (c. 500,000 sq ft across three data centre halls + auxiliary buildings) on Plots 1 & 2, plus outline permission for a warehouse building.

This transaction has driven group level value growth and facilitates investment in the region, catalysing economic growth, with Skelton Grange estimated to deliver c. £4bn of inward investment when the development completes."

Our powered land portfolio has a further 0.8GW of power connections, on top of our Skelton Grange site, and is well positioned to capture demand from data centre and other power-intensive sectors, providing the potential for further upside opportunities, delivering strong group level value gains and attractive shareholder returns."

body:
• Net new customers +50,000 in the quarter to 723,000 (+22% YoY, +7% QoQ) — record quarterly growth.
  • Channel split: advised customers 189,000 (+7% YoY, +2% QoQ); D2C customers 534,000 (+28% YoY, +9% QoQ).
  • Assets under administration (AUA) £108.7bn (+20% YoY, +1% QoQ); market movements reduced AUA growth by ~2% in the quarter (management notes market levels improved post quarter-end).
  • Platform flows: gross inflows £5.6bn (+40%); net inflows £2.7bn (+42%) (both record vs prior year quarter).
  • Investment business AUM £9.8bn (+31% YoY, +3% QoQ); net inflows £0.3bn (prior year: £0.4bn).
  • CEO Michael Summersgill said:"I am delighted to report an excellent quarter of growth for our dual-channel platform, as we delivered a record 50,000 net new customers and £2.7 billion of net inflows. This performance reflects the early benefits of our previously announced increased investment in our brand and propositions."Our D2C platform delivered its strongest quarter to date, achieving record customer growth - over 50% higher than the same quarter last year - alongside record net inflows. This significant increase in new customers reflects the value placed on our low-cost propositions, ease of use and trusted brand. These factors also contributed to heightened inbound account transfers from other platforms within the market. Our Advised platform delivered record-equalling gross inflows, with strong growth partially offset by anticipated outflows associated with ongoing adviser consolidation."We operate a digital-first platform, while recognising that at key moments in the investment journey customers and advisers may want to speak to us directly. The tax year-end is the busiest time of the year for customer activity and throughout this period we maintained excellent service standards, with customers and advisers waiting an average of just eight seconds to reach our customer services team. This focus on service quality is reflected in our market-leading 4.9-star Trustpilot rating and our Which? Recommended Provider status for an eighth consecutive year."We have a proven track record of growing across different market conditions. Whilst recent market volatility impacted asset values at the end of the quarter, customer appetite to invest remained strong in the run-up to the tax year-end. The UK platform market continues to offer significant structural growth opportunities, and our diversified revenue model and highly scalable business model position us well to continue to invest for long-term, sustainable growth."
  • Interim results scheduled: 21 May 2026 (six months ended 31 March 2026).

In the quarter, we acquired Lettings businesses in the high-growth, complementary markets of Birmingham and Milton Keynes. This, combined with organic growth and increasing take up of our property management services, meant that Lettings revenues increased 5% in the period."The implementation of the Renters' Rights Act on 1 May 2026 is expected to create growth opportunities for Foxtons. Higher regulatory requirements further underline the importance of working with a trusted, professional agent, and Foxtons' scale, expertise and compliance capabilities position the business to protect landlords' investments and capture market share."The Sales market remains subdued and has been further affected by recent events in the Middle East, which have tempered buyer sentiment and impacted mortgage rates and availability. As ever, Foxtons is focused on what we can control by managing costs, increasing efficiencies and repositioning our Sales business to mitigate the impact of the market."We remain confident that the resilience of our Lettings and Financial Services businesses, which represents more than two thirds of revenues, alongside work to reposition the Sales business, can continue to deliver market-leading results for customers, growth opportunities for our people and long-term value creation for shareholders."

  • Leo Quinn (Executive Chair) quote:"The immediate focus is to restore confidence and ensure the right foundations are in place to support profitable growth and long-term value creation."Moving forward, the Board and management team will have a relentless focus on driving cash, cost discipline and strengthening the balance sheet. As a first step, the Board has taken the prudent decision to suspend the dividend."This is a business with a strong brand and proposition in high-footfall travel markets and the new flagship stores opened across Heathrow airport are raising the global standard for travel essentials retail."None of this is achievable without our people. Making sure our colleagues are empowered is a key priority, as engaged teams execute better, serve customers better and drive higher performance over time."While the near-term outlook is uncertain, I am confident that, with the right focus and discipline, the business can deliver superior returns for the benefit of our colleagues, partners and shareholders over the longer-term."

body:
• Simon Roberts (CEO) said:"More and more customers are choosing Sainsbury's for more of their shopping, trusting us to deliver great value day in day out. The conflict in the Middle East means customers are even more focused on the cost of living and we are absolutely committed to making sure everyone gets the best possible value when they shop with us."By staying relentlessly focused on the things that matter most - value, quality, availability and service - we have outperformed the market for the sixth year in a row. Rather than pass through the full extent of cost inflation, we invested to sustain the strength of our competitive position while also refreshing stores, improving digital experiences and increasing colleague pay by five per cent."We offer the biggest Aldi Price Match in the market, with great prices on everyday essentials and even more value through Nectar Prices and personalised Your Nectar Prices. Alongside our standout fresh food offer and the growing strength of Taste the Difference, we are well placed to be first choice for more customers."Long term partnerships with thousands of farmers and suppliers are key to delivering good food at great value. We have committed to invest more than £5 billion in British and Irish farming over the coming years, making our supply base more resilient at a time of increased challenges."Our balanced choices reflect a consistent long-term approach to creating value for shareholders: strengthening our relationships with customers, colleagues and suppliers and building a stronger Sainsbury's for the future."We will do everything we can to support our customers and colleagues over the coming months, with absolute focus on keeping prices low. We have made a positive start to the new financial year, with continued strong Grocery momentum."I would like to thank all our colleagues, farmers and suppliers for their brilliant commitment and hard work - it's their dedication that makes such a difference for our customers every time they shop with us."
  • Group revenue (ex VAT, inc fuel) £33.647bn, up 2.7% (FY25: £32.772bn).
  • Retail sales (ex VAT, ex fuel) £29.992bn, up 4.3% (FY25: £28.754bn).
  • Like-for-like sales (ex fuel) +3.9% (FY25: +3.4%); like-for-like (inc fuel) +2.5% (FY25: +1.8%).
  • FY sales (ex fuel): Sainsbury’s £25.9bn (+4.9%), Argos £4.1bn (+0.7%), Fuel £3.6bn (-8.2%).
  • Grocery sales +5.2% (strong volume growth + market share gains); Fresh food sales +8%; Taste the Difference sales ahead of £2bn target (Fresh food TTD +16%).
  • Retail underlying operating profit £1,025m (-1.1%); retail underlying operating margin 3.06% (FY25: 3.17%, -11bps). Retail underlying EBITDA margin 6.59% (FY25: 6.72%, -13bps).
  • Total underlying operating profit £1,025m (+1.1%) (FY25: £1,014m) driven by Financial Services moving from £(22)m to £0m (break-even).
  • Underlying PBT £718m (+1.3%); underlying EPS 22.3p (+3.2%).
  • Statutory profit after tax £393m (+55.3%); non-underlying items £(115)m (FY25: £(251)m).
  • Retail free cash flow £574m (+8.1%) (FY25: £531m); cash capex £843m (FY25: £825m; +2.2%).
  • Net debt (incl leases) £5.743bn (broadly flat vs £5.758bn); non-lease net debt £203m (FY25: £264m; £61m lower).
  • Proposed full-year dividend 13.7p (+0.7%); final dividend 9.6p (payable 10 July 2026, record date 5 June 2026).
  • Cash returns: ordinary dividends £316m + core buyback £200m completed; bank disposal proceeds returned via £250m special dividend + £50m buyback; FY26/27 buyback planned £300m (core £200m + additional £100m bank proceeds).
  • 2026/27 guidance (explicitly framed by Middle East uncertainty): Total underlying operating profit £975m–£1,075m; Retail free cash flow >£500m.
  • Stores/space: opened 10 supermarkets and 33 convenience stores; plan to open ~10 supermarkets and ≥20 convenience stores in 2026/27; expected net space growth impact ~0.5% to sales in 2026/27.
  • Online: Groceries Online sales +13%; OnDemand sales +69% to >£700m, now covering ~70% of UK population.
  • Cost programme: delivered ~£680m cost savings since Feb 2024; target £1bn over three years to 2026/27; delivered a further £330m structural cost savings in FY26.
  • Financial Services: exit from core banking materially completed; new partnership with NatWest announced April 2026 (loans, savings, NatWest Nectar credit card expected H2 2026); expects to surrender banking licence by July 2026; Financial Services no longer to be reported as a separate operating segment.
  • Pension: IAS 19 defined benefit surplus £525m (down £206m YoY); 2024 triennial valuation completed 20 March 2026 (surplus £171m incl ABC; £15m excl); escrow established (no funds deposited as at 28 Feb 2026).
  • Management framing on performance/cash returns: "We delivered a resilient operating profit performance despite significant cost inflation, whilst generating strong free cash flow and returning more than £800 million to shareholders."

body:
• CEO Matthew Bonning-Snook: “The Period has seen further strong progress across our business, building on the significant momentum delivered in the first half of the year. At The Bower, EC1, the resurgence of the tech occupier market that we highlighted at our Half Year Results has translated into a c.20,000 sq ft letting of two floors to an AI platform, three further floors totalling c.32,000 sq ft going under offer, as well as regears with existing occupiers being agreed on a further five floors.

Having acquired, financed and signed the main construction contract at our 240,000 sq ft development at Paddington, W2, we now have four office schemes, totalling over 700,000 sq ft, currently under construction. 100 New Bridge Street, EC4 is on track to achieve practical completion later this month, triggering completion of the forward sale of the building to State Street Corporation and a return of equity to the business. This will be followed by the completion of Brettenham House, WC2 and 10 King William Street, EC4 later in the year, with both best-in-class assets well positioned to take advantage of the strong rental growth being driven by a market with very tight supply.

This pipeline is supplemented by our equity-light 429 bed PBSA scheme at Southwark, SE1, where, in February 2026, the joint venture agreed a forward funding with Places for London. With no further equity required to be injected, this has significantly de-risked the project and should generate a very strong return on investment. Finally, yesterday, our joint venture with Places for London successfully secured a planning consent for a new 55,000 sq ft office development in Farringdon, further bolstering our exciting pipeline.”

  • 100 New Bridge Street, EC4: practical completion expected April 2026; handover to State Street to complete £333m forward sale (Helical share £166.5m); delivered in 24 months and in line with original budget.

• CEO Eduardo Landin: “We have made a solid start to the year, with a strong operational performance at our flagship Inmaculada mine in Peru whilst the turnaround programme at Mara Rosa in Brazil is progressing well, with continued improvements in the plant and filtering operations. Overall, we have delivered another quarter of strong cash generation and we are on track to meet our full-year production and cost guidance. In parallel, we have continued to advance the engineering work at our Monte Do Carmo gold project in Brazil, where we are targeting the third quarter for project approval and the commencement of construction. Finally, the Environmental Impact Study for the Royropata silver project in Peru is progressing according to plan.

With Inmaculada performing well, an improved Mara Rosa, guidance maintained and an exciting portfolio of future growth projects, we see a strong future for Hochschild and look forward to updating the market on our progress”

  • Q1 attributable production (in line with expectations): 55,252oz gold, 1.6Moz silver, 75,599 gold equivalent oz.
  • Guidance reiterated: 300,000–328,000 gold equivalent oz in 2026; AISC $2,157–$2,320/Geoz.
  • Cash: total cash, cash equivalents & short-term investments ~$412m at 31 Mar 2026 (vs $317.0m at 31 Dec 2025; +$95m / ~+30%).
  • Balance sheet swing: net cash ~ $95m at 31 Mar 2026 (vs net debt $22.7m at 31 Dec 2025).
  • Group attributable production vs prior: gold equivalent 75.60koz (Q1 2025: 81.65koz); silver equivalent 5,821koz (Q1 2025: 6,287koz).
  • Inmaculada (Peru): Q1 production 32,561oz gold and 1.21Moz silver (48,281 Geoz); moderately higher tonnage offset by lower grades (cut-off grade effect from higher prices); reverse osmosis plant completed and started up; tailings lift advanced.
  • San Jose (Argentina, 51%): Q1 production 0.699Moz silver and 17.92koz gold (26,991 Geoz); tonnage up vs Q1 2025; silver grades slightly lower; “on track” for annual target.
  • Mara Rosa (Brazil): turnaround continued (greater plant stability, maintenance reliability, higher run rates); peak quarter throughput noted (crushing 8.4kt; milling 6.9kt; filter plant 7.0kt); contractor replacement mobilisation 75% by end-March; new tailings thickener commissioning expected end-April with operations by end-May 2026; Q1 production 13,552 Geoz (below expectations due to equipment availability, weaker waste development, rainy season).
  • Prices: average realisable prices $4,471/oz gold and $89.8/oz silver (Q1 2025: $2,708/oz and $33.2/oz).
  • Monte Do Carmo (Brazil): engineering/permitting/procurement work progressed; board approval targeted in Q3 2026 (and start of construction thereafter).
  • Royropata (Peru): Environmental Impact Study progressing “according to plan”.
  • Exploration: 2026 brownfield drilling commenced at all sites; first results due from Q2 2026.
  • ESG: LTIFR 0.55 (FY 2025: 0.97); fresh water used 0.17 m³/t (FY 2025: 0.26); women in workforce 11.2% (FY 2025: 10.6%); ECO score 5.90/6 (FY 2025: 5.61).

body:
• Managing Director Tom Hickey: “We are pleased to have returned to a strong safety performance in Q1 2026, with no Lost Time Injuries incurred. Shipments were in line with the run rate of our annual guidance, and we have already drawn down almost 100,000 tonnes of inventory.

While our product markets remained soft in Q1, global supply curtailments and unplanned production disruptions are starting to reduce the oversupply of ilmenite, supporting a tighter market outlook. Encouragingly, the zircon market continues to show signs of recovery, with higher agreed prices in Q2, and we shipped more of our new product, ZrTi, in Q1 than we did in all of 2025. Although current geopolitical uncertainty has increased freight rates and affected access to some customers’ port facilities, altering our shipping schedule in Q1, the overall impact of the war has been limited to date.

There continues to be constructive and regular engagement with the Government of Mozambique regarding the renewal of Moma’s Implementation Agreement and we are focused on securing a near-term resolution.”

  • Safety: 0 LTIs in Q1; rolling 12-month LTIFR 0.07 per 200,000 hours (31 Mar 2025: 0.06).
  • Guidance: on track to achieve 2026 guidance on all metrics; finished product stockpiles drawn down 99,900t in Q1 (value-over-volume).
  • Production headwinds: HMC 217,200t (-30% YoY) driven by ongoing WCP A debottlenecking; excavated ore 8.005Mt (-14% YoY) and grade 3.26% (-23% YoY) as WCP A reaches end of Namalope mine path.
  • Ilmenite: 125,900t (-38% YoY), impacted by lower HMC and lower recoveries (spillage/inconsistent feed + retreatment campaigns); retained material to be retreated in Q2.
  • Zircon & rutile: primary zircon 8,900t (-36% YoY); rutile 1,000t (-60% YoY) (same recovery issues; partly offset by intermediate stockpile processing for zircon).
  • Concentrates: 45,200t (+397% YoY) supported by new by-product ZrTi production 35,200t.
  • Shipments: 277,900t (-10% YoY) but in line with run-rate for >1.1Mt FY guidance; includes 46,400t ZrTi; shipment mix: 207,300t ilmenite, 10,900t primary zircon, 100t rutile, 59,500t concentrates.
  • Inventory: closing HMC stock 41,000t (vs 29,200t at FY25); finished product stock 244,100t (vs 344,000t at FY25), reflecting the 99,900t drawdown.
  • WCP A upgrade: major construction/installation complete; capex rate decreased substantially in Q1; low-cost fixes implemented (dredge winch brake software/cooling; tailings pump gearbox upgrades; stable densification paddock/TSF operations; long-term rectifications after walkway turning over).
  • Early Q2 ops: improved dredge feed delivery achieved on one dredge and to be replicated; plant flowrate debottlenecking to complete “over the coming weeks”, with expectation that nameplate capacity will be substantially achieved thereafter.
  • Market: titanium feedstocks remained soft; Kenmare’s average ilmenite price declined significantly vs H2 2025 (as expected); supply curtailments/disruptions tightening outlook; strong order book for Q2.
  • Zircon market: demand exceeds Kenmare supply; higher agreed prices for Q2 2026.
  • Geopolitics/logistics: higher freight rates and port-access constraints altered shipping schedule in Q1; “overall impact of the war has been limited to date”.
  • Credit recovery: “significant progress” recovering value from Q3 2025 shipments to a distressed customer; Spanish ops new owner settled outstanding invoice in full; discussions ongoing with proposed buyer of Malaysian ops to recover value.
  • ZrTi accounting: ZrTi recognised at estimated net realisable value (c. ~$130/t in 2025 after handling/export taxes), reducing ilmenite production cost.
  • Implementation Agreement (IA): meeting with Government 19 Feb 2026 targeted renewal terms by 20 Mar 2026 (not achieved); engagement continues; Kenmare reserves right to safeguard entitlements “up to and including arbitration” if needed; mining ops are under separate framework not impacted by IA process.

time_period: Update as at 22 April 2026 (includes liquidity position to 17 April 2026) and summary unaudited results for FY 2025 (year ended 31 December 2025)
body:
• Board says an equity capital raise is “currently the only viable solution” in the required timeframe; intended to raise minimum US$100m via a conditional placing to existing/new institutional investors to support working capital and operate at reduced level for the next ~18 months (the “Intended Fundraise”).
  • Intended Fundraise launch subject to Board approval and market conditions; completion conditional on shareholder Resolutions at a General Meeting convened ASAP after launch; company does not intend to publish a prospectus.
  • Group reiterates it has sufficient net accessible cash until ~end-August 2026, assuming no material adverse changes (iron ore price/opex incl. energy, operating conditions incl. energy supply, no restrictive measures by FPM insolvency manager, no negative legal outcomes); assumes receipt of proceeds from sale of vessel “Iron Destiny”.
  • Agreed sale of owned transhipping vessel “Iron Destiny” for US$7.7m net cash; completion expected later April 2026.
  • Critical timetable: if fundraise proceeds, it is expected to be launched and completed on/before 30 April 2026 to enable publication of audited FY2025 results.
  • If the bookbuild is not completed by 30 April 2026, shares expected to be suspended from 07:30 (UK) on 1 May 2026 until audit completed and FY2025 Annual Report published; no certainty on timing of any lifting of suspension, “if at all”.
  • Company states there is no certainty the Intended Fundraise (or any alternative funding) can be executed in the timeframe, or at all; non-completion could lead to insolvency filings and shareholders potentially losing all or a substantial portion of their investment.
  • Engagement ongoing with largest shareholder Fevamotinico S.a.r.l. (holds 49.32% of shares in issue ex treasury) on support for the Resolutions and potential participation; discussions focus on dilution and implications of association with Kostiantyn Zhevago (beneficiary of The Minco Trust which wholly owns Fevamotinico).
  • Liquidity deterioration highlighted: net cash ~US$20m (net accessible cash ~US$17m, excluding funds held at MBaer Merchant Bank after its banking licence revocation in Feb 2026) as at 17 April 2026 vs US$25m (31 Mar 2026), US$30m (27 Feb 2026), US$47m (31 Dec 2025), US$50m (30 Jun 2025), US$101m (31 Dec 2024).
  • Key driver of liquidity stress: ongoing suspension of VAT refunds since March 2025; net VAT receivable balance US$90.3m at 31 March 2026; US$78.9m claimed for refund (Jan 2025–Mar 2026), with US$69.4m refused (Jan–Dec 2025) cited as due to association with Mr Zhevago and his personal sanctions in Ukraine.
  • Operations: production resumed in 2026 but remains ~25% of sustained pre-war capacity; currently running 1 of 4 pellet lines and selling primarily to European customers.
  • Q1 2026 production: 593kt total (pellets 525kt, Fe 67% concentrate 68kt).
  • Notes constraints from war impacts (energy grid attacks, costly electricity imports, logistics, conscription) and legal/regulatory actions in Ukraine; production was temporarily suspended 20 Jan 2026 due to electricity disruption, with limited resumption late Feb 2026.
  • States that aside from lease liabilities (mostly long-term over ~10 years), the Group has no outstanding interest-bearing loans/borrowings.
  • Longer-term outlook framed as multi-phase recovery dependent on war evolution, restoration/collection of VAT refunds, legal outcomes, and additional capital beyond this raise; target max capacity ~12mtpa, with an expected start of recovery to pre-war levels in 2028; highlights Belanovo greenfield optionality (1.7bn tonnes JORC resource) suitable for DR pellets.
  • Use of proceeds: primarily working capital (power, labour, consumables, logistics, maintenance) and preserving financial flexibility amid uncertainty (power, logistics, legal proceedings, VAT refund suspension).
  • Funding alternatives reviewed (debt, supplier/customer terms, trade finance, care & maintenance, asset disposals, strategic investment) but Board concludes none can raise sufficient cash in time; cites constraints from Ukrainian sanctions/KYC concerns, asset freeze orders, FPM bankruptcy process limiting disposals/security, and inability to assure stable export income to service debt.
  • Legal / regulatory milestones flagged: Supreme Court of Ukraine hearing on contested sureties claim scheduled 1 May 2026; FPM appeal hearing against opening of bankruptcy proceedings scheduled 30 April 2026.
  • FY2025 unaudited (going concern basis contingent on Intended Fundraise) summary: sales volume 6.6mt (2024: 6.8mt, -4%); Fe 65% fines price US$115/t (2024: US$123/t, -7%); revenue US$787m (2024: US$933m, -16%).
  • FY2025 production 6.1mt (2024: 6.8mt, -9%); C1 cash costs US$76.3/t (2024: US$77.5/t, -2%); write-offs/impairments US$161m (2024: US$72m, +124%).
  • FY2025 profitability: operating result loss US$197m (2024: profit US$18m; swing -US$215m); loss for period US$211m (2024: loss US$50m; loss widened by US$161m / +322%); diluted EPS -35.8c (2024: -8.5c).

body:
• Blanket Mine gold production: 14,767 oz vs 18,671 oz in Q1 2025 (-20.9% YoY).
  • Lower quarter was anticipated due to mining sequence and expected access constraints to higher grade / higher volume areas.
  • Operational impacts in the quarter: equipment availability issues and challenging ground conditions (constraining access to planned ore sources).
  • New mine shift system being implemented to move production from 6 days/week to 7 days/week.
  • Contractor appointed to accelerate access to higher-grade ore sources.
  • Milling capacity expected to increase following commissioning of an additional ball mill in Q2 2026.
  • Management remains comfortable with full-year production guidance of 72,000–76,500 oz; production expected to be weighted to H2 2026.
  • Processing performance: 202,217 tonnes milled with “good operational availability across the processing circuit”.
  • CEO Mark Learmonth comment (full quote): “Gold production in Q1 2026 was below our expectations, reflecting the lower grades mined during the Quarter; however, this is consistent with our guidance of production being weighted towards the second half of the year. Pleasingly, plant performance remained strong, with 202,217 tonnes milled and good operational availability across the processing circuit. This is an important reflection of our continued investment into the future of the processing facility. "The Quarter also included several typical operating challenges associated with deep, mature mining assets, including sequencing considerations, equipment downtime and difficult ground conditions in certain areas. These factors temporarily constrained access to some planned ore sources. "We are actively addressing these challenges through several practical measures, including the acceleration of mine development, supported by the appointment of a contractor, to improve access to planned ore sources. "Importantly, we will be introducing a revised shift system later in the year, moving the operation to a seven-day working week (up from six), which we expect will both reduce worker fatigue and support increased ore production. "Alongside these mining initiatives, we are progressing further plant improvements, including an increase in milling capacity following the commissioning of an additional ball mill. Taken together, these actions are expected to support a stronger production profile in the second half of the year and into 2027. "The challenges experienced in the first quarter do not reflect the underlying quality of the orebody or the long-term fundamentals of the operation. Blanket remains a resilient, cash-generative asset, supported by a capable and committed workforce and a processing plant that continues to perform reliably and where we are growing capacity. Management's focus is on stabilising mining areas, improving equipment availability and restoring access to planned ore sources as we progress through the year.”

body:
• Agreed sale of owned transhipping vessel “Iron Destiny” for US$7.7m net cash consideration (subject to delivery and customary closing conditions; expected to complete later this month).
  • Rationale for disposal: constrained ability to use vessel since start of the war; continued monthly maintenance and sustaining capex to keep seaworthy; uncertainty on timing of end of war; vessel approaching end of useful life; sale provides immediate cash injection and removes ongoing maintenance / future capex burden.
  • Net accessible cash runway: including expected proceeds from Iron Destiny sale, Ferrexpo estimates runway extended from at least end-June 2026 to approximately end-August 2026 (subject to iron ore price volatility, opex including energy costs, operating conditions, potential actions by the insolvency manager at FPM, and outcomes of ongoing proceedings).
  • Funding options: Board says an equity capital raise is currently the most viable solution within the required timeframe (after discussions with existing and certain potential new institutional investors).
  • Possible Fundraise: likely structured as a conditional placing of new shares to institutional investors to raise a minimum of US$100m to support working capital and short-term operational requirements while operating at a reduced level for the next 18 months.
  • Fundraise conditionality: would require shareholder resolutions at a general meeting to be convened “as early as possible” following launch.

As a significant shareholder with a long term belief in ATG I will be an interested observer in its future success.”

time_period: Analyst reaction to outlook for year to March 2027; referenced recent trading metrics and disposal programme progress
body:
• Workspace warned of a “substantial step down” in profit as it invests to become the “first-choice provider of space” for start-ups and small businesses.
  • Share price reaction described: shares slumped 9.5% to 337.99p; intraday low cited as 313.10p (down as much as 16%); shares also cited as down 22% over the past year.
  • JPMorgan: outlook "not in current market expectations"; focus is on factors driving a "substantial step down" in trading profit in FY2027 vs FY2026.
  • JPMorgan estimated profit headwinds of ~GBP10m–GBP15m from a combination of: lower starting rents, disposals, higher debt costs, reduced capitalised interest, and increased operating expenses.
  • JPMorgan implied FY2027 trading profit of ~GBP45m–GBP50m based on those headwinds.
  • JPMorgan said this implies an 18%–26% downgrade to consensus forecasts (per the article).
  • Dividend pressure flagged: move to 1.2x dividend cover suggests high single-digit % cuts to FY2026 dividend expectations (per JPMorgan).
  • JPMorgan: applying the 1.2x cover approach into FY2027 implies potential dividend reductions up to 32% (per the article).
  • JPMorgan quote: "This is a challenging update with earnings, dividends and NAV expectations now needing to move lower,".
  • Strategy support (JPMorgan): portfolio is "made up of quality buildings in good locations with long-term structural demand"; opportunity is repositioning so Workspace "owns the value category"; but "this repositioning will take some time" and the market will want progress before re-engaging.
  • Berenberg view: company is "laying the groundwork for a sustainable recovery", but expects near-term earnings to fall; expects trading profit towards the "high GBP40 millions" (around 17% below their previous estimates and ~22% below consensus, per the article).
  • Trading metrics cited by Berenberg: occupancy 81.6%; rent per square foot down 0.9%.
  • Peel Hunt: two consecutive quarters of occupancy improvement is "encouraging that this is not a structural problem", but expects a trading profit downgrade; models FY2027 trading profit in the mid- to high-GBP40m range (implying ~25% downgrade, per the article).
  • Peel Hunt dividend impact (per the article): forecasts ~10% reduction in FY2026 dividend and 25%–30% cuts for FY2027.
  • Panmure Liberum: rebasing is "the required medicine to put the business in a position to grow", but warned shares are vulnerable to near-term weakness.
  • Disposal programme: GBP125.7m completed/agreed so far out of GBP200m target (i.e., ~62.9% of the programme achieved); some disposals completed at “significant discounts” to prior valuations, highlighting softer pricing conditions.

time_period: War-risk insurance capacity for Hormuz transits during the current Middle East conflict
body:
• Beazley will lead a “marine war consortium” to provide USD1 billion in additional war insurance coverage for vessels sailing through the Strait of Hormuz.
  • The extra capacity will be provided via Lloyd’s of London.
  • Beazley statement: "The consortium is designed to support the maritime sector with additional war insurance capacity as it deals with a complex and evolving situation in and around the Strait of Hormuz,".
  • Beazley statement: "The facility will be offered to vessels and their cargoes whilst transiting the Strait of Hormuz; coverage will be in line with Beazley's risk appetite and in compliance with all global sanctions".
  • CEO Adrian Cox: the arrangement will help "in keeping global trade moving".
  • Article context: war has driven up shipping insurance payments; about 30 vessels have reported being hit or targeted in the area (per the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre cited).
  • Article context: Iranian forces have restricted passage through the strait to “all but a trickle” of ships since the war erupted on 28 February (as stated in the article).
  • Lloyd’s Market Association (trade body) position: "Safety concerns, not insurance availability, (are) driving reduced vessel traffic,".
  • Additional corporate context in the article: Beazley earlier this year accepted a GBP8.2 billion takeover approach from Zurich Insurance Group AG.

time_period: Short-term jet fuel supply disruption at Italian airports; resolved within a day
body:
• CEO said Wizz Air experienced jet fuel shortages at three Italian airports: Venice, Brindisi and Catania.
  • CEO Jozsef Varadi: "We had problems because of a shortage of jet fuel in three Italian airports – Venice, Brindisi and Catania".
  • Varadi: "It was all resolved within a day and in some cases within hours, without having to cancel flights."
  • The issue followed warnings about jet fuel supplies linked to the blockage/effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz due to the war in Iran.
  • Article context: Europe normally imports about half of its jet fuel from Gulf countries.
  • Varadi: "In no other European country, so far, have we experienced a fuel shortage,".
  • Varadi: "I think we are currently watching each other (between airlines) to understand how serious the situation might become."
  • Varadi: "Jet fuel has been supplied adequately across Europe, with a minor hiccup in Italy,".
  • Varadi: "For the time being, I think the situation in Europe is not that alarming; the problems are more serious in Asia than in Europe,".
  • Varadi: "I believe we will overcome this crisis as well and that it will not be too damaging."
  • Mitigation approach if shortages recur: first ensure planes carry enough fuel for another journey; only then consider reducing services at the affected airport.
  • Demand commentary: Varadi said "Demand is hesitant" and "People are waiting to see what will happen" for the coming weeks.

summary: UBS upgrades BP to buy, citing new CEO and potential for cost savings and deleveraging
body:
Time Period Analyst note (focus areas ahead of a likely strategy update later in 2026; deleveraging scenarios out to 2028)

  • UBS upgraded BP to ‘buy’ (from ‘neutral’); price target raised to 700p (from 650p).
  • UBS framing: new CEO Meg O’Neill “takes over at a critical turning point,” with “work to regain investor confidence” after “52% underperformance versus peers since 2018”.
  • Cost base: UBS estimates potential unproductive cost savings of USD3 billion–USD6 billion.
  • Growth: UBS wants clearer definition of key growth opportunities, noting importance of growing the business following buyback suspension.
  • Balance sheet: UBS highlights BP’s sector-high leverage ratio (~47%); expects deleveraging helped by higher oil prices, with leverage potentially falling to ~27% by 2028 in base case (earlier in upside case).
  • Distributions: UBS argues the equity case would be supported by clarifying distribution policy and conditions for reintroducing buybacks.

summary: Dunelm Q3 sales growth slowed to 2.1% amid March consumer softening and value-seeking
body:
Time Period 13 weeks ended 28 March 2026 (Q3 FY26); year-to-date FY26

  • Q3 sales +2.1% to GBP472 million.
  • Year-to-date sales +3.1% to GBP1.40 billion.
  • Growth cadence: Q3 improved vs Q2 (+1.6%), but slowed vs Q1 (+6.2%) and vs prior-year Q3 (+6.3%).
  • Trading: “the third quarter started well… however more recently, and particularly in March, we experienced a period of broad-based softening,”

Over the last year, despite cost pressures from new regulation, we have increased our investments in keeping prices low, further improving quality and offering even better service. Customers are choosing to shop more with us as a result, leading to our highest market share for over a decade. Our investments have been made possible by our Save to Invest programme, which has delivered over £2.2bn of savings over the last four years, funding lower prices for customers and higher pay for colleagues, including our recent 5.1% increase in UK hourly pay. Recognising their exceptional service over the last year, I am also pleased to announce a £65m special performance award for colleagues in our stores, distribution centres and customer engagement centres. Our further investments in value included tripling the number of products on Everyday Low Prices to 3,000, running alongside over 10,000 Clubcard Prices and more than 600 Aldi Price Match lines. summary: Ashmore's AuM fell 3.4% to $50.7bn due to geopolitical disruption and institutional redemptions
body:
Time Period Quarter ended 31 March 2026 (Q3 FY26 AuM statement)

  • AuM down $1.8bn to $50.7bn from $52.5bn (≈ -3.4%).
  • AuM movement split: -$0.9bn investment performance and -$0.9bn net outflows.
  • By investment theme (31 Dec 2025 → 31 Mar 2026):

– External debt: $8.4bn → $8.0bn (≈ -4.8%). – Local currency: $15.7bn → $16.4bn (≈ +4.5%). – Corporate debt: $5.3bn → $5.1bn (≈ -3.8%). – Blended debt: $12.5bn → $10.5bn (-16.0%).

  • Asset class totals:

– Fixed income: $41.9bn → $40.0bn (≈ -4.5%). – Equities: $8.8bn → $8.8bn (flat). – Alternatives: $1.8bn → $1.9bn (≈ +5.6%).

  • Narrative driver: positive EM momentum from 2025 continued early in quarter but was interrupted by broadened Middle East conflict (end-Feb) → higher volatility and “wait and see” investor stance.
  • Flow colour: subscriptions “healthy” with net inflows in local currency and equities, but institutional redemption in blended debt drove net outflow there; small net outflow from external debt.
  • Market backdrop: EM indices flat to down 3% over the quarter; strong Jan/Feb then weaker March.
  • Performance messaging: Ashmore claims continued outperformance across equity and fixed income; proportion of AuM outperforming benchmarks consistent near-to-mid term, and improved over longer term.
  • Strategic development: announced strategic partnership with Japan Post Insurance Co., Ltd at period end.
  • CEO quote (Mark Coombs):

"Geopolitical events interrupted some of the macro tailwinds supporting emerging markets, but the reaction across most asset classes has so far been manageable and with limited price dislocations. In the near term, investors globally are taking a more measured stance until there is greater clarity in the outlook for the duration of the conflict and its implications for factors such as commodity prices, inflation, interest rates and currency trends. "As ever, it is paramount to understand the rich diversity of emerging markets and therefore to manage portfolios actively to deliver investment performance. Ashmore's specialist approach and long history of investing in emerging markets, across different cycles and complex geopolitical and macro events, means it is well positioned to navigate the current environment. summary: easyJet expects H1 FY26 headline loss of £540m-£560m, up 37-42% year-on-year
body:
Time Period Six months ended 31 March 2026 (H1 FY26)

  • easyJet expects headline loss before tax of £540m–£560m for H1 FY26.
  • Prior-year comparative (six months ended 31 March 2025) headline LBT was £394m (implying ~+37% to +42% larger loss YoY vs the expected range).
  • Load factor 90%, +2ppts YoY.
  • easyJet holidays customers +22% in H1.
  • Underlying H1 result described as broadly in line with expectations, with revenue/costs in line excluding:

– ~£25m incremental fuel costs in March due to Middle East conflict. – ~£30m net increase in legal provisions across historic cases.

  • Strategic investments: Milan Linate + Rome Fiumicino performed in line with expectations in first winter year (£30m investment cost).
  • YoY performance also impacted by capacity investments to drive winter utilisation and competitive overcapacity in certain markets.
  • Q2 RASK +~3% YoY, driven by modest route maturity + earlier Easter timing; strength in domestics/cities/Western Med offset by war-related softness in Egypt, Turkey, Cyprus.
  • Operational metrics:

– Airline on-time performance 78% (+1ppt YoY). – Airline customer satisfaction 84% (+2ppts YoY). – easyJet holidays customer satisfaction 85%.

  • FY26 cost outlook:

– Airline headline CASK ex fuel: full-year expectation broadly unchanged, but fuel volatility creates uncertainty for total CASK. – H1 Airline headline CASK ex fuel +~8% YoY (inflation weighted to H1; resilience measures annualisation; airport rate phasing; higher winter load factors; digitalisation; plus ~£30m legal provisions). – H2 Airline headline CASK ex fuel expected to rise low single digits YoY.

  • Fuel dynamics:

– March: Middle East escalation drove ~£25m incremental cost (unhedged March requirements 18% bought at spot). – H1 fuel CASK down ~5% YoY. – H1 Airline headline CASK up ~5% YoY overall.

  • Booking curve: conflict introduced uncertainty; booking curve shortened, reducing forward visibility.
  • Balance sheet/liquidity: net cash £434m, liquidity £4.7bn, and owns 86% of neo aircraft (flexibility).
  • Hedging + sensitivity:

– H2 FY26: 70% hedged at $706/metric tonne (spot at 15/04/26: $1,500). – Every $100 move in fuel prices ≈ £40m cost in H2 FY26.

  • Bookings:

– Q3: 63% sold, -2ppts YoY, ticket yield marginally down; 1ppt Q3 RASK ≈ £26m revenue. – Q4: 30% sold, -2ppts YoY, ticket yield modestly up; 1ppt Q4 RASK ≈ £33m revenue.

  • easyJet holidays:

– H2 currently 67% sold. – FY26 customer growth expected low double-digit YoY (competitive market).

  • Next milestone: Half-year results on Thursday, 21 May 2026.
  • CEO quote (Kenton Jarvis):

“easyJet saw continued positive demand in the first half, driven by our great value flights and holidays, alongside a continued focus on our operations and customer experience. “Despite these positives, our H1 financial performance worsened year on year, impacted by the conflict in the Middle East and the competitive environment in some markets. Following our busiest Easter holiday period ever, the operational ramp up into peak summer continues as planned. “easyJet’s financial strength from our investment grade balance sheet and £4.7 billion of liquidity mean we are well placed to navigate current geopolitical challenges while remaining focused on our medium term targets.”

body:
Time Period FY 2026 outlook update (with net cash commentary for 1 Jan 2026 to 14 Apr 2026)

summary: Ferrexpo's Q1 production plummeted 72% due to Ukrainian power infrastructure attacks
body:
Time Period First quarter 2026 (Q1)

  • Reported Q1 total commercial production 592,751 tonnes, down 72% from 2.1m tonnes a year earlier.
  • Q1 output split: premium iron ore concentrate 67,825 tonnes, down 91% year-on-year.
  • Q1 output split: premium iron ore pellets 524,926 tonnes, down 61% year-on-year.
  • Said production was “largely suspended” during Q1 due to “nationwide attacks on Ukrainian electricity generation and transmission infrastructure”.
  • Operations restarted at reduced capacity at the end of February, citing improved electricity availability and pricing.
  • Financial risk framing: continuing to monitor cash and working capital, and actively exploring funding options such as an equity raise.
  • Flagged VAT risk: if withholding of VAT refunds persists and funding issues aren’t resolved, “this could give rise to material negative consequences for the group”.
  • Interim Executive Chair Lucio Genovese on suspension decision: "The lower production numbers in the first quarter, at almost half of what we achieved in the final three months of 2025, reflect focused Russian attacks on Ukraine's power and energy infrastructure late last year and the resultant impact on our ability to operate sustainably. By January, given the supply of electricity could not be assured on a sustainable basis in the volumes required, we were forced to make the difficult decision to temporarily suspend operations and place a part of the workforce on furlough,"
  • Genovese on priorities: "Going forward, our focus remains on managing working capital and costs throughout this challenging operating environment."
  • Market reaction noted: shares down 2.9% to 43.62p on Wednesday afternoon.

summary: Tesco expects flat operating profit despite 14% revenue growth amid retail margin pressures
body:
Time Period FY to 26 February 2026 (expected results); outlook into FY2026/27

  • Expected (company-compiled consensus) revenue ex-VAT incl fuel: GBP72.55bn, up from GBP63.64bn (+GBP8.91bn; +14.0%).
  • Expected consensus group adjusted operating profit: GBP3.10bn, down from GBP3.13bn (-1.0%).
  • Reminder from January guidance: expects FY2026 group adjusted operating profit at the upper end of GBP2.9bn–GBP3.1bn range.
  • Continues to expect retail free cash flow within medium-term guidance range of GBP1.4bn–GBP1.8bn.
  • Share context given: shares +0.9% to 474.30p on Wednesday afternoon; +37% over the past year; “largely flat” since onset of the Middle East conflict (per the article).
  • Market position noted: market share “around 28%” amid competition from Aldi/Lidl and a “renewed Asda”.
  • Citi (Monique Pollard) expectation: adjusted operating profit GBP3.08bn, assuming GBP500m cost savings, and retail free cash flow GBP1.77bn.
  • Citi Q4 view: UK like-for-like growth 3.4% vs 3.1% Visible Alpha consensus (as cited).
  • Jefferies forecast: sales GBP72.28bn, adjusted operating profit GBP3.13bn, EPS 28.8p; expects a “strong end to 25/26 and resilient margin performance”.
  • Jefferies capex/FCF angle: “4.5% below cons FCF” in 26/27 as capex grows to GBP1.6bn.
  • Weather/comps watchpoint: “tough comparisons” in Q1; analysts watching if wet weather has dampened sales.
  • Michael Hewson on the margin/outlook risk: "If things weren't already tough for retailers when it comes to margins, the outlook appears set to get even worse, with the effects of the conflict in the Middle East set to muddy the outlook further. Higher employment costs, along with higher fuel prices are likely to exert upward pressure on margins as look towards the new fiscal year... Guidance is likely to be key here, with all UK food retailers having to bear the costs of higher energy prices, labour costs, as well as increased competition as Aldi and Lidl continue to open new stores."
  • AJ Bell on inflation dynamics and competitive stance: "Tesco's defensive credentials have seen it in demand even during the recent market turbulence, with the weekly shop being a non-negotiable for most people. However, investors will be looking for an update on how renewed inflationary pressures might impact the business... Inflation should nominally boost sales figures and translate into increased revenue, but volumes may be affected as consumers cut back and margins, which are always thin in the supermarket game, will come under pressure. A key question will be the extent to which Tesco seeks to take on some pain in order to protect its competitive position."
